Results: Based on the FSSCTA, 10.4% (91/876) of patients were reclassified to the low-risk group, and 2.9% (25/876) of patients were reclassified to the intermediate-to-high-risk group. MACEs occurred in 16.6% (145/876) of patients over a median follow-up period of 19.4 months. FSSCTA and invasive coronary angiography-based SS (SSICA) were independently associated with the risk of MACEs regardless of whether they were in continuous or categorical form (FSSCTA: c continuous HR 1.082, 95% CI 1.038-1.128; categorical HR 1.865, 95% CI 1.138-2.305. SSICA: continuous HR 1.045, 95% CI 1.012-1.079; categorical HR 1.520, 95% CI 1.128-2.048). FSSCTA showed the best predictive power for MACEs compared with SSCTA and SSICA (all comparisons with FSSCTAp < 0.05). Conclusions: FSSCTA, SSCTA and SSICA were all independent predictors of MACEs in patients undergoing PCI, and FSSCTA showed a significantly better predictive value for MACEs than SSCTA and SSICA.

Title: Admission Route and In-Hospital Mortality Among Trauma Patients Admitted to a Regional Trauma Center in South Korea: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
Abstract: Background: Studies comparing interhospital transfer with direct admission have reported inconsistent associations with mortality, and Korean evidence is limited. We evaluated admission-route associations with in-hospital mortality among patients admitted to a South Korean regional trauma center and explored mortality-associated factors after transfer. Methods: This retrospective receiving-center cohort included trauma admissions during 2022-2024. Patients arriving in cardiac arrest who died without return of spontaneous circulation were excluded. Logistic regression estimated adjusted associations; additional analyses varied adjustment sets and cohort restrictions, and transferred-subgroup analyses were exploratory. Results: Among 2464 patients, 1504 arrived directly and 960 were transferred; mortality was 18.6% vs. 12.0%. Transfer was associated with lower adjusted mortality odds (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.54; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.39-0.75) within this selected receiving-center cohort. Omitting arrival physiology and injury-to-center time yielded an aOR of 0.42 (95% CI, 0.32-0.55). Age and arrival Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) scores were associated with mortality among transferred patients (aOR, 2.03 [95% CI, 1.68-2.46] for age 70 vs. 60 years and 0.75 [0.71-0.79] per 1-point GCS increase). Conclusions: In this receiving-center cohort, transfer was associated with lower in-hospital mortality. Among transferred patients, older age and lower arrival GCS scores were exploratory prognostic markers. These associations should not be interpreted as causal, because transferred patients had to survive until arrival, prehospital severity was unmeasured, and arrival measures may reflect prior care.

Title: Anticoagulation for Splanchnic Vein Thrombosis in Moderate-Severe Acute Pancreatitis: In-Hospital Outcomes from a Prospective Cohort Study.
Abstract: Background: Splanchnic vein thrombosis (SVT) is a common complication of acute pancreatitis (AP), but the role of anticoagulation (AC) during acute hospitalization remains unclear. We aimed to evaluate the impact of in-hospital AC on SVT recanalization and bleeding risk. Methods: We conducted a single-center prospective cohort study (2023-2026) including patients with moderate-severe AP and CT-confirmed SVT. The primary outcome was SVT recanalization at discharge; secondary outcome was in-hospital bleeding complications. Results: Among the 258 included patients, 89 (34.5%) received AC. The median AC duration was 42 days (range 1-83). SVT recanalization did not differ between AC and non-AC groups (15.7% vs. 16.6%, p = 0.862). Bleeding risk was significantly higher with AC (27.0% vs. 9.5%, p < 0.001), driven predominantly by clinically significant hemoglobin decline (7.9% vs. 1.2%, p = 0.015), while major bleeding did not differ significantly between groups. Among the anticoagulated patients, those with recanalization had a higher rate of necrosectomy (78.6% vs. 53.3%, p = 0.080). Conclusions: In this observational cohort, in-hospital AC was not associated with improved short-term SVT recanalization but was associated with a higher incidence of bleeding complications, driven predominantly by clinically significant hemoglobin decline. These observations require confirmation in randomized trials.

Title: Long-Term Outcomes According to the Initially Intended Stenting Strategy for Unprotected Distal Left Main Bifurcation PCI: A Single-Centre Retrospective Cohort Study.
Abstract: Background: Optimal stenting for distal unprotected left main coronary artery (LMCA) bifurcation disease remains uncertain. We evaluated long-term outcomes by initially intended strategy. Methods: This retrospective, single-centre cohort included 234 consecutive patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) without acute coronary syndrome, classified by intended strategy irrespective of crossover. Cox models for all-cause mortality were adjusted for strategy, age, left ventricular ejection fraction, SYNTAX score, and diabetes, with anatomical and propensity-score sensitivity analyses. Secondary and subgroup analyses were exploratory. Results: Provisional and upfront two-stent strategies were intended in 145 and 89 patients. Two-stent patients had greater anatomical complexity. During median 49-month follow-up, mortality did not differ significantly (two-stent versus provisional: 16.9% versus 21.4%; p = 0.499; adjusted hazard ratio, 0.83; 95% confidence interval, 0.43-1.60; p = 0.579), with consistent sensitivity analyses. Older age, lower ejection fraction, and higher SYNTAX score were associated with mortality. Target-lesion revascularisation (7.8% versus 2.1%; p = 0.033) and in-hospital stroke (5.6% versus 0.7%; p = 0.031) were more frequent with intended two-stent PCI; other secondary outcomes did not differ significantly. Exploratory unadjusted comparisons showed lower target-lesion and target-vessel revascularisation with double-kissing crush (n = 74) versus conventional culotte (n = 15), limited by small samples and selection bias. Intravascular ultrasound was associated with lower mortality in exploratory adjusted analyses. Mortality was numerically lower with elective intra-aortic balloon pump support at ejection fraction ≤40%, without statistical significance. Conclusions: No, statistically significant association between initially intended bifurcation strategy and long-term all-cause mortality was observed. Limited precision precludes an inference of equivalence, and exploratory differences in target-lesion revascularisation and in-hospital stroke warrant caution. These findings provide a long-term real-world perspective on individualised distal LMCA PCI, integrating lesion complexity, ventricular reserve, procedural technique, and intravascular imaging.

Title: Renal Complications After Pediatric Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Kidney-related complications contribute substantially to morbidity in children undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), although evidence in pediatric populations remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate the incidence of acute kidney injury (AKI), chronic kidney disease (CKD), and hypertension within the first two years following HSCT and to investigate factors associated with these complications. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed 70 pediatric patients who underwent HSCT at the İnönü University Pediatric Bone Marrow Transplantation Unit between November 2017 and December 2023; patients who died during follow-up were excluded. Renal function was assessed using serum creatinine, the glomerular filtration rate was measured by 24-h urine collection or estimated using the Schwartz formula, and renal imaging was performed. The Acute Kidney Injury Network criteria were used to classify AKI, whereas CKD was defined according to the Kidney Disease Outcomes Quality Initiative criteria. Associations with demographic characteristics, primary disease, conditioning regimen, nephrotoxic drug exposure, graft-versus-host disease, veno-occlusive disease, and infections were evaluated. Results: AKI occurred in 54.3% of patients during the first 100 days, comprising stage 1 in 30.0%, stage 2 in 17.1%, and stage 3 in 7.1%. Primary diagnosis, conditioning regimen, nephrotoxic drug use, and transplantation-related complications were not significantly associated with AKI. Hypertension developed in 32.9% of patients, with most cases occurring during the early period after transplantation. A significant association was observed between hypertension and myeloablative conditioning without total body irradiation (p = 0.014). CKD was present in 45.7% of evaluated patients at month 6 and 44.6% at month 12. Amphotericin B use was significantly associated with CKD at month 6 (p = 0.015). No patient developed end-stage kidney disease or required dialysis. Conclusions: Renal complications were common after pediatric HSCT. AKI occurred frequently during the first 100 days, while CKD remained prevalent at 6 and 12 months. Younger age and amphotericin B exposure were associated with CKD in this cohort. Early recognition of renal injury and long-term kidney follow-up are warranted after pediatric HSCT.

Title: Management and Prognosis of Sustained Ventricular Tachycardia in the Emergency Department: A Retrospective, Observational, Single-Centre Study.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT) is a potentially life-threatening arrhythmia requiring prompt Emergency Department (ED) assessment and management. However, data on its frequency, real-world treatment, and prognosis in the ED remain limited. We aimed to describe the clinical characteristics, acute management, and short- and long-term outcomes of patients presenting with VT. Methods: We retrospectively included consecutive patients presenting to the ED between January 2018 and December 2024 with a primary diagnosis of sustained VT with a pulse. We collected baseline characteristics, hemodynamic status, underlying cardiac disease, and acute treatment. In-hospital events and 30-day and 1-year outcomes were assessed. Results: A total of 103 patients were identified, accounting for approximately 0.025% of all ED visits during the study period; 84.5% were male. Chest pain (31.1%) and palpitations (25.2%) were the most common presenting symptoms. Structural heart disease was present in 90% of the cases, predominantly of ischemic origin (61%). Nearly half of the patients (49.5%) had a prior history of VT. Electrical cardioversion was performed in 28.2% of the cases. The majority of the patients (95/103; 92%) required hospitalization. Mortality was 4.9% at 30 days and 17% at 1 year. After adjustment for age, a left ventricular ejection fraction ≤ 30% and in-hospital arrhythmic recurrence were independently associated with 1-year mortality. Conclusions: Sustained VT is an uncommon but high-risk ED presentation, mainly affecting patients with ischemic structural heart disease. A discrepancy was observed between real-world clinical practice and guideline recommendations. The substantial mortality observed, particularly among patients with impaired left ventricular function or in-hospital arrhythmic recurrence, highlights the need for prompt risk stratification and optimized, guideline-concordant acute management.

Title: Minimally Invasive Aortic Valve Replacement and Perioperative Stroke Risk: A Propensity-Matched Analysis.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Stroke is a devastating complication after aortic valve replacement (AVR). Whether minimally invasive AVR (miniAVR) reduces perioperative stroke risk versus conventional sternotomy remains uncertain. Methods: This single-center retrospective cohort study used propensity score matching (PSM) in 1741 consecutive patients undergoing isolated AVR (2014-2025). After exclusions, 1:1 PSM using 10 covariates created 155 matched pairs with excellent balance (all standardized mean differences < 0.20). The primary endpoint was in-hospital stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA); secondary endpoints were 30-day and 5-year mortality and major complications. Firth penalized logistic regression identified independent predictors of stroke/TIA. Results: Stroke/TIA occurred in 0/155 (0.0%) miniAVR versus 7/155 (4.5%) conventional patients (p = 0.015); the rule-of-three upper 95% limit for miniAVR was ~1.9%. Thirty-day mortality was similar (0.6% vs. 2.6%; p = 0.371). Five-year survival favored miniAVR (94.6% vs. 87.2%; log-rank p = 0.047). miniAVR was independently associated with lower stroke/TIA odds (odds ratio [OR] 0.052; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.003-0.832; p = 0.037); longer cardiopulmonary bypass time was associated with higher odds (OR 1.014/minute; 95% CI 1.001-1.028; p = 0.032). Conclusions: miniAVR was associated with zero observed perioperative strokes and higher 5-year survival; however, this survival comparison is limited by short median follow-up in the miniAVR group (1.9 years). Given the small number of events and the single-center design, these findings should not be interpreted as proof of a causal neuroprotective effect. Multicenter validation with longer, balanced follow-up is required.

Title: Correlates of Fetal Aortic Isthmus Diameter in Fetuses Considered Structurally Normal on Second-Trimester Assessment.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Fetal aortic isthmus reference data have characterized its size as a function of gestational age; whether aortic and pulmonary valve diameters are associated with isthmic caliber in addition to gestational age has not been systematically examined. We examined the correlates of aortic isthmus diameter in fetuses considered structurally normal on second-trimester assessment. Methods: This retrospective single-center cohort study included 472 fetuses considered structurally normal on second-trimester assessment at 19 + 0-24 + 6 weeks. Aortic isthmus (AoI), aortic valve (AV), pulmonary valve (PV) and thymic transverse diameters were measured by a single operator. Three-step hierarchical linear regression modeled the AoI diameter (Model 1, gestational age; Model 2, +AV and PV; Model 3, +thymus), with variance inflation factors, regression diagnostics and internal validation conducted via repeated five-fold cross-validation (100 repeats). For sensitivity analyses, the gestational-age equivalents recorded in the clinical reports for femur length, biparietal diameter and head circumference were converted into total days and analyzed as continuous variables in place of the clinical gestational age. Results: AoI diameter was correlated with gestational age (r = 0.512), AV (r = 0.507), PV (r = 0.516) and thymic diameter (r = 0.397) (all p < 0.001). Gestational age alone accounted for 26.2% of the variance (R2 = 0.262). Adding AV and PV increased the explained variance (ΔR2 = 0.060; total R2 = 0.322; p < 0.001); both AV (β = 0.186; p = 0.005) and PV (β = 0.187; p = 0.006) were independently associated with isthmic caliber, and the highest VIF in Model 2 was 3.22. Adding thymic diameter produced no meaningful increment (ΔR2 = 0.0003; p = 0.636). Across the four size-index specifications, the valve-term increment ranged from 0.037 to 0.060. Internal validation via repeated five-fold cross-validation gave a mean cross-validated R2 of 0.299 (SD of repeat-specific means, 0.011). Conclusions: In fetuses considered structurally normal on second-trimester assessment, aortic isthmus diameter was associated with gestational age, and, in addition, with aortic and pulmonary valve diameters, which accounted for a modest further share of the variance. No independent association with thymic diameter was demonstrated.

Title: Low PHASES-Estimated Rupture Risk Among Patients Presenting with Ruptured Intracranial Aneurysms: A Retrospective Single-Centre Observational Study.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: The PHASES score is widely used to estimate the 5-year rupture risk of unruptured intracranial aneurysms, yet many patients present with aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage despite low calculated risk. This study aimed to characterise the demographic and aneurysm-related profile of patients with ruptured aneurysms classified as low risk by PHASES. Methods: This retrospective single-centre observational study included 243 consecutive patients with radiologically confirmed ruptured intracranial aneurysms treated between 2013 and 2021. PHASES scores and estimated 5-year rupture risks were calculated retrospectively. Age, sex, arterial hypertension, aneurysm size, location, and multiplicity were analysed using non-parametric statistical methods. Results: The mean PHASES score was 5.16 ± 3.43 points. An estimated 5-year rupture risk below 1% was assigned to 125 patients (51.44%), and 54 patients (22.22%) had PHASES scores of 0-2. Ruptured aneurysms measuring ≤7 mm occurred in 147 patients (60.49%), and 210 patients (86.42%) were younger than 70 years. Internal carotid artery aneurysms were the most frequent overall, whereas anterior communicating artery aneurysms had the smallest median diameter while remaining among the most common rupture sites. Arterial hypertension was associated with larger aneurysm diameter. Conclusions: Low PHASES-estimated risks were common in this cohort of patients presenting with aneurysm rupture. Because the study included no comparison group with unruptured aneurysms, it cannot assess PHASES calibration or predictive performance. PHASES should therefore be used as a population-based decision-support tool rather than a stand-alone predictor of individual rupture risk, with morphology, imaging findings, documented growth, and patient-specific factors incorporated into clinical assessment.

Title: Artificial Intelligence in Ocular Surface Oncology: A Narrative Review of Multimodal Imaging, Smartphone-Based Screening, and Clinical Decision Support.
Abstract: Ocular surface malignancies include ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN), con-junctival melanoma, and conjunctival lymphoma. These rare disorders may threaten vi-sion and, in some cases, life. Early identification may be difficult because malignant le-sions can resemble benign ocular surface conditions. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, has emerged as a potential aid to detection, classi-fication, and referral. This structured narrative review, organized with reference to SANRA principles, synthesizes PubMed/MEDLINE literature on AI applications in ocular surface oncology available through 29 August 2026. We examine slit-lamp photography, anterior segment optical coherence tomography, in vivo confocal microscopy, ultrasound biomicroscopy, and smartphone imaging. Deep-learning models have shown promising performance in selected binary OSSN tasks, whereas multiclass studies report lower sen-sitivity for rare malignancies such as conjunctival melanoma and lymphoma. Smartphone-based screening has also been evaluated in a prospective referral pathway, although the reference standard and verification process limit interpretation of popula-tion-level sensitivity. Dataset imbalance, image-acquisition variability, limited external and prospective validation, explainability, and workflow integration remain barriers to implementation. Future work should prioritize multicenter datasets, standardized acquisition, calibrated thresholds, and prospective human-AI evaluations. Current evidence supports further evaluation of AI as an adjunct for detection and referral, not as a re-placement for specialist assessment or histopathology.

Title: Real-World Management and Outcomes of Probable and Indeterminate UIP Patterns on HRCT: A Retrospective Cohort Study and Implications for the 2022 IPF Guideline.
Abstract: Background: The 2018 ATS/ERS/JRS/ALAT guideline conditionally recommended surgical lung biopsy (SLB) for patients with probable or indeterminate usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) patterns on high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT). This study assessed the real-world use of this recommendation and outcomes of patients with probable or indeterminate UIP. Methods: HRCT scans of 1255 patients with interstitial lung disease (ILD) followed between 2012-2021 were retrospectively reviewed. A total of 185 patients met the inclusion criteria. We re-evaluated the HRCT scans and classified them through multidisciplinary discussion (MDD) involving one thoracic radiologist, one pulmonary pathologist, one rheumatologist, and at least three pulmonologists specializing in ILD. We analyzed clinical features, biopsy rates, final diagnoses, and survival outcomes. Results: SLB was performed in 10.8% of patients and met the predefined criteria for clinical biopsy success in 50%. Among patients with probable UIP who were ultimately diagnosed with IPF, 32 of 38 (84.2%) received the diagnosis without SLB. The remaining six (15.8%) underwent SLB, of whom five met predefined criteria for clinical biopsy success. Final diagnoses included IPF (23.8%), hypersensitivity pneumonitis (16.8%), and connective tissue disease-associated ILD (16.2%). Crude mortality proportions did not differ significantly between the probable and indeterminate UIP groups (p = 0.173). However, time-to-event analyses demonstrated shorter survival in the probable UIP group (log-rank p = 0.019), and probable UIP was associated with a higher mortality hazard after adjustment for age, sex, and smoking history (adjusted HR 1.91, 95% CI 1.06-3.42; p = 0.030). This association was attenuated and no longer statistically significant after additional adjustment for cardiovascular disease (adjusted HR 1.71,95% CI 0.93-3.14; p = 0.082). Conclusions: These findings support an individualized, multidisciplinary diagnostic approach and are consistent with the diagnostic flexibility introduced in the 2022 IPF guideline.

Title: Preoperative High-Resolution Ultrasound-Guided Design of the Fibula Osteoseptocutaneous Flap: A Structured Surgeon-Performed Protocol.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: The fibula osteoseptocutaneous flap is an established option for head and neck reconstruction. Preoperative planning requires assessment of donor-limb arterial anatomy and localization of cutaneous perforators. This study describes a structured surgeon-performed Conventional High-Frequency Ultrasound (CHFUS) protocol and evaluates its correlation with intraoperative findings. Methods: This retrospective study included patients undergoing reconstruction with a fibula osteoseptocutaneous free flap between January 2024 and December 2025. A standardized two-phase CHFUS workflow was used to assess infrapopliteal arterial anatomy and identify, characterize, and mark perforators at their deep fascial emergence. Preoperative findings were compared with intraoperative anatomy. Results: Ten patients underwent fibula flap reconstruction. Eighteen perforators were mapped, with a mean of 1.80 ± 0.63 per patient. The most common Kim-Lippert vascular pattern was type I (90%). Mean peroneal artery diameter at its origin was 2.83 ± 0.15 mm, and mean dominant perforator diameter at deep fascial emergence was 1.04 ± 0.14 mm. All 10 patients met the predefined anatomical agreement threshold of ≤1 cm (100%; exact two-sided 95% confidence interval, 69.2-100%). No flap required intraoperative redesign because of perforator anatomy. All flaps survived, without partial skin-paddle necrosis, donor-site ischemia, or vascular complications. Conclusions: This structured surgeon-performed CHFUS protocol was feasible and useful for fibula osteoseptocutaneous flap planning, enabling assessment of arterial anatomy, reliable perforator localization, and translation of preoperative findings into skin-paddle design. CHFUS should be considered complementary to CT angiography. Larger prospective studies are required to evaluate interoperator reproducibility and the diagnostic performance of CHFUS for clinically relevant arterial variants.

Title: Impact of Functional Frailty Measured by Short Physical Performance Battery Test on the Effectiveness of SGLT2 Inhibitors in Elderly Patients with Acute Heart Failure:PROFUND-IC Registry.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Acute heart failure (AHF) is the leading cause of hospitalization among patients over 65 years and is frequently associated with frailty. Sodium-glucose cotransporter type 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) currently represent the only drug class recommended across the entire ejection fraction spectrum, although evidence regarding their effectiveness according to frailty status remains limited. Aims: To determine whether functional frailty, measured by the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) test, influences the effectiveness of SGLT2i in reducing hospital readmission and mortality in elderly patients with AHF. Methods: Observational study of 794 polypathological patients admitted to Internal Medicine with AHF. An interaction analysis assessed whether SPPB, as a continuous variable, modified the association between SGLT2i and the composite outcome (hospital readmission or death), using a Cox model. The sample was further divided by SPPB test score (below 4 (N = 477) or ≥4 (N = 317)) for exploratory analyses. Descriptive and comparative analyses were performed according to SGLT2i administration, using the chi-squared test for qualitative variables and Student's t-test for quantitative ones (Fisher's and Mann-Whitney U test as appropriate). Survival analysis was done using Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox regression, with multivariable adjustment for confounders. Results: No significant interaction was found between SPPB score and SGLT2i (p = 0.506). When SPPB was dichotomised, SGLT2i treatment was associated with significantly lower all-cause mortality (3.7% vs. 12.0%; p = 0.018) and readmission (30.3% vs. 45.2%; p = 0.021) in SPPB ≥ 4, with mortality and readmission also numerically lower, without reaching statistical significance, in SPPB < 4 (mortality 12.9% vs. 16.9%, p = 0.410; readmission 34.5% vs. 42.0%, p = 0.220). After adjustment, SGLT2i treatment in the SPPB ≥ 4 group remained associated with a numerically lower hazard for the composite outcome (HR 0.652; 95% CI 0.418-1.018; p = 0.060). Conclusions: No evidence was found that functional frailty modifies the effectiveness of SGLT2i in elderly polypathological patients with AHF. An exploratory analysis suggested a possible gradient of greater association with SPPB ≥ 4, although this should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating.

Title: Comparative Effects of Myo-Inositol, Metformin, Berberine, and Combination Therapy on Metabolic, Anthropometric and Hormonal Parameters in Women with Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: A 6-Month Observational Cohort Study.
Abstract: Background: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is the most prevalent endocrine condition among women of reproductive age. It is marked by metabolic and reproductive irregularities and is often linked to insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and obesity. Diverse methods of treatment are employed to enhance metabolic and hormonal parameters, including inositol-based supplements, metformin, and novel compounds such as berberine. Objective: To describe changes observed over six months in anthropometric, metabolic, lipid, and hormonal metrics among women with PCOS undergoing myo-inositol, metformin, berberine, or a combination of metformin and berberine in standard clinical settings, and to investigate if disparities among treatment groups remained after controlling for initial characteristics. Materials and Methods: This retrospective observational cohort study included 148 women with PCOS diagnosed according to the Rotterdam criteria who completed six months of treatment with myo-inositol (n = 38), metformin (n = 52), berberine (n = 28), or combined metformin-berberine therapy (n = 30). Anthropometric, metabolic, lipid, and androgen parameters were assessed at baseline and after six months. Within-group changes were evaluated with correction for multiple testing using the Holm method. Given the non-random treatment allocation and baseline differences among groups, supplementary baseline-adjusted analyses were performed for the continuous outcomes. Results: Treatment groups differed significantly in several baseline metabolic variables including body mass index (BMI), fasting plasma glucose (FPG), fasting insulin and homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR). After Holm correction for multiple testing, the metformin group showed significant reductions in BMI, FPG, markers of insulin resistance, lipid parameters, and androgen-related hormonal parameters, together with an increase in high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C). In the myo-inositol group, significant reductions were observed in fasting insulin, HOMA-IR, total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), triglycerides, androstenedione, and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS). In the berberine group, significant reductions were observed in BMI, fasting insulin, HOMA-IR, total cholesterol, triglycerides, and androstenedione. In the combined metformin-berberine group, significant reductions were observed in BMI, fasting insulin, HOMA-IR, total cholesterol, LDL-C, triglycerides, testosterone, androstenedione, DHEAS, and 17-hydroxyprogesterone, together with an increase in HDL-C. In the baseline-adjusted analyses, no significant overall treatment-group effects remained for the principal metabolic outcomes after correction for multiple testing, whereas significant overall treatment-group effects were observed for DHEAS and 17-hydroxyprogesterone. Conclusions: In this real-world observational cohort, six months of treatment with metformin, myo-inositol, berberine, or combined metformin-berberine therapy was associated with changes in several metabolic and hormonal parameters. However, substantial baseline differences among the clinically selected treatment groups and the absence of significant baseline-adjusted between-group effects for the principal metabolic outcomes preclude conclusions regarding comparative treatment efficacy. The observed between-group differences in selected hormonal outcomes warrant further investigation in prospective comparative studies.

Title: Systemic Inflammatory Markers, Thyroid Autoimmunity, and Neuroretinal Structure in Graves' Disease: A Comparative OCT Study According to Ophthalmopathy Status.
Abstract: Background: Graves' disease is a systemic autoimmune disorder that may affect ocular structures even in the absence of clinically apparent ophthalmopathy. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) enables objective assessment of neuroretinal structures, but the relationships between OCT findings, systemic inflammatory indices, thyroid hormone levels, and thyroid autoimmunity markers in Graves' disease remain incompletely defined. This study aimed to evaluate the associations between OCT-derived neuroretinal measurements and systemic inflammatory, hormonal, and autoimmune markers according to ophthalmopathy status. Methods: This retrospective cross-sectional study included 161 participants: 60 healthy controls, 50 Graves' disease patients with ophthalmopathy (GO+), and 51 Graves' disease patients without ophthalmopathy (GO-). Central macular thickness (CMT) and circumpapillary retinal nerve fiber layer (cpRNFL) thickness measurements were obtained using spectral-domain OCT. Macular RNFL (mRNFL) thickness was not evaluated. Laboratory evaluation included complete blood count, glucose, urea, creatinine, aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), total cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), triglycerides, C-reactive protein (CRP), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), free triiodothyronine (fT3), free thyroxine (fT4), anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO), and anti-thyroglobulin (anti-Tg) antibodies. Results: In the primary three-group OCT analysis, significant differences were observed for superior (p = 0.010, q = 0.0125), inferior (p < 0.001, q = 0.0024), temporal (p = 0.002, q = 0.0050), and nasal cpRNFL thickness (p = 0.006, q = 0.0092), and all remained significant after FDR correction; CMT did not differ among the groups (p = 0.925, q = 0.925). The lowest cpRNFL thickness values were observed in the GO- subgroup, particularly in the inferior quadrant (116.39 ± 27.52 vs. 136.65 ± 20.01 µm, post hoc p < 0.001); however, this finding should be interpreted cautiously because standardized GO activity and severity staging was not consistently available. Systemic inflammatory indices were largely similar between groups, whereas CRP levels were higher in Graves' disease in the exploratory analysis (3.87 ± 3.40 vs. 1.86 ± 1.11 mg/L, nominal p < 0.001). Several weak correlations between cpRNFL parameters and fT4, CRP, and anti-TPO reached nominal significance; however, none remained statistically significant after FDR correction. In multivariable analysis restricted to patients with Graves' disease, GO+ status remained associated with greater inferior cpRNFL thickness compared with GO- status, whereas anti-TPO was not associated with inferior cpRNFL thickness after adjustment. Conclusion: Sectoral cpRNFL differences were observed among the control, GO+, and GO- groups, whereas CMT remained comparable. However, the lower cpRNFL measurements in patients classified as GO- should be interpreted cautiously because of retrospective ophthalmopathy classification, potential misclassification, differential exclusion rates, and residual confounding. These findings are strictly exploratory and hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation. Biomarker-OCT correlations did not remain statistically significant after FDR correction.

Title: The Gut-Vascular Axis as a Therapeutic Hub: Rationale and Evidence for Combined Gut-Directed and Endothelium-Directed Interventions.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: The gut-vascular axis linking gut microbiota, intestinal barrier, and vascular endothelium is a key pathophysiological interface in chronic metabolic diseases. Dysbiosis and "leaky gut" enable bacterial products and gut-derived metabolites to enter the circulation, driving systemic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction. Single-target interventions show limited efficacy; combined gut-directed and endothelium-directed strategies remain underexplored.
METHODS: PubMed was searched from database inception to 31 August 2026 using a predefined search strategy combining terms for the gut-vascular axis, intestinal barrier, microbiota/metabolites, endothelial dysfunction, and combined interventions. Preclinical and clinical studies evaluating gut barrier integrity, microbiota modulation, or endothelial protection, alone or in combination, were included. No formal risk-of-bias scoring was performed; study design, sample size, endpoint type, follow-up, and limitations were appraised.
RESULTS: (1) The axis comprises three core components: gut barrier, endothelium, and microbial metabolites. (2) Pathological activation involves leaky-gut-driven endotoxemia, dysbiosis-induced metabolic inflammation, and immune crosstalk sustaining vascular inflammation. (3) Animal models demonstrate that combined interventions can reduce atherosclerotic plaque, improve endothelium-dependent relaxation, and lower systemic inflammation to a greater extent than some monotherapies; however, most studies have not directly compared combination therapy with both corresponding monotherapies or performed formal interaction testing, so true synergy remains unproven. (4) Limited clinical studies in metabolic syndrome and heart failure suggest improvements in surrogate endpoints, but large-scale randomised trials with hard cardiovascular endpoints are lacking.
CONCLUSIONS: The gut-vascular axis is a promising therapeutic framework for cardiometabolic diseases, with a strong biological rationale. Combined gut- and endothelium-directed interventions offer a rational multi-target approach, but direct evidence that they provide superior clinical outcomes remains limited. Future research must prioritise hard-endpoint trials, standardised interventions and endpoints, long-term safety, reproducibility, multi-omics-based patient stratification, and next-generation microbiome therapies.

Title: Beyond BMI: Associations of Body-Shape Indices with CBC-Derived Systemic Inflammatory Indices in Adults with Metabolic Syndrome: A Cross-Sectional Study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) is characterized by central adiposity, metabolic dysregulation, and low-grade inflammation, but body mass index (BMI) may not fully capture body-shape variation in established MetS. We investigated whether body-shape indices were associated with complete blood count (CBC)-derived systemic inflammatory indices after accounting for BMI.
METHODS: In this cross-sectional study with prospective data collection, 331 adults with MetS were evaluated. Weight-adjusted waist index (WWI) was the primary anthropometric variable and systemic inflammation response index (SIRI) the primary inflammatory variable. Body roundness index (BRI), a body shape index (ABSI), conicity index, waist-to-height ratio (WHtR), and waist-to-hip ratio (WHR) were assessed as secondary anthropometric measures, together with the systemic immune-inflammation index (SII), neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), and lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio (LMR). Multivariable linear regression models were adjusted for age, sex, current smoking, and BMI.
RESULTS: WWI was not significantly associated with log-SIRI after adjustment for age, sex, current smoking, and BMI (standardized β = 0.067, 95% CI -0.052 to 0.185; p = 0.268). Adding WWI increased R2 from 0.091 to 0.094 (ΔR2 = 0.0034; partial R2 = 0.0038). None of the secondary anthropometric-inflammatory associations was statistically significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Restricted cubic spline analysis showed no evidence of a nonlinear WWI-SIRI association (P-nonlinear = 0.582). Additional covariate analyses in which C-reactive protein, diabetes, estimated glomerular filtration rate, coronary artery disease and heart failure were added separately did not materially alter the WWI estimate.
CONCLUSIONS: In adults with established MetS, we did not detect significant associations between WWI or other body-shape indices and CBC-derived systemic inflammatory indices after adjustment for BMI. These findings do not exclude smaller associations that may not have been detectable in this cohort.

Title: Tail-Risk-Aware Model Predictive Control for Hypoglycemia Mitigation in Automated Insulin Delivery.
Abstract: Background: Automated insulin delivery must maintain glycemic control despite partial observability, physiological heterogeneity, and sensing and actuation errors. Cohort-average metrics may nevertheless conceal hypoglycemia in vulnerable virtual patients. Methods: We developed a tail-risk-aware model predictive control framework that combines a Transformer-based latent world model, unguided iterative cross-entropy method planning over perturbed rollouts, and a deterministic Safety Layer that projects insulin actions onto programmed bounds. Reinforcement-learning-guided proposal sampling was evaluated separately as an exploratory search variant. The primary controller was evaluated in Simglucose using 10 virtual patients, three random seeds, and five prespecified operating conditions. Results: Under nominal conditions, it achieved a cohort-average time in range (TIR) of 77.6% and time below range (TBR) of 3.8%, but worst-k TBR was 11.0% and increased to 37.4% under 5% random CGM missingness. In the risk-objective ablation, combining variance penalization with TailMean increased TIR by 2.8 percentage points and reduced cohort-average and worst-k TBR by 2.3 and 7.4 percentage points, respectively, relative to mean-only planning. The Safety Layer modified every proposed action in the analyzed run, indicating strong dependence on the programmed bounds. Conclusions: These results show that average target attainment can coexist with substantial patient-level risk. They support tail-aware evaluation and identify patient-specific safeguards as a priority for future validation, but do not establish clinical safety or efficacy.

Title: Weight Regain After Discontinuation of GLP-1 and GIP/GLP-1 Receptor Agonists: A Systematic Review.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Weight regain and loss of cardiometabolic benefit commonly follow the withdrawal of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) and dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/GLP-1 receptor agonists, yet maintenance strategies are incompletely characterized.
METHODS: We conducted a systematic review reported according to PRISMA 2020 of primary studies in adults with overweight or obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes. PubMed/MEDLINE, Europe PMC and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from inception to September 2026, supplemented by backward/forward citation searching and cross-checking of recent systematic reviews. Eligible reports quantified weight or cardiometabolic outcomes at least 12 weeks after planned or unplanned treatment cessation, or tested a post-cessation maintenance strategy. Randomized reports were assessed with RoB 2 and non-randomized reports with ROBINS-I. Owing to incompatible estimands, follow-up schedules, cointerventions and overlapping trial families, results were synthesized narratively without a new pooled estimate.
RESULTS: Eighteen reports representing 16 study families were included. Randomized withdrawal trials showed renewed weight gain after treatment cessation: +6.9% over 48 weeks after switching from semaglutide to placebo in STEP 4, and +14.0% over 52 weeks after switching from tirzepatide to placebo in SURMOUNT-4. In the STEP 1 extension, participants regained 11.6 percentage points over one year, approximately two-thirds of their prior loss, while several cardiometabolic measures moved toward baseline. Real-world estimates were smaller and more variable because discontinuation was often inferred from prescriptions, follow-up weights were missing, and many patients restarted or switched therapy. Cardiometabolic rebound was associated with the degree of weight regain, but clinical cardiovascular events were not evaluated. Evidence for maintenance strategies was sparse: one randomized post-treatment study supported supervised exercise, with the exercise-plus-liraglutide group retaining an additional 5.1 kg of weight loss one year after both interventions ended compared with liraglutide alone; a small pilot supported sitagliptin plus metformin after liraglutide in polycystic ovary syndrome. No eligible controlled trial isolated a specific diet after cessation.
CONCLUSIONS: Weight regain is frequent after stopping GLP-1-based therapy, although magnitude varies by drug, design, follow-up and subsequent treatment. Structured exercise may help reduce regain and preserve lean mass, but evidence for dietary, behavioral, tapering or pharmacologic transition strategies remains limited. Discontinuation should therefore be planned as part of chronic obesity care, with explicit monitoring and shared decision-making, rather than presented as a predictable short course.

Title: HDL Cholesterol and Atherogenic Lipid Indices in Hidradenitis Suppurativa: Associations with BMI and Hurley Disease Severity.
Abstract: Background: Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a chronic inflammatory disease associated with cardiometabolic comorbidities and increased cardiovascular risk. Methods: This retrospective case-control study evaluated serum lipid parameters and atherogenic indices-including the atherogenic index of plasma (AIP), Castelli risk index I (CRI-I), Castelli risk index II (CRI-II), and the atherogenic coefficient (AC)-in 176 patients with HS compared with 132 controls frequency-matched for age and sex and examined their associations with BMI and Hurley stage using multiple linear regression models. Results: BMI was significantly higher in patients with HS than in controls (median 29.4 vs. 26.1 kg/m2, p < 0.001), and subsequent regression analyses were therefore adjusted for BMI. Patients with HS exhibited higher triglyceride, LDL-C, and non-HDL-C levels, lower HDL-C levels, and higher atherogenic indices than controls, whereas total cholesterol did not differ significantly between the groups. After BMI adjustment, differences in triglyceride, LDL-C, and non-HDL-C lost significance, whereas HDL-C and all atherogenic indices remained significantly altered. In ordinal trend analyses, increasing Hurley stage showed modest associations with lower HDL-C and higher LDL-C, non-HDL-C, CRI-I, CRI-II, and AC, whereas triglycerides and AIP showed no significant trends after FDR correction. Conclusion: However, residual confounding by unmeasured cardiometabolic and lifestyle factors cannot be excluded, and the present findings do not establish increased cardiovascular risk or the clinical predictive utility of these indices. These findings should therefore be considered hypothesis-generating and warrant confirmation in prospective studies incorporating comprehensive cardiometabolic covariates, inflammatory biomarkers, and direct measures of subclinical atherosclerosis.

Title: Adiposity, Body Composition, and Cardiometabolic Outcomes in Women with and Without Gestational Diabetes.
Abstract: Aims: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is associated with increased long-term cardiometabolic risk. The value of body composition measures in predicting adverse cardiometabolic outcomes after GDM remains uncertain. Methods: In this prospective observational study, 757 women (300 controls and 457 with GDM in their index pregnancy) attended a postnatal assessment at a median of 5.8 (IQR 5.1-7.1) months after delivery. Anthropometric measures, biochemical markers, cardiovascular assessments, and body composition by bioelectrical impedance analysis were obtained. Outcomes included dysglycaemia, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, metabolic syndrome and liver steatosis. Multivariable logistic regression models evaluated associations and predictive performance. Results: Compared with controls, women with prior GDM had higher BMI, central adiposity, and fat mass (all p < 0.001). They also had a higher prevalence of dysglycaemia (42.9% vs. 16.7%), hypertension (30.2% vs. 18.7%), dyslipidaemia (6.3% vs. 3.0%), and liver steatosis (33.3% vs. 14%; all p < 0.05). BMI and waist-to-height ratio improved prediction of adverse outcomes beyond maternal characteristics alone. Body composition measures were associated with cardiometabolic outcomes but did not show superior discriminatory performance compared with conventional anthropometric measures. Conclusions: Women with prior GDM have a high burden of postpartum cardiometabolic abnormalities. While body composition provides additional biological insight, simple anthropometric measures remain the practical first-line tools for risk stratification.

Title: WingShape-Warn: A Morphology-Driven Early-Warning Pipeline for Mosquito-Borne Disease Surveillance.
Abstract: Environmental stressors-including climate change, urbanisation, and pollution-are increasingly altering the wing morphology of mosquito vectors. These morphological shifts, particularly in wing geometry, can serve as early-warning indicators for mosquito abundance and arboviral disease outbreaks. However, quantitative wing-shape analysis remains underutilised in operational mosquito surveillance and public health early-warning systems. This Technology and Code article presents WingShape-Warn, a reproducible, open-source pipeline that integrates geometric morphometrics, deep learning-based image segmentation, association-rule mining, and Neo4j knowledge-graph construction to detect, quantify, and visualise morphology-driven mosquito-borne disease risk. The protocol comprises seven steps: (1) stratified collection of mosquito wing images along environmental gradients; (2) image preprocessing and deep learning-based landmark/semilandmark extraction; (3) generalised Procrustes analysis (GPA), principal component analysis (PCA), and Apriori association-rule mining on wing-shape variables; (4) Neo4j knowledge-graph construction linking wing-shape traits, environmental variables, and disease outcomes; (5) design of a morphology-based early-warning rule base; (6) automated report generation with a knowledge-update trigger; and (7) validation via retrospective forecasting and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. WingShape-Warn has been validated on 1200 wing images of Aedes albopictus and Anopheles spp. (2020-2024, five climate zones), demonstrating that wing-shape PC1 explains 42.3% of the variance and predicts mosquito abundance with an AUC of 0.89. WingShape-Warn has been measured and validated on 1200 wing images of Aedes albopictus and Anopheles spp. (2020-2024, five climate zones)-the only corpus measured in this study-demonstrating that wing-shape PC1 explains 42.3% of the variance and predicts mosquito abundance with an AUC of 0.89. Two reporting conventions are adopted throughout: results obtained on this mosquito corpus are reported as measured results, whereas all cross-taxa material is reported as illustrative, literature-mapped examples and is labelled [Illustrative] wherever it appears. An ablation on the held-out chronological test set shows that adding wing-shape PCs to environmental variables alone raises the AUC from 0.74 to 0.89 (ΔAUC = +0.15, DeLong p < 0.001; NRI = 0.21, IDI = 0.14), while a permuted-shape control returns the model to baseline (AUC 0.75, p = 0.62). The U-Net landmark detector reaches a mean radial error of 1.34 ± 0.41 px against manual digitisation under five-fold cross-validation, i.e., below the pre-registered 2 px tolerance and within human inter-operator repeatability (1.12 ± 0.33 px). While the measured validation is currently limited to mosquito wings, the modular "analyze-detect-warn" architecture can be reused or adapted by researchers for other arthropod vectors (e.g., ticks, sandflies) or additional environmental stressors; such extensions are presented here as proof-of-concept demonstrations and require independent validation before operational use.

Title: The Integrated Hemostatic Network in Pediatric ECMO: A Systems-Level Framework for Precision Hemostasis.
Abstract: Pediatric extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is associated with complex hemostatic disturbances arising from interactions among blood-circuit interfaces, developmental hemostasis, endothelial dysfunction, coagulation, fibrinolysis, inflammation, and disease- and treatment-related factors. Conventional approaches focused on individual laboratory abnormalities may not adequately capture this complexity. This review proposes the Integrated Hemostatic Network (IHN) as a unified conceptual framework for understanding ECMO-associated dyshemostasis and informing precision hemostatic management. This narrative review synthesized literature identified iteratively through PubMed searches addressing pediatric ECMO hemostasis and related mechanistic and clinical domains. Priority was given to pediatric studies, prospective comparative studies, randomized trials, systematic reviews, and consensus or guideline documents. Adult and non-ECMO evidence was considered when relevant pediatric data were limited. The evidence was integrated across developmental hemostasis, blood-circuit interactions, platelet and von Willebrand factor biology, coagulation and anticoagulant pathways, fibrinolysis, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, complement activation, and hemolysis, with implications for multimodal monitoring and individualized management. The evidence supports a systems-level interpretation of pediatric ECMO-associated dyshemostasis, in which interacting determinants evolve over time. Bleeding, thrombosis, and their coexistence may arise from overlapping disturbances rather than isolated abnormalities or anticoagulation intensity alone. Three proposed working hemostatic states-bleeding-predominant, thrombosis-predominant, and mixed bleeding-thrombotic-provide a conceptual structure for clinical assessment and therapeutic reasoning but are not validated biological categories, prediction models, or treatment algorithms. The IHN integrates developmental and clinical context, laboratory and functional assessment, anticoagulant effects, and patient and circuit findings to support longitudinal interpretation beyond isolated laboratory targets. By explicitly integrating these interacting determinants and their temporal evolution, the IHN provides a unified conceptual architecture for understanding pediatric ECMO-associated dyshemostasis. Its clinical utility requires prospective multicenter evaluation to establish reproducibility and determine whether its application improves patient-centered outcomes.

Title: The Role of Urocortin 2 in Arterial Stiffness and Hypertension in Children with Obesity.
Abstract: Background: Childhood obesity is associated with hypertension (HT), arterial stiffness, and increased cardiovascular risk. Urocortin 2 (UCN2), a member of the corticotropin-releasing factor family, exerts vasodilatory and cardioprotective effects; however, its role in obesity-related vascular dysfunction in children remains unclear. We aimed to investigate the relationship between circulating UCN2 levels, HT, and arterial stiffness parameters in children with obesity. Methods: This prospective, single-center, cross-sectional case-control study included 154 children aged 10-18 years: 95 with obesity and 59 healthy controls. Anthropometric measurements, serum UCN2 concentrations, and metabolic parameters were assessed. Brachial-based oscillometric pulse wave analysis was performed to obtain estimated pulse wave velocity (PWV), augmentation index corrected for a heart rate of 75 beats/min (AIx@75), central systolic blood pressure (cSBP), and other hemodynamic parameters. Multivariable linear regression analyses were used to identify independent predictors of UCN2 and arterial stiffness. Results: Children with obesity had significantly higher PWV, cSBP, pulse pressure, cardiac output, and HT prevalence compared with controls (all p < 0.001). Although UCN2 levels tended to be lower in children with obesity, the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.196). In children with obesity, UCN2 was negatively correlated with body mass index (r = -0.31, p = 0.003) and pulse pressure (r = -0.22, p = 0.031), and log-transformed UCN2 levels were negatively correlated with PWV (r = -0.22, p = 0.034). The independent negative association between UCN2 concentrations and PWV indicates an inverse relationship with arterial stiffness in childhood obesity. However, further longitudinal and mechanistic studies are required to determine whether this association reflects a underlying physiological involvement or therapeutic target. Conclusions: Childhood obesity is associated with adverse vascular alterations and increased arterial stiffness. The independent inverse association observed between UCN2 and PWV highlights a biological link with vascular stiffness in childhood obesity. However, whether UCN2 possesses biomarker utility or therapeutic relevance remains speculative and warrants evaluation in prospective longitudinal and clinical studies.

Title: Epidemiological, Clinical and Laboratory Characteristics of Hospitalized Children with SARS-CoV-2 Infection During Three Consecutive Pandemic Years: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) generally follows a milder clinical course in children than in adults. The clinical characteristics of pediatric severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection have evolved throughout the pandemic and longitudinal data comparing successive pandemic years remain limited.
OBJECTIVE: To compare the epidemiological, clinical, and laboratory characteristics of children hospitalized with SARS-CoV-2 infection during 2020-2022 and to identify factors associated with disease severity.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of children aged 1 month to 18 years hospitalized with laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection at a tertiary pediatric hospital in Bucharest, Romania, between January 2020 and December 2022.
RESULTS: Of 669 eligible patients, 519 met the inclusion criteria (118 in 2020, 168 in 2021, and 233 in 2022). The proportion of hospitalized infants increased over time, whereas adolescent admissions declined (p < 0.001). Respiratory manifestations remained predominant, while gastrointestinal involvement was consistently common. Respiratory manifestations increased from 61.9% in 2020 to 77.3% in 2022 (p = 0.01), while gastrointestinal manifestations remained consistently frequent. Cardiovascular manifestations were reported in 28.9% of patients, without significant differences across the study years (p = 0.06). Neuromuscular manifestations declined from 43.2% in 2020 to 12.0% in 2022 (p < 0.001). Leukocyte count, lymphocyte count, and hemoglobin differed significantly across the study period, whereas C-reactive protein remained unchanged. Moderate-to-severe disease was associated with digestive, cardiovascular, and reno-urinary involvement but not with sex or residence.
CONCLUSIONS: The epidemiological and clinical profile of hospitalized children with SARS-CoV-2 infection changed substantially across the first three years of the pandemic. These findings highlight the importance of continued surveillance and comprehensive clinical assessment to optimize the management of pediatric COVID-19.

Title: Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia Requiring ECMO: Current Evidence, Controversies, and Unresolved Questions.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) requiring extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) remains one of the most challenging conditions in neonatal critical care. Despite advances in prenatal assessment and neonatal management, substantial uncertainty persists regarding ECMO selection, mode and duration of support, and timing of diaphragmatic repair. This review summarizes the available evidence and critically examines the major unresolved questions in the management of infants with CDH requiring ECMO. Methods: A narrative review was conducted based on a literature search in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library for studies published between June 2005 and June 2026. Additional relevant publications were identified through reference screening, and selected foundational studies predating the search period were included when appropriate. Prospective and retrospective studies, registry-based analyses, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and relevant consensus statements were considered. Evidence was narratively synthesized, with particular attention to disease severity, methodological limitations, and survivor bias. Results: Available evidence highlights substantial heterogeneity in disease severity and management. Prenatal and postnatal markers aid risk stratification, but no single parameter reliably predicts ECMO requirement or defines the optimal management strategy. To date, no clear survival advantage has been demonstrated for either veno-arterial or veno-venous ECMO, although veno-arterial ECMO remains the predominant mode of support in most centers; mode selection should therefore be individualized according to cardiopulmonary physiology, patient characteristics, anatomy, and institutional expertise. Surgical timing remains particularly controversial. While repair after ECMO decannulation has been associated with favorable outcomes, recent observational analyses suggest that early repair during ECMO may be beneficial in selected patients, although the optimal timing remains uncertain. Prolonged ECMO may provide additional time for pulmonary and cardiovascular recovery, although this potential benefit must be weighed against the cumulative morbidity of prolonged support. Conclusions: Management should be individualized according to disease severity, clinical trajectory, cardiopulmonary recovery, and institutional expertise. Current evidence does not support a universal strategy for ECMO initiation, mode, surgical timing, or duration. Prospective multicenter studies using standardized definitions and adequately accounting for disease severity are needed to reduce practice variation and better define optimal management.

Title: Machine Learning to Distinguish Physiologic Causes of Hypoxemia After Bidirectional Glenn Using Bedside Markers.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hypoxemia after bidirectional Glenn palliation can result from distinct physiological mechanisms that may produce similar arterial oxygen saturation. We evaluated whether routinely available bedside markers could recover physiological states encoded in a mechanistic virtual-patient model.
METHODS: A steady-state zero-dimensional closed-loop model generated five causes of Glenn hypoxemia: elevated pulmonary vascular resistance, veno-venous collateral shunting, pulmonary gas-exchange impairment, increased metabolic demand, and ventricular dysfunction. Hidden physiological variables were withheld from the classifier; inputs were SpO2, heart rate, mean arterial pressure, hemoglobin, Glenn/SVC pressure, and SVC oxygen saturation. Because bedside patterns arise downstream from prespecified equations and phenotype perturbations, classification was interpreted as internal mechanistic recoverability rather than clinical diagnostic performance.
RESULTS: Of 150,000 generated states, 127,162 passed broad physiological criteria and 66,269 met strict hypoxemia/hemodynamic criteria. After balancing, 26,400 virtual patients were analyzed (5280 per mechanism; 19,800 training and 6600 held-out testing). SpO2 alone achieved 26.1% accuracy (macro-AUROC 0.580); the primary bedside model achieved 56.1% accuracy (95% CI 55.0-57.4%) and macro-AUROC 0.845 (95% CI 0.840-0.851). Elevated PVR was the most readily recovered phenotype. Glenn/SVC pressure and SVC saturation provided the largest incremental contributions, while broader measurement-error assumptions substantially reduced performance.
CONCLUSIONS: Within this mechanistic simulation, multivariable bedside patterns allowed partial recovery of physiological states encoded by the model. Because phenotypes and their observable consequences were generated from prespecified assumptions, the reported performance quantifies internal recoverability under those assumptions and should not be interpreted as diagnostic accuracy or as independent evidence of bedside information content in patients. The model identifies testable physiologic signatures and areas of overlap for prospective clinical validation.

Title: Beyond the Normal Ejection Fraction: Can Strain Echocardiography Unmask Early Myocardial Impairment in Adolescents with Substance-Use Disorders.
Abstract: Background: Substance use among adolescents is a growing global health problem, and psychoactive substances may damage the myocardium before conventional echocardiographic parameters change. We aimed to determine whether two-dimensional speckle-tracking strain echocardiography can unmask early myocardial impairment in adolescents with substance-use disorder. Methods: In this retrospective cross-sectional case-control study, 29 adolescents with substance-use disorder followed at a Child and Adolescent Substance Dependence Treatment Center and 29 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent conventional echocardiography and strain analysis (segmental, territorial, and global longitudinal strain [GLS]) performed by two blinded pediatric cardiologists. Between-group comparisons were adjusted for multiple testing; discriminative performance was assessed by receiver operating characteristic analysis with bootstrap internal validation, and multivariable logistic regression tested the independence of the association. Results: Patients had a median substance exposure of 3 years, and 75.9% reported polysubstance use (most commonly pregabalin, 41.4%, and methamphetamine, 34.5%). Current cigarette smoking was reported by 75.9% of patients and none of the controls. Ejection fraction was lower in patients but remained within the normal range (62.3% vs. 68.4%; p = 0.016). GLS was significantly impaired in the patient group (-17.0% vs. -20.4%; p < 0.001; median difference 3.4 percentage points; Hedges' g = 2.00), with diffuse segmental involvement across all three apical views. GLS discriminated patients from controls with an area under the curve of 0.913; at the Youden-optimal cut-off of -19.3%, sensitivity was 79.3% and specificity 96.6%. Conclusions: Strain echocardiography can unmask early myocardial impairment in adolescent substance and tobacco users, while ejection fraction and other conventional parameters, although differing modestly, remained within their normal reference ranges. Adding GLS to routine cardiac surveillance may improve early detection; however, reversibility with abstinence and prognostic value require prospective longitudinal studies.

Title: Specific Factors Associated with Iatrogenic Withdrawal Syndrome in Children After Cardiac Surgery.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Iatrogenic withdrawal syndrome (IWS) is common but underrecognized in critically ill children, and data from pediatric cardiac intensive care units (pCICUs) remain limited. This study determined the frequency of IWS after cardiac surgery and the factors associated with it. Methods: Retrospective, single-center cohort study of all pediatric patients admitted to a pCICU after cardiac surgery over 15 months. IWS screening was performed using the Withdrawal Assessment Tool-1 (WAT-1) at least three times daily post-extubation. IWS was defined as at least one WAT-1 score of 3 or higher. A prespecified multivariable logistic regression model with ten perioperative variables was fitted in the complete-case population. A subgroup analysis in ventilated children examined sedative and analgesic exposure, including the grouped duration of remifentanil infusion, in an adjusted model. Results: Of 311 patients, 294 (94.5%) were screened, and IWS occurred in 136 patients (46.3%, 95% CI 40.6-52.0). In the complete-case population (n = 286), univentricular physiology (OR 2.51, p = 0.044), suspected postoperative infection (OR 5.28, p = 0.023), and invasive ventilation for 10-100 h (OR 2.75, p = 0.021) or beyond 100 h (OR 5.29, p = 0.003) were independently associated with IWS, whereas postoperative lactatemia (>2 mmol/L for >6 h) was associated with lower odds (OR 0.39, p = 0.039). In mechanically ventilated children (n = 162), after adjustment, no sedative or analgesic exposure was significantly associated with IWS, while odds were substantially higher in patients receiving remifentanil beyond 48 h (OR 2.64, p = 0.114) and midazolam (OR 3.95, p = 0.057). Conclusions: In our institution, IWS was highly frequent after pediatric cardiac surgery, in particular in patients with univentricular physiology. In sedated patients, midazolam and prolonged remifentanil showed substantially higher, though not statistically significant, odds of developing IWS. These hypothesis-generating associations require prospective confirmation.

Title: Early Cardiotoxicity in Pediatric Patients with Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia and Hodgkin Lymphoma: Incidence, Risk Factors, and Clinical Implications.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cardiotoxicity is a major adverse effect of antineoplastic therapy in pediatric oncology, potentially leading to long-term morbidity. This study aimed to evaluate the incidence, spectrum, and risk factors of early cardiovascular (CV) complications in children treated for acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and Hodgkin lymphoma (HL).
METHODS: In this retrospective cohort study, 109 patients diagnosed with ALL or HL between 2013 and 2019 were analyzed. All patients were under 18 years at diagnosis. CV assessment included electrocardiography, echocardiography, blood pressure and Holter monitoring, and additional imaging where available. Early cardiotoxicity was defined as CV events occurring during or shortly after therapy, including echocardiographic abnormalities, arrhythmias, arterial hypertension, and other CV complications. Descriptive and exploratory statistical analyses were performed to identify potential risk factors.
RESULTS: Early CV events occurred in 69% of ALL patients and 68% of HL patients. Multiple CV events were observed in 32% of ALL and 36% of HL patients. Most cardiotoxic effects were subclinical or transient; clinically significant CV complications were rarely detected. These comprised treatment-requiring heart failure, arterial hypertension, and thromboembolic events. Persistent CV abnormalities were also observed, including subclinical cardiac dysfunction, arterial hypertension, and cardiac arrhythmias. The majority of CV complications occurred within the first 500 days after therapy initiation. Increased cardiotoxicity was associated with older age, higher treatment risk groups, and disease relapse, while no significant sex differences were identified.
CONCLUSIONS: CV abnormalities were frequent in children and adolescents receiving treatment for ALL or HL, although most were subclinical or transient. Clinically significant CV complications were uncommon. These findings support systematic CV surveillance during and after pediatric cancer therapy, with particular attention to persistent abnormalities and potentially treatable complications.

Title: Factors Associated with Transplant-Specific Psychological Adaptation Among Heart and Kidney Transplant Recipients.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Psychological adaptation after solid organ transplantation extends beyond graft survival and includes transplant-specific emotional responses that may influence long-term health outcomes. However, factors associated with transplant-specific psychological adaptation remain insufficiently understood, particularly in Central European populations.
METHODS: A multicentre cross-sectional study was conducted among 224 adult heart (n = 107) and kidney (n = 117) transplant recipients attending three Polish transplant centers. Participants completed the Transplant Effects Questionnaire (TxEQ), Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), General Self-Efficacy Scale (GSES), Life Orientation Test-Revised (LOT-R), and SF-36. We performed univariable and multivariable linear regression analyses separately for heart and kidney transplant recipients to identify factors associated with transplant-specific psychological adaptation.
RESULTS: Overall psychological adaptation was favorable. Adherence demonstrated the highest TxEQ scores, whereas donor-related guilt and disclosure concerns were relatively low. Approximately 20.53% of participants reported clinically relevant anxiety symptoms and 14.2% reported depressive symptoms. In heart transplant recipients, better mental health-related quality of life was independently associated with greater adherence (β = 0.025, p = 0.003). Among kidney transplant recipients, higher donor-related guilt was associated with transplantation center, while greater disclosure was associated with male sex, transplantation center, and shorter time since transplantation (all p < 0.05). Several psychological variables were associated with selected domains of transplant-specific psychological adaptation, whereas demographic and clinical variables showed fewer significant associations.
CONCLUSIONS: These findings indicate that several psychological variables were associated with transplant-specific psychological adaptation in long-term heart and kidney transplant recipients. Routine assessment of anxiety, mental health-related quality of life, and transplant-specific emotional responses may facilitate identification of recipients who could benefit from further psychosocial evaluation. Prospective studies are needed to determine whether these associations translate into improved long-term outcomes.

Title: A Configurable Multi-Modal Clinical Time-Series Platform for Predictive Modeling in Cardiology.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVE: Predictive models for cardiovascular disease rely predominantly on electronic health records (EHRs), whereas wearable devices, home monitoring, and patient-reported outcomes offer new opportunities for multimodal risk prediction; however, integrating these heterogeneous sources into a reproducible, clinically usable machine learning workflow remains challenging. This study aimed to develop an end-to-end architecture for explainable multimodal time-series prediction in patients with heart failure (HF), left ventricular assist device (LVAD) recipients, and heart transplant (HT) recipients.
METHODS: The modular architecture harmonizes Health Level Seven Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (HL7 FHIR) and non-FHIR telemonitoring data into a unified event log, which leakage-aware temporal preprocessing converts into patient-day feature matrices. Configurable adverse-event tasks (HF hospitalization, cardiac decompensation, transplant rejection, and mortality) are modeled using gradient-boosted trees or temporal neural networks, with optional probability calibration. Explanations combine SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) for tabular models with temporal-perturbation attribution and integrated gradients for sequence models. The pipeline is declaratively configured, tracked with MLflow, and deployable via command-line and web interfaces. It was developed alongside the prospective multicenter RETENTION trial of a telemonitoring-based care pathway and was subsequently applied to data collected within the trial.
RESULTS: Applied to the RETENTION cohort, the framework executed the complete workflow, from heterogeneous source data to per-patient-day probability estimates for each prediction task, with feature- and time-level explanations presented as clinician-facing narratives. The cohort served to demonstrate the architecture, not to establish clinical predictive performance or prospective clinical validation.
CONCLUSIONS: This study provides a reproducible, end-to-end architecture that unifies data harmonization, temporal processing, machine learning orchestration, explainability, and deployment for multimodal clinical prediction. Its modular, disease-agnostic design supports adaptation to other diseases, settings, and data sources, laying a foundation for prospective validation and clinical translation.

Title: Complications and Hospital Resource Utilization Associated with ECMO in COVID-19 ARDS with Acute Kidney Injury: Insights from United States National Inpatient Sample, 2020-2022.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common complication of COVID-19-associated acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), yet the impact of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) on outcomes in this high-risk population remains unclear.
METHODS: We performed a retrospective, survey-weighted study using the National Inpatient Sample (NIS) database from 2020-2022 to compare outcomes among adults hospitalized with COVID-19-associated ARDS and AKI managed with invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) alone versus IMV and ECMO. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality, while secondary outcomes included renal replacement therapy (RRT), complications, hospital length of stay (LOS), and healthcare utilization.
RESULTS: Among 198,395 hospitalizations with COVID-19 ARDS complicated by AKI, 4730 received IMV and ECMO. ECMO use was not associated with statistically significantly lower adjusted in-hospital mortality (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.96, 95% CI 0.81-1.12). However, ECMO was associated with greater odds of RRT, intracranial hemorrhage, disseminated intravascular coagulation, cardiogenic shock, vasopressor use, tracheostomy, acute liver failure, deep vein thrombosis, ischemic stroke and ICU-acquired weakness. ECMO was also associated with longer LOS and higher hospitalization charges.
CONCLUSIONS: Among hospitalizations with COVID-19-associated ARDS and AKI, ECMO was not associated with statistically significantly lower adjusted in-hospital mortality but was associated with markedly higher complication burden, longer hospitalization, and substantially greater healthcare resource utilization.

Title: Dexmedetomidine Versus Dexamethasone in Pediatric Cardiac Surgery with Cardiopulmonary Bypass: An Exploratory Randomized Controlled Trial of Inflammatory Biomarkers and Opioid Consumption.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) triggers a systemic inflammatory response in children undergoing congenital heart surgery. Although dexmedetomidine has been proposed as an alternative to corticosteroids, the two agents have not previously been directly compared in a pediatric randomized trial. This study aimed to compare the effects of dexmedetomidine and dexamethasone on inflammatory biomarkers and analgesic outcomes in children undergoing congenital heart surgery with CPB. Methods: In this prospective, randomized, controlled exploratory trial, 50 children aged 6 months to 18 years undergoing elective congenital heart surgery with CPB were randomized 1:1 to dexamethasone (n = 25) or dexmedetomidine (n = 25), using institutional regimens that were not equipotent anti-inflammatory doses. Serum interleukin-6 (IL-6) and interleukin-8 (IL-8) were measured at baseline, immediately after separation from CPB (post-CPB), and 12 h postoperatively. The primary endpoint was IL-6 at the two postoperative time points; IL-8 was a secondary biomarker outcome. Secondary outcomes also included Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability (FLACC) pain scores, fentanyl consumption, and time to first rescue analgesia. Effect estimates included Hodges-Lehmann (HL) median differences with 95% confidence intervals (CIs); a post hoc baseline-adjusted mixed-effects model of log-transformed concentrations served as a sensitivity analysis. Secondary and exploratory analyses were not adjusted for multiple comparisons. Results: All 50 randomized children were analyzed. Median IL-6 was lower in the dexmedetomidine group at 12 h (50 vs. 178 pg/mL; HL difference 86 pg/mL, 95% CI 59 to 144; p < 0.001); the post-CPB difference (46 vs. 77 pg/mL; HL difference 34 pg/mL, 95% CI 0 to 112; p = 0.045) was imprecise and not significant after post hoc Bonferroni correction for the two primary comparisons. In the post hoc baseline-adjusted sensitivity model, the ratio of geometric mean IL-6 concentrations (dexmedetomidine/dexamethasone) was 0.35 (95% CI 0.22 to 0.58; p < 0.001). Among secondary and exploratory outcomes, for which p-values are nominal, IL-8 was also lower post-CPB (159 vs. 381 pg/mL; p = 0.001) and at 12 h (120 vs. 311 pg/mL; p = 0.002). Dexmedetomidine was associated with lower intraoperative (83.0 ± 30.7 vs. 142.6 ± 51.7 µg; p < 0.001) and cumulative 24-h fentanyl consumption (53.8 ± 17.4 vs. 105.4 ± 32.8 µg; p < 0.001), analyzed in absolute units with incompletely documented intraoperative doses, and a longer time to first rescue analgesia (4.68 ± 0.73 vs. 1.84 ± 0.23 h; p < 0.001). Time to extubation did not differ significantly (median 2 vs. 1 h; p = 0.204). Intensive care unit length of stay, an exploratory outcome recorded in days, was distributed toward shorter stays with dexmedetomidine (median 2 [interquartile range 1-2] vs. 2 [2-3] days; p = 0.007).
