BACKGROUND: Chronic diseases are highly prevalent and driven in part by modifiable behaviors including diet and physical activity. Most US adults do not meet behavioral guidelines. Rhode Island (RI)'s 14 Health Equity Zones (HEZs) address chronic disease through place-based efforts to support healthier behaviors statewide.
PURPOSE: To characterize the strategies used by the RI HEZs to implement programs to improve nutrition access and opportunities for physical activity.
METHODS: Annual process evaluations from RI HEZs were reviewed using retrospective content analysis to categorize HEZ implementation efforts related to improving diet and physical activity. Activities were coded using the established Behavior Change Technique (BCT) Taxonomy v1, and Expert Recommendations for Implementing Change (ERIC) strategies.
RESULTS: In each HEZ, 0-62 BCTs and ERIC strategy instances were used to increase physical activity or improve nutrition access. Coding identified 30 out of 93 BCTs and 33 out of 73 ERIC strategies. The most frequently coded BCTs were: Restructuring the social environment (n = 40), social support (practical) (n = 35), instruction on how to perform a behavior (n = 33), adding objects to the environment (n = 22), and restructuring the physical environment (n = 12). The most frequently coded ERIC strategies were: promote network weaving (n = 49), build a coalition (n = 23), access new funding (n = 20), develop resource sharing agreements (n = 18), and tailor strategies (n = 14). HEZs used BCTs and ERIC strategies primarily to implement programs to reduce food insecurity, increase access to nutritious foods, and support physical activity opportunities.
CONCLUSIONS: HEZs utilized social-driven BCTs and ERIC strategies to provide accessible nutrition and physical activity programming. Results inform strategies for future community-driven chronic disease prevention efforts.

Title: A Classification of Safety Risks in Medical AI.
Abstract: AbstractIn clinical practice, patient safety is paramount, guided by the principle "first, do no harm." For medical AI to become a core component of clinical care, safety cannot be determined by its performance or accuracy alone, but by whether or not it protects patients from harm. However, consequences of medical AI models - used either independently or in combination with clinicians - may result in harms that can emerge years after the initial AI-enabled diagnosis or intervention, are difficult to attribute to the original AI model, and are irreversible (e.g., serious morbidity or mortality). We propose a four-level clinical safety classification for medical AI. S1 refers to narrow, testable uses; S2 to decision support that clinicians can review before acting; S3 to uses in which important harms may appear only after follow-up and therefore require surveillance and outcome monitoring before wider rollout; and S4 to high-risk autonomous actions that should be prohibited or allowed only under exceptional safeguards. Using a real-world prospective study of DeepDR-LLM, an integrated image-language system that combines a large language model with image-based deep learning for primary diabetes care and diabetic retinopathy screening, we illustrate how the same AI function may remain classified as S2 when used as clinician-reviewed decision support, become S3 when safety depends on referral completion and follow-up outcomes, or approach S4 if used to bypass clinical judgment. We propose multiwindow postdeployment surveillance that captures near-term signals, scheduled follow-up checkpoints, and long-horizon monitoring beyond 12 months through registry or claims linkage and postimplementation surveillance studies, strengthening medicine's core commitment to "first, do no harm - both now and in the future."

Title: From Technical Performance to Clinical Readiness: A Phase-Based Framework for Evidence Standards in Clinical Artificial Intelligence.
Abstract: AbstractClinical AI is moving rapidly from technical development to patient care, yet evidence standards remain inconsistent. Many studies emphasize model discrimination and retrospective validation, while fewer assess calibration, transportability, prospective clinical impact, implementation readiness, or postdeployment safety. We propose a phase-based framework for evidentiary maturity in clinical AI, using cardiovascular AI as a representative use case. The framework spans model development and representation learning, internal validation, external validation, prospective evaluation of decision impact and implementation readiness, and postdeployment monitoring. Each phase is linked to a core question, expected evidence, and the type of claim that can reasonably be supported. By aligning claims with phase-appropriate evidence, this framework is intended to help investigators, reviewers, regulators, health systems, and clinicians distinguish technical feasibility from clinical readiness and identify when additional prospective evaluation, monitoring, or governance is needed.

Title: TRIALSCOPE - A Framework for Clinical Trial Simulation from Real-World Data.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: The rapid digitization of real-world data presents an unprecedented opportunity to optimize health care delivery and accelerate biomedical discovery. However, these data are often found in unstructured forms, such as clinical notes in electronic medical records (EMRs), and are typically plagued by confounders, making it challenging to generate robust real-world evidence (RWE). Therefore, we present TRIALSCOPE, a framework designed to distill RWE from population-level observational data at scale.
METHODS: TRIALSCOPE leverages biomedical language models to structure clinical text at scale, employs advanced probabilistic modeling for denoising and imputation, and incorporates state-of-the-art causal inference techniques to address common confounders in treatment effect estimation.
RESULTS: Extensive experiments were conducted on a large-scale dataset of over 1 million cancer patients from a single large health care network in the United States. TRIALSCOPE was shown to automatically curate high-quality structured patient data, expanding the dataset and incorporating key patient attributes only available in unstructured form. The framework reduces confounding in treatment effect estimation, generating comparable results with randomized controlled lung cancer trials. In addition, we demonstrate simulations of unconducted clinical trials - including a pancreatic cancer trial with varying eligibility criteria - using a suite of validation tests to ensure robustness. Thorough ablation studies were conducted to better understand key components of TRIALSCOPE and establish best practices for RWE generation from EMRs.
CONCLUSIONS: TRIALSCOPE was able to extract cancer treatment data from EMRs, overcoming limitations of manual curation. We were also able to show that TRIALSCOPE could reproduce the results of lung and pancreatic cancer clinical trials from the extracted real-world data.

Title: TARGET-AI: A Foundational Approach for the Targeted Deployment of Artificial Intelligence Electrocardiography in the Electronic Health Record.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence (AI) applied to electrocardiograms (ECGs) offers promise for structural heart disease (SHD) screening, yet clinical integration remains challenged by high false-positive rates and a lack of tailored deployment strategies.
METHODS: We developed TARGET-AI, a multimodal approach that integrates longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) with ECGs to define patient phenotypes and support targeted SHD screening opportunities. TARGET-AI uses an EHR foundation model applied to 118 million events from 159,322 individuals, to generate temporal patient-level embeddings and identify screening candidates, and a contrastive vision-language model trained on 754,533 ECG image-echocardiogram report pairs, to detect distinct SHD subtypes with tunable characteristics. We evaluated this in 5198 individuals referred for a transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) within 90 days of an ECG (temporal validation) and in geographically distinct cohorts, including 33,518 UK Biobank participants undergoing protocolized ECG and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, and an inpatient cohort of 3628 patients from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC)-IV database with ECG-TTE pairs. We compared discrimination metrics between targeted and untargeted strategies, with bootstrap-derived 95% confidence intervals excluding zero considered significant.
RESULTS: The TARGET-AI ECG model discriminated 26 SHD subtypes, including left ventricular systolic dysfunction (area under the receiver operating curve [AUROC] of 0.90), severe aortic stenosis (AUROC of 0.85), and elevated right ventricular systolic pressure (AUROC of 0.82). Compared with untargeted screening, targeted screening in the temporal validation set (n=5198) was associated with a significant increase in F1 scores (median: 0.25; range: 0.09 to 0.75) and a decrease in the number of false positives (median: -303; range: -715 to -77) across 26 SHD labels. Similar results were seen in the UK Biobank (n=33,518; median change in false positives: -819 [range: -3521 to -459] across seven SHD labels) and MIMIC-IV (n=3628; median false-positive change: -255 [range: -716 to -86] across five SHD labels) participants.
CONCLUSIONS: TARGET-AI may guide the targeted deployment of AI-ECG for SHD screening across health systems. (Funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute of the National Institutes of Health and others.).

Title: Effect of diet-induced plasma ceramide on human in vivo microvascular endothelial function.
Journal: American journal of physiology. Heart and circulatory physiology
Abstract: Elevated plasma ceramides and microvascular endothelial dysfunction are separately implicated in the incidence of cardiovascular disease. Exogenous exposure and endogenous accumulation of ceramide causes microvascular endothelial dysfunction in isolated human microvessels ex vivo; however, the impact of increased plasma ceramide on in vivo human microvascular function is unknown. We measured peripheral microvascular endothelial function in young, healthy adults before and after increasing plasma ceramide levels via high-fat meal. We hypothesized that acute increases in plasma ceramide would induce peripheral microvascular dysfunction. Twenty-three healthy adults (12 males and 11 females) participated in this double-blind, randomized controlled, crossover trial. In vivo microvascular function and perfusion were assessed with laser Doppler flowmetry (LDF) using local heating and incident dark-field microscopy imaging, respectively. Plasma ceramides were quantified and microvascular function was assessed at baseline and 2 and 4 h post ingestion of a meal rich in long (LCT)- or medium (MCT)-chain fatty acids. Acute consumption of a LCT meal increased (P < 0.001) circulating ceramide concentrations in female participants only. Nitric oxide-dependent and maximal dilation, assessed via LDF, were similarly reduced after the intake of either a MCT or LCT meal, with no sex differences observed. No change in microvascular density and perfusion was observed after the consumption of either meal. Results suggest that an acute increase in plasma ceramide is not sufficient to further impair postprandial microvascular function, as both meals similarly reduced microvascular function despite ceramide elevations occurring only after the LCT meal. Future studies should investigate how repeated elevations in ceramide levels affect microvascular function.NEW & NOTEWORTHY Acute consumption of a long-chain fatty acid-rich meal increased circulating ceramides in a sex-specific manner, with elevations observed only in females. Despite this, in vivo microvascular endothelial function was similarly impaired after both medium- and long-chain fatty acid-rich meals, with no differences observed between sexes. Further studies are needed to define the role of ceramide-induced microvascular dysfunction and the long-term cardiovascular impact of repeated exposure.

Title: Generating Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Images from Electrocardiograms - A Multicenter Study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) requires early and accurate diagnosis to improve outcomes. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging provides gold-standard functional and structural insights but remains limited by accessibility and complexity. Electrocardiogram (ECG) is widely available but lacks CMR's granularity. We propose CardioNets, a deep learning framework that translates 12-lead ECG into CMR-aligned functional parameters and synthetic images, enabling scalable, low-cost cardiac assessment.
METHODS: CardioNets aligns the ECG with CMR-derived latent representations via crossmodal contrastive learning, then generates CMR images from the ECG using masked autoregressive modeling. The study utilized 159,819 samples from the U.K. Biobank (UKB), the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC) IV ECG database, and two external clinical datasets for model development and evaluation. The performance in cardiac measurement regression and disease detection was evaluated against ECG-only and CMR-based baseline models, and the synthesized CMR image quality was compared with state-of-the-art methods. A reader study compared CardioNets with physicians using ECG and clinically acquired CMR images.
RESULTS: In the UKB dataset, CardioNets improved cardiac measurement regression (R2=0.310; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.304 to 0.315) compared with the best ECG baseline (R2=0.269; 95% CI, 0.265 to 0.272; P<0.0001). For cardiomyopathy detection, CardioNets achieved an area under the receiver operator curve (AUROC) of 0.890 (95% CI, 0.836 to 0.944), outperforming the best ECG baseline (AUROC=0.867; 95% CI, 0.812 to 0.921; P<0.01), and demonstrating performance comparable to a CMR-based model (AUROC=0.906; 95% CI, 0.890 to 0.922; P=0.514). In MIMIC-IV for pulmonary hypertension detection, CardioNets (AUROC=0.879; 95% CI, 0.853 to 0.903) outperformed the best ECG baseline (AUROC=0.853; 95% CI, 0.824 to 0.881; P<0.001). Synthesized CMR images by CardioNets achieved a structural similarity index measure of 0.205 (95% CI, 0.202 to 0.208), outperforming the state-of-the-art method (0.122; 95% CI, 0.120 to 0.125; P<0.0001). In the reader study, CardioNets achieved an accuracy of 0.874 (95% CI, 0.800 to 0.923), outperforming participating readers.
CONCLUSIONS: CardioNets translates ECGs into CMR-level insights, improving CVD detection performance and enabling scalable accessibility. Prospective studies are warranted to validate clinical deployment. (Funded by the National Key Research and Development Program of China and others.).

Title: Artificial Intelligence-Enhanced Auscultation to Identify Left Ventricular Dysfunction - Development and External Validation in Prospective Multicenter Studies.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Left ventricular dysfunction (LVD) is common and associated with adverse prognosis, even in asymptomatic individuals. Early treatment improves outcomes, underscoring the need for efficient strategies to identify patients who may benefit from echocardiographic evaluation. This study aimed to develop and externally validate an AI auscultation method to detect LVD among patients referred for clinically indicated echocardiography.
METHODS: In this prospective, multicenter study, adult patients referred for echocardiography were enrolled to undergo digital auscultation at four standard auscultation sites with simultaneous single-lead ECGs. LVD was defined as a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) less than or equal to 40% on concurrent echocardiography. An ensemble model combining a transformer-based network and a one-dimensional convolutional neural network was trained on multicenter data and externally validated. The model's performance was compared with a seven-cardiologist reader substudy and clinical logistic regression models incorporating clinical variables, single-lead ECG-derived features, and B-type natriuretic peptide levels.
RESULTS: The multicenter training cohort included 2359 patients (mean age, 69.7±13.5 years; 40.4% female; 8.9% with reduced LVEF). The external validation cohort of 964 patients (mean age, 68.6±15.4 years; 38.9% female; 7.6% with reduced LVEF) was obtained from another independent multicenter registry. The four-site AI auscultation outperformed ECG-only models and the clinical logistic models, achieving an area under the receiver operator curve (AUROC) of 0.926 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.911 to 0.939) in the training cohort. In the external validation cohort, AUROC was 0.904 (95% CI, 0.876 to 0.930) and sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were 86.3%, 74.2%, and 75.1%, respectively. In a 100-patient reader substudy, AI auscultation outperformed cardiologist consensus in accuracy (82.0% vs. 62.0%; P=0.004). Model performance was consistent across prespecified subgroups. The simplified two-site auscultation model retained high accuracy in the external validation cohort (AUROC, 0.903; 95% CI, 0.878 to 0.927).
CONCLUSIONS: AI auscultation accurately detected LVD among patients referred for clinically indicated echocardiography, supporting its potential as a scalable and accessible pre-echocardiographic risk-enrichment tool. Further validation is warranted before broader screening applications. (Funded by AMI Inc. and the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science KAKENHI program [grant number 25K19371].).
Publication Types: Journal Article; Multicenter Study; Validation Study

Title: Changes in Anthropometric, Metabolic, and Micronutrient Features Among Patients with Severe Obesity Awaiting Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Due to high demand for metabolic and bariatric surgery, patients often face significant waiting periods before undergoing the procedure. This study aimed to investigate trends in weight and metabolic changes among patients with severe obesity awaiting surgery, given the potential impact of preoperative metabolic changes on perioperative outcomes.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study included patients with severe obesity who had been waiting for metabolic and bariatric surgery for at least six months. Weight, body composition analysis parameters, and biochemical tests were recorded every six to eight weeks for these candidates.
RESULTS: Among the 2926 patients studied, the average age was 39.7 years, with 74.8% being women. The mean weight was 124.65 kg, while the mean BMI was 46.14 kg/m². Seventy-five percent of the patients had obesity-related comorbidities. Adjusted models based on generalized estimating equations (GEE) approach showed that weight, FBS, insulin, and TG have an increasing trend over time. Male sex was associated with significantly higher weight (+25.78 kg), FBS (+4.11 mg/dL), insulin (+8.47 µIU/mL), TG (+15.39 mg/dL), SGPT (+17.59 IU/L), and SGOT (+6.93 IU/L), as well as lower HDL (-3.89 mg/dL), and a small but statistically significant increase in BUN. Age showed small but significant effects, with increases linked to reduced weight, insulin, TG, and SGPT, but slightly higher FBS, LDL, HDL, and BUN values. Dyslipidemia was significantly associated with higher TG (+38.20 mg/dL), while type 2 diabetes mellitus was linked to large increases in FBS (+61.63 mg/dL) and TG (+18.04 mg/dL) and a decrease in LDL (-7.50 mg/dL). The presence of cardiovascular disease was related to higher insulin (+7.22 µIU/mL), but lower TG (-4.02 mg/dL) and LDL (-13.84 mg/dL).
CONCLUSION: Lengthening the waiting time for surgery can lead to worsening glycolipid status and weight gain in patients. Therefore, if possible, reducing wait times or providing more regular and thorough nutritional and psychological consultations can improve metabolic conditions, resulting in better outcomes after surgery.

Title: Effect of Activin Type II Receptor Signaling in Patients With HFpEF and Pulmonary Hypertension: A Critical Analysis of Biological Mechanisms and Clinical Trials.
Abstract: The totality of evidence indicates that the mechanisms underlying the increase in pulmonary vascular resistance in patients with combined postcapillary and precapillary pulmonary hypertension (CpcPH) associated with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) differ meaningfully from those responsible for the increase in pulmonary vascular resistance in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension. CpcPH-HFpEF is a complex disorder involving the pulmonary veins, left atrium, and pulmonary arterioles, but recent evidence has highlighted a potentially central role for pulmonary venous and left atrial (LA) dysfunction. Epicardial adipose tissue occupies anatomical proximity to both structures, allowing derivative secretory products to influence their structure and function. The most well-characterized proinflammatory adipokine released from an expanded epicardial fat mass is activin A, which causes fibrosis and cardiomyocyte stiffness and senescence in underlying tissues by signaling through activin type II receptor signal transduction. Such signaling regulates pulmonary venular responses to mechanical stretch, and circulating activin A is elevated in patients with HFpEF who have enlarged LA chambers, pulmonary venous hypertension and increased pulmonary vascular resistance. The adipokine hypothesis of HFpEF identified activin A and activin type II receptor signaling as key adipokine mediators in the pathogenesis of HFpEF. Experimentally, activin A signaling promotes the development of both atrial myopathy and HFpEF, and activin type II receptor ligand traps alleviate HFpEF and ameliorate both the pulmonary vascular and left heart abnormalities in experimental models in which CpcPH-HFpEF is induced by obesity. These collective observations led to the prospective hypothesis that adipokine modulation by sotatercept would mediate benefits on the left heart in patients with CpcPH-HFpEF. These expectations were validated when the CADENCE trial showed that sotatercept decreased both pulmonary artery wedge pressures and left atrial volume index in patients with CpcPH-HFpEF, which are effects that could not explained by a decrease in pulmonary vascular resistance. Activin A released from an expanded epicardial adipose tissue promotes both pulmonary venous and left atrial remodeling and fibrosis in vivo, which (in turn) are effects that can be attenuated by an activin A decoy. The efficacy of sotatercept to slow the progression of CpcPH-HFpEF is now being tested in a phase III outcomes trial.

Title: Correction to: 2026 Guideline for Adult Stroke Rehabilitation and Recovery: A Guideline From the American Heart Association and American Stroke Association.
Impact of broadly targeted enhanced recovery after surgery protocols in hysterectomy versus other gynecologic surgeries.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The opioid epidemic in the United States poses a major public health challenge, with postoperative prescribing recognized as a significant source of initial opioid exposure. Midwestern states, including Iowa, have experienced substantial opioid-related morbidity and mortality, reflecting broader national trends of opioid misuse, diversion, and overdose. Excess postoperative opioid prescribing increases the availability of unused medications, which are often retained in households and pose ongoing risks for diversion and nonmedical use. These challenges highlight the need for effective, scalable strategies to reduce opioid exposure at surgical discharge. Accordingly, this study investigated the impact of a broadly targeted Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) pathway on opioid prescribing at discharge for hysterectomy patients compared to other gynecologic procedures.
METHODS: A retrospective chart review was conducted across six Iowa hospitals implementing the "Billion Pill Pledge" ERAS pathway. Two groups of patients underwent surgery between November 3, 2022 and April 4, 2024: those undergoing hysterectomy (n = 63) and those undergoing other gynecologic surgeries (n = 30), including cervical hysteroscopy, cesarean section, endometriosis excision or ablation, and sterilization procedures. Pre-ERAS and post-ERAS implementation data from the postoperative period were analyzed between the two groups in terms of average opioid pill counts prescribed, percent reduction in pill counts prescribed after ERAS implementation, and percent of prescribed pills remaining unused.
RESULTS: Pre-ERAS data showed no significant difference in mean opioid pill counts prescribed at discharge between hysterectomies and other gynecologic surgeries (p = 0.3). Post-ERAS data displayed significantly higher mean pill counts for hysterectomies (23 pills) versus other gynecologic surgeries (16 pills) (p < 0.001). Patient-reported post-ERAS prescription quantities were significantly lower than surgeon-estimated pre-ERAS prescribing quantities for both hysterectomies (27 pills versus 23 pills) (p < 0.001) and other gynecologic surgeries (29 pills versus 16 pills) (p < 0.001). The hysterectomy group had a significantly smaller percent reduction in prescribed pill counts than the other gynecologic group (14% versus 40%) (p < 0.001). There was no significant difference in the proportion of prescribed pills left unused between the hysterectomy group (55%) and the other gynecologic group (65%) (p = 0.08). No prescription refills were reported within 30 days postoperatively.
CONCLUSION: Patient-reported opioid prescription quantities prescribed at discharge following implementation of the Billion Pill Pledge ERAS pathway were significantly lower than surgeon-estimated pre-ERAS prescribing quantities across gynecologic surgeries, with a larger difference observed among non-hysterectomy procedures. Despite lower post-ERAS prescription quantities, over half of prescribed pills on average remained unused, highlighting the need for ongoing efforts to optimize postoperative opioid disposal practices. These findings suggest that broadly targeted ERAS pathways may be associated with lower postoperative opioid prescribing in gynecologic surgery.

Title: MRI-guided microwave ablation of hepatic malignancies: 4-year institutional outcomes.
Abstract:
PURPOSE: We assessed the safety and efficacy of magnetic resonance (MR)-guided microwave ablation for treating hepatic malignancies.
METHODS: This retrospective single-center review evaluated patients who underwent MR-guided microwave ablation for hepatic malignancies between 02/15/2017-04/22/2020. Complications were classified following CIRSE guidelines. Local tumor progression (LTP), local tumor recurrence (LTR), non-target progression (NTP), progression-free survival (PFS) and time to progression (TTP) were assessed, with data presented as mean ± standard deviation.
RESULTS: Sixteen patients (60.75 ± 14.4 years; 9 males, 7 females) underwent 17 MR-guided microwave ablation for 21 hepatic malignancies (17 (81.0%) hepatocellular carcinoma, 1 (4.8%) cholangiocarcinoma, 2 (9.5%) metastases, and 1 (4.8%) suspicious lesion in a patient with primary sclerosing cholangitis). Lesion size was 12.2 ± 4.8 mm and total procedure time 138 ± 53 minutes. Complications included fever (N = 2), abdominal pain (N = 2), biloma (N = 1), and reactive cholecystitis (N = 1). These resolved with pain medication for one patient and antibiotics for another. No tumor recurrence was observed at ablation sites (LTP and LTR = 0%) at 36.7 ± 28.2 months. NTP occurred in 11 patients (68.8%) with a TTP of 14.8 ± 11.4 months. PFS was 44 months (95% CI: 10-85 months). Three patients died during follow-up - one from complications after liver transplantation and two from disease progression. Post-ablation liver transplantation was performed in two patients.
CONCLUSION: MR-guided microwave ablation for hepatic malignancies is safe and effective, with no local tumor recurrences noted over a follow-up period of 36.7 ± 28.2 months.
CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: MR-guided microwave ablation is a promising minimally invasive treatment for hepatic malignancies, demonstrating no LTR at 36.7 ± 28.2 months. Precise, radiation-free needle placement in real-time and effective targeting of small tumors may further improve future patient care.

Title: Prevalence of osteosarcopenia and associated factors among older Vietnamese outpatients: A cross-sectional study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Osteosarcopenia - the concurrent presence of sarcopenia and low bone mass, including osteopenia or osteoporosis - is emerging as a significant health issue in aging populations. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of osteosarcopenia and identify factors associated with prevalent osteosarcopenia among older Vietnamese outpatients.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted on 389 outpatients aged ≥60 years at Can Tho University of Medicine and Pharmacy Hospital from 01/202511/2025. Osteosarcopenia was defined by coexistent low bone mass (osteopenia/osteoporosis via DXA) and sarcopenia defined according to AWGS 2019 as low muscle mass accompanied by low muscle strength, low physical performance or both. Logistic regression analyses were used to assess factors associated with osteosarcopenia. All data were analysed using R version 4.5.5.
RESULTS: The overall prevalence of osteosarcopenia was 26.7% (95% CI 22.6-31.3%). Prevalence was similar in women and men (26.3% vs 28.6%, p = 0.68). On multivariable analysis, older age (per 1-year increase; OR 1.06, 95% CI 1.02-1.10), lower BMI (per 1 kg/m2 increase; OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.50-0.65), coronary artery disease (OR 2.07, 95% CI 1.09-3.95), and diabetes (OR 2.48, 95% CI 1.35-4.56) were independently associated with osteosarcopenia.
CONCLUSION: Osteosarcopenia affected about one in four older outpatients in this Vietnamese cohort. Older age, lower body mass index, coronary artery disease, and diabetes were independently associated with osteosarcopenia. These findings highlight the importance of early screening and integrated management of bone and muscle health in older adults.

Title: MIF inhibitor ISO-1 attenuates ischemia-reperfusion injury in a rat model of donation after circulatory death liver transplantation.
Abstract: Macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) is an early mediator of ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI), however, the evidence on its role in orthotopic liver transplantation (OLT), particularly with donation after circulatory death (DCD) grafts is limited. Given its key regulatory function, this study investigated the effects of IRI on graft injury and assessed whether the use of ISO-1, a small-molecule MIF-inhibitor, affect IRI in a rat DCD-OLT model. 196 male Lewis rats were randomized into DBD control, DCD-30 min, DCD-60 min, DCD-30 + ISO-1, and DCD-30 + vehicle groups (n = 7/group/time-point). ISO-1 was administered before controlled cardiac arrest (0-60 min) and 3 h cold preservation before arterialized OLT. Animals were sacrificed at 1, 3, 24, and 168 h post-reperfusion. DCD grafts showed marked injury, with the DCD-60 group exhibiting lethal IRI. ISO-1 significantly reduced early hepatocellular injury compared with vehicle (AST:294 ± 63 vs 867 ± 211 IU/L, p = 0.017) and resulted in values comparable to DBD controls. Serum HMGB-1 (11 ± 2.8 vs 26 ± 6.2 pg/mL, p = 0.045) and MIF (45 ± 5.3 vs 144 ± 27.5 ng/mL, p = 0.034) levels were similarly decreased following ISO-1 application. ISO-1 improved graft microcirculation at 24 h, attenuated histological injury, and was associated with an altered time course of CD163 + macrophage infiltration. ISO-1 pre-treatment attenuated hepatocellular injury and was associated with improved graft microcirculation and reduced DAMP release, supporting further mechanistic and translational evaluation in DCD liver transplantation.

Title: From structural repair to biomechanical compatibility: Aortic stiffness after open and endovascular aortic repair.
Abstract: Evaluation of aortic repair has traditionally prioritised perioperative safety, exclusion of the diseased segment and durability. As endovascular treatment expands to younger patients, attention is turning towards the biomechanical compatibility of prosthetic grafts with the native aorta. Native aortic compliance supports Windkessel function, whereas grafts create a compliance transition that may accelerate pulse-wave transmission, alter wave reflection and increase left-ventricular load. This narrative review distinguishes established evidence from emerging concepts after open surgical repair, endovascular aneurysm repair and thoracic endovascular aortic repair. Carotid-femoral pulse-wave velocity (cfPWV) is the accepted reference non-invasive measure of regional aortic stiffness; cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR)-derived segmental pulse-wave velocity and distensibility provide complementary information. Brachial-ankle pulse-wave velocity, the cardio-ankle vascular index, and augmentation index assess different territories or haemodynamic properties and are not interchangeable with cfPWV. Left-ventricular strain and mass are downstream cardiac outcomes. Clinical evidence generally reports increases in measured arterial-stiffness indices after endovascular repair, whereas findings after open repair are heterogeneous. Treatment length, landing-zone location, oversizing, anatomy and baseline vascular phenotype may be as important as graft fabric or stent-frame category. Conflicting comparisons of polyester and expanded polytetrafluoroethylene arise from small, non-randomised studies using non-equivalent endpoints and do not support a reliable ranking of commercial devices. Emerging 4D-flow CMR, simulation and compliant graft materials illustrate a shift from structural exclusion alone towards compliance-aware repair, but evidence of improved outcomes remains insufficient. Future studies should use standardised longitudinal stiffness, blood-pressure and cardiac assessments and relate biomechanical changes to hypertension, ventricular remodelling and cardiovascular outcomes.

Title: Skeletal Muscle in Vulnerable Populations Receiving Cardiorenal-Metabolic Therapies: SGLT2 Inhibitors, Incretin-Based Therapies, and the Challenge of Precision Medicine.
Abstract: The introduction of sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors and incretin-based therapies has transformed the management of obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease by delivering substantial metabolic, cardiovascular, and renal benefits. However, their effects on skeletal muscle have become a growing area of interest. While SGLT2 inhibitors induce modest weight loss, their catabolic metabolic effects have prompted questions regarding skeletal muscle preservation, particularly in individuals with limited physiological reserve. Conversely, the profound weight loss achieved with incretin-based therapies has raised concerns about accompanying reductions in lean tissue and their potential functional consequences. In this narrative review, we critically evaluate the available evidence regarding the effects of these therapeutic classes on skeletal muscle, integrating findings from randomized controlled trials, observational studies, systematic reviews, and mechanistic investigations. We compare their distinct biological mechanisms; summarize clinical evidence on changes in muscle quantity, quality, strength, and physical performance; and discuss their implications for older adults; individuals with frailty, sarcopenia, or sarcopenic obesity; and patients with heart failure or chronic kidney disease. Overall, current evidence indicates that both SGLT2 inhibitors and incretin-based therapies preferentially reduce adipose tissue, whereas the accompanying reductions in lean tissue are generally proportional to the magnitude of weight loss. Importantly, reductions in lean tissue should not be equated with treatment-induced sarcopenia, as current evidence does not consistently demonstrate clinically meaningful impairment in muscle strength or physical performance. Nevertheless, the populations most susceptible to skeletal muscle dysfunction remain underrepresented in clinical trials. We discuss a phenotype-based approach that integrates skeletal muscle health into therapeutic decision-making and outline practical strategies-including resistance exercise, adequate protein intake, and individualized monitoring-to preserve muscle function during treatment. Future research should prioritize standardized functional outcomes and dedicated studies in vulnerable populations to enable precision cardiorenal-metabolic medicine.

Title: Postmenopausal Hormone Replacement Therapy is not Associated with Increased Postoperative Complications After Breast Surgery: A Propensity Matched Study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Breast surgery and reconstruction rates in the USA continue to rise, with over 90% of new breast cancer diagnoses occurring in peri- or postmenopausal women. Despite the relevance of menopause to wound healing, postoperative outcomes in this population remain understudied. Estrogen hormone replacement therapy (HRT) may aid wound healing and menopausal symptoms, but carries prothrombotic risk. We investigate postsurgical outcomes after breast surgery and reconstruction among postmenopausal patients on HRTs compared to those without HRT use.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: Using the TriNetX database, we compared patients with and without HRT use within 1 year preceding breast reconstruction. Mastectomy and reconstruction procedures were identified using CPT codes. HRT use was identified using ICD-10 and RxNorm codes. Cohorts were propensity-matched for demographics and comorbidities. Risk differences with 95% confidence intervals were calculated for outcomes within 90 days postoperatively. Analyses were performed within TriNetX, with significance set at P < 0.05.
RESULTS: Two cohorts were generated, with 3750 HRT+ and 75503 HRT- patients. After propensity matching, two cohorts of 3750 patients each were created. After propensity adjustment, there was no significant association between HRT use and postoperative mortality, VTE, or wound healing complications, which were comparably low across all surgery types. Among patients undergoing autologous reconstruction, 1-year revision rates were higher in the HRT+ cohort.
CONCLUSIONS: Systemic hormone replacement therapy was not associated with an increased complications after breast reconstruction, including mortality, thrombosis, infection, and wound dehiscence. Further prospective studies across surgical populations are needed to validate these findings.

Title: Naxos disease: current insights from early clinical observations to genetics and precision medicine.
Abstract: Naxos disease is the prototype of the Naxos disease cardiocutaneous spectrum, a group of inherited desmosomal disorders characterised by distinctive hair and skin abnormalities that precede the development of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM). Since its original clinical description in 1986 and the subsequent identification of the first ACM-causing gene (JUP), Naxos disease has provided fundamental insights into the pathogenesis, diagnosis and management of inherited desmosomal cardiomyopathies. This review provides current insights into the evolving clinical spectrum, encompassing the characteristic cutaneous signature, early electrical abnormalities, progressive structural myocardial remodelling, inflammatory ("hot-phase") episodes, ventricular arrhythmias and heart failure. We discuss the expanding genotype-phenotype relationships involving JUP, DSP and DSC2, highlighting how distinct genetic substrates influence ventricular involvement, disease severity and clinical outcomes while sharing common desmosomal mechanisms. Particular emphasis is placed on early clinical recognition, multimodality imaging, genetic diagnosis, risk stratification and lifelong multidisciplinary management. Finally, we discuss the emerging role of international collaborative registries, including NAXCARE, in generating prospective real-world evidence to refine genotype-informed surveillance, improve risk prediction and support precision medicine. Nearly four decades after its original description, Naxos disease has evolved from a rare inherited syndrome into the prototype of desmosomal cardiomyopathy, demonstrating how careful clinical observation can drive molecular discovery, precision medicine and improved patient care.

Title: Myocardial contraction fraction and mortality in cardiac amyloidosis: a prospective single-center cohort study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) often remains normal in cardiac amyloidosis (CA) because declines in stroke volume (SV) parallel reductions in end-diastolic volume. The myocardial contraction fraction (MCF), the ratio of SV to myocardial volume, has been proposed as superior to LVEF in predicting mortality in CA.
METHODS: Thirty patients with confirmed CA underwent echocardiography and were followed for a mean of 18.2 ± 5.8 months. MCF was calculated from standard two-dimensional echocardiographic measurements. Cox proportional hazards modeling with Lasso-penalized selection was used to evaluate the association of MCF with all-cause mortality.
RESULTS: Mean age was 70.1 ± 8.6 years; 76.7% were male. Thirteen patients (43.3%) died. MCF was lower among those who died compared with survivors (21.9% vs 38.2%; p < 0.0001); 87.5% of patients with MCF ≤ 25% died, compared with 27.3% of those with MCF > 25%. MCF ≤ 25% was independently associated with mortality (HR: 5.456; 95% CI: 1.628-18.29; p = 0.006); modeled as a continuous variable, each 5-percentage-point increase in MCF was associated with lower mortality (HR: 0.57; p = 0.002), while MAPSE < 10 mm and grade 3 diastolic dysfunction were retained in the multivariable model but did not reach significance after penalization.
CONCLUSIONS: MCF ≤ 25% demonstrated numerically greater discriminative ability for all-cause mortality compared with LVEF (C-statistic 0.83 vs 0.71) and was the only echocardiographic parameter to remain an independent predictor after Lasso-penalized multivariable adjustment. These hypothesis-generating findings, from a small single-centre cohort, require validation in larger, subtype-specific studies.

Title: A Phase III, Open-Label, Single-Arm, Multicentric Study of Tildrakizumab in Indian Patients with Moderate-to-Severe Plaque Psoriasis.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory disease linked to significant morbidity and reduced quality of life (QoL). Prospective data on interleukin-23 (IL-23) inhibitors in Indian patients remain limited. This phase III, open-label, multicentre, single-arm bridging study assessed the efficacy, safety and immunogenicity of tildrakizumab 100 mg in Indian patients.
METHODS: Adults with plaque psoriasis for ≥ 6 months, body surface area (BSA) involvement of 10-50%, Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) score ≥ 12 and Physician's Global Assessment (PGA) rating ≥ 3 received tildrakizumab 100 mg subcutaneously at weeks 0, 4 and 16, followed through week 28. The primary endpoint was PASI 75 (≥ 75% reduction in a patient's PASI score compared to their baseline score before treatment) at week 12. Secondary endpoints included PASI 90 (≥ 90% reduction in PASI score), PGA rating, Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI), safety and immunogenicity.
RESULTS: Among the 115 patients participating in the study, mean (± standard deviation) psoriasis duration was 7.4 ± 6.9 years, baseline PASI was 21.1 ± 7.8 and BSA involvement was 23.9 ± 9.6%. PASI 75 response rose from 62.3% at week 12 to 93.9% at week 28. PASI 90 was achieved by 78.1% of participants at week 28, and PGA 0/1 with ≥ 2-grade improvement was achieved by 91.2%. DLQI improved markedly (mean change - 13.2 ± 7.43; p < 0.0001). Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) occurred in 30 patients (26.3%), of which most were mild. One serious TEAE (acute myocardial infarction, unrelated to study drug) was reported. Anti-drug antibodies were detected in 7.1% of patients at week 28.
CONCLUSION: In this short-term, single-arm bridging study, tildrakizumab 100 mg demonstrated sustained skin clearance and meaningful QoL improvement through week 28 after three doses, with a favourable safety profile in Indian patients. Longer-term comparative data are needed to confirm durability and relative effectiveness.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: CTRI/2023/06/053784.

Title: Prognostic role of selective beta-1 blockers in patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors.
Journal: Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer
Abstract:
PURPOSE: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have revolutionized cancer care and prognosis. Beta-adrenergic activation contributes to cancer initiation and progression. While non-selective beta-blockers were found to improve the efficacy of ICIs therapy, the role of beta-1 (β1)-selective beta-blocker (β1B) is unknown. We aimed to evaluate the association between baseline selective β1-blocker therapy and all-cause mortality and cardiovascular immune-related adverse events (CV irAEs) among patients treated with ICIs.
METHODS: We performed a retrospective single-center study including patients diagnosed with cancer and treated with ICIs therapy.
RESULTS: Among 2409 patients, 591 (25%) were pretreated with β1B. Patients in the β1B group were older (72 ± 9 vs. 64 ± 13 years, p < 0.001) with a higher prevalence of cardiac risk factors and CV diseases including ischemic heart disease (40% vs. 8%, p < 0.001), heart failure (HF) (9% vs. 2%, p < 0.001) and atrial fibrillation (AF) (15% vs. 3%, p < 0.001). Patients pretreated with β1B showed significantly increased all-cause mortality (68% vs. 57%, p < 0.001) and CV irAEs (14% vs. 7%, p < 0.001), mainly HF (7% vs. 3%, p < 0.001) and AF (7% vs. 3%, p < 0.001). In a multivariate analysis, β1B remained a strong independent predictor for all-cause mortality (Hazard Ratio (HR) 1.21 [95% CI 1.05-1.39]), p = 0.010), however, not for CV irAEs (HR 1.22 [95% CI = 0.84-1.77], p = 0.290). The association between baseline selective β1-blocker treatment and increased all-cause mortality was consistent among patients with or without baseline CV disease.
CONCLUSIONS: Baseline β1B therapy may be an independent predictor of increased all-cause mortality in patients treated with ICIs.

Title: German multicenter biobank and registry for phenotype-specific genomic research in thoracic aortic disease.
Abstract:
PURPOSE: To establish a national multicentre biobank and registry for future genomic and genotype-phenotype studies of distinct thoracic aortic disease entities and to report the study design and current recruitment status.
METHODS: A prospective multicenter registry with integrated biobanking was established in May 2024 across eight German vascular and cardiovascular centres. Patients with Stanford type B aortic dissection (STBAD), thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA), intramural hematoma (IMH), or penetrating aortic ulcer (PAU) were enrolled. Clinical characteristics, treatment, imaging parameters, and longitudinal outcomes were collected in a centralized pseudonymized database, and EDTA blood samples were stored at - 80 °C for future genomic analyses. An established retrospective Heidelberg cohort of 118 patients with isolated STBAD serves as a hypothesis-generating cohort, while the prospective multicenter cohort provides an independent population for subsequent validation and extension of genetic findings. No genomic analyses were performed for the present report.
RESULTS: As of May 2026, 274 patients had been included: 118 patients with STBAD from the hypothesis-generating Heidelberg cohort and 156 patients from the prospective multicenter cohort comprising 84 patients with STBAD, 40 with TAA, 13 with IMH, and 19 with PAU. The most prominent descriptive difference between disease entities was age distribution. Among patients with STBAD, 116/202 (57.4%) were younger than 60 years, compared with 6/40 (15.0%) with TAA, 2/13 (15.4%) with IMH, and 2/19 (10.5%) with PAU. A positive family history of thoracic aortic disease was reported in 14 patients (5.1%), and hypermobility or other connective tissue features were documented in 12 patients (4.4%), and two patients (0.7%) had a documented connective tissue disorder. Overall, 217 patients (79.2%) underwent surgical or endovascular treatment. Median imaging follow-up ranged from 1.5 months in IMH to 48 months in the retrospective Heidelberg cohort.
CONCLUSION: This national multicenter biobank and registry provides a deeply phenotyped platform for future investigation of the genetic basis of distinct thoracic aortic disease entities. The observed difference in age distribution provide a rationale for phenotype-specific genomic investigation but should not be interpreted as evidence of differing genetic contributions per se. Continued recruitment and longitudinal follow-up will enable future future genomic and genotype-phenotype analyses.

Title: [Camelid-assisted interventions in mental disorders : Effects on psychological and physiological parameters in a controlled study].
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Animal-assisted interventions are increasingly used in psychiatric care; however, evidence on the use of camelids, which are characterized by a calm and low-intensity interaction behavior, remains scarce.
OBJECTIVE: This study therefore aimed to investigate the short-term effects of a camelid-assisted intervention in individuals with mental disorders.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: In an exploratory pilot study using a controlled naturalistic fixed-sequence within-subject design, 68 psychiatric inpatients participated in a group intervention with llamas and alpacas. An outdoor group session without animals served as the control condition. Psychological and physiological outcomes were assessed before and after the intervention.
RESULTS: Compared with the control condition, the camelid-assisted intervention was associated with significantly greater increases in visual analogue scale scores for relaxation and calmness of thought; descriptively, a similar (nonsignificant) pattern was observed for mental well-being, emotional stability, self-confidence and energy. States of anxiety and affective distress decreased slightly in both conditions. Overall, physiological findings for salivary cortisol, salivary alpha-amylase, and heart rate variability were inconsistent.
DISCUSSION: The findings suggest short-term positive psychological changes in psychiatric patients in association with the camelid-assisted intervention. The stability and generalizability of these changes remain to be examined in larger randomized studies with follow-up assessments.

Title: Traditional Chinese medicine in CKD: myths, facts, and evidence.
Journal: Nephrology, dialysis, transplantation : official publication of the European Dialysis and Transplant Association - European Renal Association
Abstract: Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) is increasingly used among patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), particularly in regions where healthcare resources, accessibility and cultural acceptance influence treatment choices. However, its role in the treatment of CKD remains controversial, with conflicting perceptions ranging from therapeutic promise to concerns regarding unproven efficacy and potential toxicity. In this review, we critically examine some myths and facts surrounding TCM use in CKD through the framework of evidence-based medicine. Randomized evidence remains limited, but a few trials have reported clinically relevant signals. In patients with type 2 diabetes and CKD, the multicenter SCHEMATIC trial found that add-on Rehmannia-6-based Chinese medicine was associated with a slower decline in eGFR over 48 weeks. In membranous nephropathy, an earlier multicenter randomized trial of Shenqi particle reported reductions in proteinuria and remission outcomes comparable with conventional immunosuppressive therapy. These findings are hypothesis-supporting rather than definitive: neither trial established a reduction in kidney failure, cardiovascular events or mortality, and independent confirmation is lacking. Importantly, safety should not be inferred from natural origin or historical use. Product quality, botanical authentication, pharmacokinetics, toxicological evaluation, herb-drug interactions and pharmacovigilance are essential components of responsible clinical evaluation. Future research should move beyond the broad question of whether 'TCM works' and instead focus on product-specific assessment using rigorous trial methodology, standardized manufacturing, precision CKD phenotyping and internationally applicable outcome measures. Chinese herbal medicines should neither be dismissed solely because they are traditional nor accepted solely because they are natural. Their future role in CKD care should be determined by the same principles applied to any therapeutic intervention: reproducible quality, demonstrated clinical benefit and an acceptable benefit-risk profile.

Title: First-trimester Cardiac Assessment in Fetuses With Increased Nuchal Translucency: A Diagnostic Accuracy Study.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the independent and incremental value of a standardized first-trimester binary cardiac assessment for screening severe congenital heart disease (CHD) in fetuses with increased nuchal translucency (NT).
METHOD: This single-center retrospective diagnostic accuracy study included 223 singleton fetuses with NT ≥ 3.0 mm at 11-13+ 6 weeks of gestation who underwent prenatal screening at our hospital between January 2019 and December 2023. First-trimester binary cardiac assessment was performed through blinded review of archived ultrasound images. Clinical and screening variables, including NT thickness and pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A), were collected. Missing serum marker data were addressed using multiple imputation. Logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses were used to assess the predictive and diagnostic performance of the cardiac assessment alone and in combination with conventional screening indicators. The DeLong test was used to compare the baseline model (NT + PAPP-A) with the incremental model (NT + PAPP-A + cardiac assessment).
RESULTS: A positive first-trimester cardiac assessment was independently associated with severe CHD (adjusted OR = 4.02, 95% CI: 1.09-14.87). In the primary imputed analysis, the baseline model (NT + PAPP-A) had an AUC of 0.840 (95% CI: 0.772-0.912), and the incremental model adding cardiac assessment had an AUC of 0.879 (95% CI: 0.812-0.945); however, the DeLong test did not show a statistically significant difference (p = 0.243). The cardiac assessment showed particularly high sensitivity for left-sided obstructive cardiac malformations (90.0%).
CONCLUSION: A standardized first-trimester cardiac assessment is independently associated with severe CHD in fetuses with thickened NT. Adding it to NT thickness and maternal PAPP-A did not significantly improve model discrimination in this retrospective cohort, although the AUC increased numerically. Prospective multicenter studies are needed to determine whether this combined strategy provides incremental value.

Title: Stroke and Bleeding Risk in Long-Term Care Residents With Atrial Fibrillation Who Discontinue Anticoagulation.
Abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Atrial fibrillation (AF) leads to more than 100 000 cases of stroke yearly and is particularly prevalent in long-term care (LTC) residents. Anticoagulation (AC) is the mainstay of stroke prevention, but given its risks, clinicians and residents may consider discontinuation at the time of LTC entry.
OBJECTIVE: To estimate the association between AC discontinuation and stroke and bleeding risk among LTC residents with AF.
DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This comparative effectiveness research study with target trial emulation used claims data (2020-2021) from LTC facilities in the US serving Medicare beneficiaries. Medicare beneficiaries with AF receiving AC who entered LTC between April 1 and December 31, 2020, were included; those with additional indications for AC, including prosthetic heart valve or venous thromboembolism, were excluded. Analysis was performed in August 2026.
EXPOSURE: Discontinuer vs continuer assignment.
MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: The main outcomes were stroke (including ischemic stroke, transient ischemic attack, and systemic embolism) and bleeding, assessed using Medicare claims. A target trial emulation was conducted with clone censor weighting (CCW) analysis. Specifically, eligible LTC residents were assigned (cloned) to each of 2 strategies: AC discontinuation or AC continuation. Clones were then censored when they deviated from their assigned strategy, and inverse probability of censoring weighting was applied to address informative censoring: residents who deviated differing systematically from those who did not. Subdistribution hazard ratios (sHRs) for stroke and bleeding were then calculated to account for competing mortality and a cause-specific hazard ratio (HR) for death.
RESULTS: This study included 15 426 LTC residents (mean [SD] age, 82.6 [7.6] years). Most were female (62.6%). AC discontinuers had 187 strokes, 297 bleeding events, and 3684 deaths over a mean (SD) of 128.9 (177.9) days. AC continuers had 321 strokes, 493 bleeding events, and 5475 deaths over a mean (SD) of 279.6 (204.9) days. Discontinuers had similar stroke risk (sHR, 1.07; 95% CI, 0.93-1.23) and bleeding risk (sHR, 1.02; 95% CI, 0.92-1.13) compared with continuers, but discontinuers had higher mortality risk (HR, 1.27; 95% CI, 1.23-1.31).
CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this target trial emulation with CCW in a cohort of LTC residents with AF, AC discontinuation was not associated with higher stroke or bleeding risk. Very high mortality, unmeasured confounding, and reliance on claims-based outcome ascertainment may have limited the ability to better understand the consequences of AC discontinuation on stroke and bleeding.

Title: Evaluation of Serum Pentraxin-3 and Heavy Metal Levels in Patients with Acute Coronary Syndrome.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Vascular inflammation and vasculotoxic heavy metals have each been linked to acute coronary syndrome (ACS) but have rarely been studied together. This study compared serum pentraxin-3 (PTX-3), a proposed marker of local vascular inflammation, and whole-blood lead (Pb), arsenic (As), and nickel (Ni) between ACS patients and controls.
METHODS: In this single-center, cross-sectional case-control study, 50 patients with angiographically confirmed ACS were compared with 50 age- and sex-comparable emergency department controls with minor non-cardiac complaints.
RESULTS: PTX-3, Pb, As, and Ni were higher in ACS patients (all false discovery rate-adjusted q < 0.001). Between-group discrimination was highest for Pb (area under the curve [AUC] 0.962) and PTX-3 (AUC 0.951). PTX-3 and Pb remained independently associated with ACS after adjustment for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and smoking and, separately, for age, diabetes, and renal function. Within the ACS group, PTX-3 was not significantly correlated with the Gensini score (ρ = 0.12, p = 0.41).
CONCLUSIONS: PTX-3 and whole-blood Pb, As, and Ni were markedly elevated in ACS, with PTX-3 and Pb showing the strongest and most robust associations. Prospective multicenter studies in patients with suspected ACS are needed to confirm these findings and establish whether these biomarkers add value beyond established clinical assessment.

Title: Outcomes of Intravitreal Anti-VEGF Therapy for Neovascular Age-Related Macular Degeneration in Kazakhstan.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD) is a leading cause of irreversible vision loss among older adults. Although randomised controlled trials have demonstrated the robust efficacy of intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy, real-world outcomes often differ markedly from trial findings. This study aimed to evaluate the anatomical and functional outcomes of anti-VEGF therapy in a clinical cohort of nAMD patients, including a subgroup that received adjunctive rescue photodynamic therapy (PDT) with verteporfin.
METHODS: This single-centre, retrospective observational cohort study included 568 patients (634 eyes) with nAMD treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections. Bevacizumab was used in 49% of eyes, ranibizumab in 44%, and aflibercept in 7%. Best recorded visual acuity (BRVA) and central retinal thickness (CRT) measured by optical coherence tomography (OCT) were recorded at baseline and at the final documented follow-up. Eyes with eccentric fixation were excluded from BRVA analysis but were retained for CRT analysis.
RESULTS: Mean patient age was 71.7 ± 8.8 years, and 67.6% of eyes were from female patients. The mean number of anti-VEGF injections was 5 ± 5.3 per eye; the mean follow-up duration was 11.5 months. Mean CRT decreased significantly from 347.3 ± 27.5 μm at baseline to 324.9 ± 28.8 μm at final follow-up (p < 0.001). Mean BRVA (logMAR) improved modestly from 0.98 ± 0.55 (Snellen ~20/190; ~35 ETDRS letters) to 0.93 ± 0.56 (Snellen ~20/175; ~37.5 ETDRS letters) (p < 0.001), with 67.9% of eyes demonstrating BRVA stability (change < 0.1 logMAR). Rescue PDT was administered in 10.3% of eyes.
CONCLUSIONS: In this real-world cohort, anti-VEGF therapy was associated with significant anatomical improvement, as measured by CRT reduction, while functional outcomes were characterised by visual stabilisation rather than substantial gains.

Title: Cross-Sectional and En Face Optical Coherence Tomography of Outer Retinal Morphological Changes Following Retinal Detachment Repair.
Abstract:
PURPOSE: To characterize short-term outer retinal changes in silicone oil-filled eyes after primary macula-involving rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) repair using en face and cross-sectional optical coherence tomography (OCT), and to examine the association of outer retinal features, including foveal ellipsoid zone rosettes (FEZRs), with 12-week postoperative best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA).
METHODS: This prospective observational study included 35 patients with primary macula-involving RRD who underwent pars plana vitrectomy with silicone oil tamponade with follow-up at 3, 6, and 12 weeks. BCVA, external limiting membrane (ELM)/ellipsoid zone (EZ) integrity, persistent subretinal fluid (PSRF), outer retinal folds (ORFs), and FEZR were evaluated.
RESULTS: Mean BCVA improved from 1.96 logMAR at baseline to 0.64 logMAR at 12 weeks, with progressive restoration of foveal ELM/EZ integrity. En face OCT showed high agreement with cross-sectional OCT for PSRF and ORF detection. PSRF was detected in 25.7%, ORFs in 5.7%, and FEZR in 22.9% of eyes; FEZR were more frequent in eyes with poor 12-week visual outcomes.
CONCLUSION: Cross-sectional and en face OCT provided complementary information on early outer retinal remodeling after RRD repair with silicone oil tamponade. Progressive ELM/EZ restoration was associated with better 12-week BCVA, whereas FEZR presence was associated with worse 12-week BCVA. These findings support further prospective evaluation of FEZR as a potential early negative prognostic imaging marker.

Title: Dietary Nitrate Supplementation and Exercise Performance in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Dietary nitrate supplementation improves exercise performance in recreationally active individuals, but efficacy in athletes remains debated. This meta-analysis evaluated the effects of dietary nitrate supplementation on six exercise performance and physiological/perceptual outcomes-peak power (PP), mean power (MP), maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max), heart rate (HR), blood lactate (LAC), and rating of perceived exertion (RPE)-in athletes across diverse sports and protocols. Methods: Forty-five randomized, placebo-controlled trials involving 659 healthy athletes (Tier 2 or higher) were included. Random-effects meta-analyses calculated pooled Hedges' g. Subgroup, sensitivity, and publication bias analyses were conducted. Results: No statistically significant overall effect was found for any of the six outcomes (all p > 0.05). In exploratory subgroup analyses, PP showed a positive effect in male-only studies (g = 0.29, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.56, p = 0.04), but the interaction with mixed-sex studies was not significant (p = 0.11). Beetroot and nitrate salts did not differ in VO2max. And trim-and-fill imputed five studies, reducing this estimate to zero. Subgroup analyses by sport type and exercise type (endurance, intermittent team sports, strength/power) revealed no significant differences. Conclusions: Dietary nitrate supplementation produced no statistically significant pooled ergogenic effects in athletes. Any potential benefit appears small and context-dependent, and the possible role of vascular endothelial function in high-performance athletes warrants further investigation. The absence of statistically significant effects should not be regarded as definitive evidence of no effect.

Title: Impact of Acute Hex-Bar Deadlift Exercise on Subsequent Cycling Performance and Skeletal Muscle Oxygenation.
Abstract: Post-activation performance enhancement (PAPE) strategies are used to improve power-dependent performance, but their impact on endurance exercise and skeletal muscle oxygenation is less clear. We tested the hypothesis that acute hex-bar deadlift (HBD) exercise would improve cycling performance and vastus lateralis muscle oxygen saturation (SmO2). Twenty-five healthy young adults (15 men, 10 women) completed moderate- and severe-intensity cycling after HBD or dynamic stretching (DYN) in a randomized crossover design. HBD consisted of 3 × 5 repetitions at 70-80% of one-repetition maximum, followed by ~8 min of recovery before cycling. Severe-intensity time-to-exhaustion was the primary outcome, while heart rate, arterial blood pressure, pulmonary oxygen uptake (V̇O2), and SmO2 were assessed as secondary physiological outcomes. Time-to-exhaustion was not different between HBD and DYN (394 ± 36 vs. 381 ± 34 s; p = 0.692). Resting and end-contraction V̇O2 and SmO2 were not different between conditions during moderate- or severe-intensity cycling. Similarly, SmO2 kinetics and area under the SmO2 curve remained unchanged. No condition-related differences in V̇O2 kinetics remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Contrary to our hypothesis, acute HBD exercise did not enhance vastus lateralis muscle oxygenation or severe-intensity cycling tolerance in healthy adults.

Title: Effects of a High-Sodium, Carbohydrate-Free Multi-Electrolyte Supplement on 15 km Treadmill Time-Trial Performance in Warm and Humid Conditions: A Randomized, Single-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Crossover Trial.
Abstract: Sodium ingestion may support fluid balance and endurance performance in the heat, but most previous studies have used sodium-loading, hyperhydration, or carbohydrate-electrolyte protocols. This study examined the effects of a high-sodium, carbohydrate-free multi-electrolyte supplement (HSES) on 15 km treadmill time-trial performance and physiological responses in trained male runners under warm-humid conditions. In a randomized, single-blind, counterbalanced crossover design, ten trained male runners (V̇O2max: 57.3 ± 8.1 mL·kg-1·min-1) completed two 15 km treadmill time trials at 26.7 °C and 60% relative humidity. Participants received HSES or a flavor-matched placebo (PLA) 30 min before exercise and every 15 min of running time. Repeated-measures analysis of cumulative completion time showed a significant main effect of condition (p = 0.034) and a significant condition × distance interaction (p = 0.023). Segment pace also showed a significant condition × segment interaction (p = 0.001); participants ran faster during HSES over the opening 0-5 km (p < 0.001), pace did not differ during 5-10 km (p = 0.091), and participants ran faster during PLA over the final 10-15 km (p = 0.032). Mean final 15 km completion time was 68.76 ± 12.28 min during HSES and 70.18 ± 13.33 min during PLA, a mean difference of 1.42 min (~2.0%). However, the direct paired comparison of final completion time did not reach statistical significance (HSES - PLA: -1.42 min; 95% CI, -3.60 to 0.77 min; p = 0.176; Cohen's dz = -0.46). No significant between-condition differences were observed in measured hydration-related, cardiovascular, metabolic, or perceptual outcomes. Estimated core temperature was higher during HSES at 15 km and 10 min post-exercise. Pacing differed between conditions during the 15 km time trial, with a faster opening 5 km during HSES and a faster final 5 km during PLA. Final 15 km completion time was approximately 2.0% faster during HSES, although the difference was not statistically significant.

Title: The Influence of Sleep and Autonomic Recovery on Performance in World-Class Swimmers at Major Competitions: The Qualifying Trials, World Championships, and Olympic Games.
Abstract: Sleep deprivation is one of the main risk factors for impaired performance in elite athletes, but the changes in sleep and autonomic regulation in response to competitions of varying levels within the same Olympic year remain unknown. In this prospective, longitudinal, observational study, we monitored parameters related to sleep quality and quantity, as well as heart rate variability and resting heart rate, in a cohort of eight Olympic swimmers (n = 8) during the World Championships in Doha, the qualifying trials, and the 2024 Paris Olympic Games, using the Oura Ring Gen3 under real-world conditions throughout the pre-competition, competition, and post-competition phases of each event. The Olympic Games were the only event where sleep efficiency fell below the commonly used reference threshold of 85% during the competition phase accompanied by a reduction in the total sleep score and an increase in resting heart rate. The Olympic setting was accompanied by temporary changes in sleep and autonomic markers, but no sleep parameter or autonomic marker showed a statistically significant association with intra-individual competitive performance, although the limited sample size constrains the power to detect such relationships.

Title: Preprocedural CT Radiomic Features of the Basal Ganglia Are Associated with Post-Thrombectomy Hyperdense Transformation: A LASSO-Based Logistic Regression Analysis.
Abstract: Purpose: To investigate whether radiomic characteristics of visually unremarkable basal ganglia on preprocedural non-contrast computed tomography (CT) are associated with subsequent post-thrombectomy hyperdense transformation (HT) in patients with acute ischemic stroke. Materials and Methods: This retrospective single-center study included a derivation cohort of 84 patients with preserved Alberta Stroke Programme Early CT Scores (ASPECTS ≥ 8), no visually appreciable basal ganglia abnormality, anterior circulation large-vessel occlusion, and complete reperfusion after mechanical thrombectomy between January 2022 and July 2023. An independent temporal validation cohort comprised 31 consecutive eligible patients treated between August and November 2023. The ipsilateral basal ganglia were manually segmented on preprocedural non-contrast CT, and radiomic features were extracted using LIFEx. Candidate features underwent interobserver reproducibility assessment and correlation filtering before least absolute shrinkage and selection operator logistic regression with 10-fold cross-validation. The final model was applied without modification to the temporal validation cohort. Nested cross-validation and learning-curve analysis were additionally performed to assess model-development optimism and stability. Results: The final model retained two texture features, Gray-Level Run Length Matrix Short Runs Emphasis and Gray-Level Size Zone Matrix Grey Level Variance. In the derivation cohort, the model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.760 (95% CI, 0.652-0.855), with 48.8% sensitivity, 95.3% specificity, and 72.6% accuracy. When applied without modification to the independent temporal validation cohort, the AUC was 0.677 (95% CI, 0.475-0.858), with 33.3% sensitivity, 93.8% specificity, and 64.5% accuracy. Nested cross-validation yielded a mean AUC of 0.673 ± 0.037, with variability in feature selection across resampling iterations. Learning-curve analysis showed an early plateau, with little improvement in cross-validated discrimination as the training sample increased within the evaluated range. Conclusions: Radiomic analysis of visually unremarkable basal ganglia on preprocedural non-contrast CT identified an exploratory two-feature imaging signature associated with subsequent post-thrombectomy HT. The model retained modest discriminatory ability in temporal validation, although internal resampling demonstrated model-development optimism and limited feature-selection stability. These findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and warrant further evaluation using larger datasets, alternative modeling approaches, and independent multicenter validation.

Title: Assessing Calcified Coronary Lesions to Guide Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: From Angiography to Intracoronary Imaging.
Abstract: Background/Objectives: Coronary artery calcification is a leading cause of stent failure and a strong predictor of adverse outcomes after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Accurate characterization of calcium burden, depth, and morphology is central to procedural planning, targeted treatment, and better outcomes. This review summarizes the contemporary armamentarium for imaging calcified coronary lesions, from coronary angiography and computed tomography to advanced intracoronary imaging, and how it facilitates treatment. Methods: We synthesized evidence from landmark studies, validated imaging scoring systems, registries, and current guideline and consensus documents addressing the assessment and imaging-guided treatment of coronary calcification. Results: Invasive angiography shows poor diagnostic accuracy for coronary calcium detection, characterization, and quantification. Coronary CT angiography noninvasively quantifies calcium (Agatston score and three-dimensional volume) and supports preprocedural planning, although it may overestimate calcium volume. Intravascular imaging by means of intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) and optical coherence tomography (OCT) effectively detects coronary calcium. Their use is associated with improved clinical outcomes compared with sole angiographic guidance. The addition of near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS-IVUS) characterizes lipids within calcified plaque and high-risk calcified nodules. OCT provides the highest spatial resolution and uniquely measures calcium thickness and longitudinal calcium length, while the utilization of artificial intelligence further enhances calcium assessment. Integration of these modalities into a morphology-based, imaging-guided approach facilitates calcium detection and modification and supports PCI optimization. Conclusions: Intravascular imaging, along with coronary CT angiography, has transformed the assessment of calcified coronary lesions. Combining their strengths enables precise, lesion-specific preparation; randomized trials show that intravascular imaging guidance improves outcomes in complex PCI, while CT-guided PCI planning is emerging as a complementary strategy whose clinical value is now being tested in randomized trials.

Title: Black-Blood Cinematic Rendering of the Pulmonary Vasculature: A Negative-Contrast Intraluminal Preset.
Abstract: Cinematic rendering (CR) is a physically based three-dimensional (3D) computed tomography (CT) visualization technique that has been applied chiefly to the external surface morphology of vascular structures. Intraluminal CR has previously been described for the cardiac chambers as black-blood cinematic rendering (BBCR), in which the opacity assigned to the contrast-enhanced blood pool is suppressed. Here, we describe the adaptation of that principle to the pulmonary vasculature as a negative-contrast intraluminal preset, in which the opacified blood pool is rendered semi-transparent so that the vessel lumen is displayed as a low-signal channel delineated by the enhancing vessel wall. We report the acquisition and rendering conditions under which the appearance was obtained in a single illustrative case performed for chest pain and showing no pulmonary vascular pathology, together with the rendering platform, base preset, and lighting configuration; the attenuation-band settings that define the appearance were tuned for the individual examination rather than applied as a fixed parameter set, were not recorded, and cannot be supplied as numerical values, so a stepwise construction procedure is given in their place. Intermediate rather than maximal compartment-specific opacification was required for the transfer function to separate lumen from wall; the case presented was acquired in an early pulmonary arterial phase, and a late split-bolus acquisition is an alternative route to the same condition that was not used here. In the case presented, the lumen of segmental and up to third-order subsegmental pulmonary arterial and venous branches was visually demonstrated on qualitative assessment by a single reader, and the preset remained stable when applied unchanged across the reconstructed 40-80% R-R window for four-dimensional display, which is a partial rather than a complete cardiac cycle reconstruction. Preset construction was less successful at the central pulmonary arteries and veins, where dense opacification and proximity to the cardiac blood pool reduced the contrast available to the transfer function. This is a single-case technical description. It demonstrates that the appearance can be produced under defined conditions and sets out the procedure by which it was constructed; it does not establish that the exact parameter values are recoverable or transferable, and it does not establish diagnostic performance, which will require prospective comparison against conventional reformats in adequately powered studies.

Title: Immune Network Dysregulation Predicts Adverse Outcomes in Infective Endocarditis.
Abstract: Infective endocarditis (IE) is characterized by systemic inflammation, yet the contribution of cytokine network dysregulation to clinical outcomes remains poorly understood. We aimed to evaluate cytokine co-expression patterns in IE and identify immune network signatures associated with in-hospital mortality and major complications. We conducted a prospective cohort study of adult patients hospitalized with IE at a quaternary public hospital in Brazil (2012-2024). Serum cytokines and chemokines were measured at one to three time points during hospitalization. Weighted topological overlap (wTO) and Co-expression Differential Network Analysis (CoDiNA) were used to characterize cytokine interactions in baseline. Logistic mixed-effects models assessed associations between individual cytokines and in-hospital mortality. Of 305 screened patients, 160 met inclusion criteria (41 deaths; in-hospital mortality 25.6%).
