However, randomized trials and meta-analyses have linked ESA use to increased thrombotic risk. Contemporary real-world data across diverse cancer populations and ESA formulations remain limited. We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX Research Network (from 1 January 2015 to 31 July 2024) evaluating adult patients with cancer-related anemia. Patients receiving ESAs were propensity score-matched 1:1 with patients not receiving ESAs based on demographics, cancer type, and comorbidities. Individuals with previous thrombotic events or anticoagulant use were excluded. Outcomes included incident deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), new anticoagulant use, and 1-year survival. Risk differences, relative risks, and Kaplan-Meier survival analyses were performed. After matching, 1606 patients were included in each cohort, with prostate, breast, bladder, colon, and kidney cancers being the predominant cancer. There was no significant difference in DVT (1.5% vs 2.1%; P = .19) or PE (0.75% vs 1.1%; P = .27) between ESA and non-ESA groups. New anticoagulant use was significantly lower in patients treated with ESAs (6.3% vs 10.2%; risk ratio, 0.52; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.49-0.78; P < .001). One-year survival was higher in the ESA cohort (73% vs 69%; hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.72-0.94; P = .004). In this large real-world cohort, ESA use was not associated with increased short-term thrombotic risk and was associated with lower anticoagulant use and improved 1-year survival. These findings suggest that guideline-concordant ESA use may be safe in selected patients with cancer-related anemia.

Title: Acute Effects of Inspiratory Muscle Training with Different Loads on Peripheral Muscle Oxygenation Kinetics and Autonomic Response in Patients with COPD: A Protocol for a Randomized Crossover Study.
Journal: International journal of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) leads to inspiratory muscle weakness, which may contribute to an altered cardiovascular response during the respiratory cycle. In this context, inspiratory muscle training (IMT) emerges as one of the available tools for the treatment and monitoring of patients with respiratory muscle dysfunction.
METHODS: This is a randomized crossover study, with blinding of both the evaluator and the researcher responsible for statistical analysis. The study will evaluate the acute effects of IMT on peripheral muscle metabolism and the autonomic response in 30 patients with COPD. The primary outcomes will be peripheral muscle oxygenation kinetics, assessed by near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), and autonomic response, assessed through heart rate variability (HRV). Participants will be randomly assigned to undergo three different intervention conditions at separate times, with a minimum interval of 48 hours between each session: IMT-S (Strength), aimed at improving inspiratory muscle strength; IMT-E (Endurance), focused on enhancing inspiratory muscle endurance; and Sham, consisting of a Sham IMT intervention. For statistical analysis, continuous variables will be presented as mean ± standard deviation, and data normality will be assessed using histograms and the Shapiro-Wilk test. All analyses will follow the intention-to-treat principle. In cases of missing data due to dropouts or absence in crossover sessions, participants with incomplete data will be retained in the analysis, assuming that data are missing at random. Between-intervention differences will be analyzed using mixed linear models with Bonferroni adjustment for multiple comparisons. The level of statistical significance will be set at 0.05.
CONCLUSION: This study may help to better understand the effects of IMT performed at different loads on peripheral muscle oxygenation behavior, as well on the autonomic response in patients with COPD. These findings may improve the understanding of the physiological impacts of this therapy and support its application in pulmonary rehabilitation programs.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinical Trial Registry NCT06827379.

Title: Impact of motor guided imagery therapy on stroke patients with pain symptoms: a three-level meta-analysis and systematic review of randomized controlled trials.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Post-stroke pain is a common and intractable complication that hinders neurorehabilitation progress. Motor Guided Imagery (MGI), an emerging rehabilitation technique based on brain-computer interaction principles, has shown potential in relieving post-stroke pain, yet high-quality evidence on its multi-dimensional efficacy remains insufficient. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the effects of MGI on pain, sensorimotor function, sleep quality, life status, and psychological mood in stroke patients using a three-level meta-analysis.
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to quantitatively assess the therapeutic effects of Motor Guided Imagery for stroke-related pain and explore potential intervention moderators using a three-level meta-analysis framework.
METHODS: Eight Chinese and English databases were searched from inception to June 29, 2025, to collect randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of MGI for stroke patients with pain. A three-level random-effects model was adopted to pool Hedges' g effect sizes, accompanied by heterogeneity testing, moderator analysis, influence analysis, and publication bias assessment. Influence-based outlier detection was implemented; analyses retaining all effect-size observations were treated as the primary main analysis, while outlier-removed analyses were reported only as supplementary sensitivity checks.
RESULTS: Motor-guided imagery training significantly relieved pain (g = -0.524, 95% CI -0.779 to -0.269, p = 0.0006; negative Hedges' g indicates clinical improvement for this outcome) and improved sleep quality (g = -1.658, 95% CI -2.115 to -1.201, p < 0.001; negative Hedges' g indicates clinical improvement for this outcome) in stroke patients. Meanwhile, it significantly enhanced motor function (g = 1.395, 95% CI 0.963 to 1.826, p < 0.001), life status (g = 1.757, 95% CI 0.966 to 2.549, p = 0.0012), and psychological-emotional status (g = 1.729, 95% CI 1.045 to 2.413, p = 0.0002); positive Hedges' g indicates clinical improvement for the latter three outcomes. Moderator analysis indicated that acute-phase intervention (≤4 weeks) and high-frequency regimens (>5 sessions/week) tended to produce better analgesic effects, while age, gender, single-session duration, and pain location had no significant moderating effects.
CONCLUSION: MGI may produce beneficial rehabilitation effects that can alleviate post-stroke pain and synergistically improve motor function, sleep, daily-living ability, and psychological state of stroke patients. Exploratory subgroup trends indicated potentially larger effects for early implementation within the acute phase and high-frequency short-duration regimens. However, these observations should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating clues given non-significant overall moderator tests. Further high-quality research is required to confirm these findings.
REGISTRATION: The systematic review protocol was retrospectively registered with PROSPERO under registration ID CRD420261278812, after literature search and full-text screening had been completed.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261278812; identifier: CRD420261278812.

Title: Left atrial and left ventricular radiation exposure predict long-term cardiovascular events after breast cancer radiotherapy.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adjuvant breast cancer (BC) radiotherapy (RT) improves survival and local control, but cardiovascular (CV) toxicity remains a concern.
AIM: This retrospective study investigated the association between RT doses to cardiac substructures and CV toxicity 15 years after BC RT.
METHODS: Women with unilateral BC diagnosed between 2007 and 2008, treated with RT at [Anonymous] were retrospectively included. Patients with major adverse cardiac events (MACE) were matched to controls by CV risk factors, anthracycline and anti-HER2 therapy. Cardiac substructures were delineated on simulation scans, and multivariable logistic regression was performed to assess associations between RT doses to these substructures and MACE or other CV events.
RESULTS: After a median follow-up of 16.5 years (IQR 16.1-17.1), and inclusion of 878 patients, 173 patients experienced MACE and were matched to 167 controls. All patients underwent adjuvant RT using 3-dimensional conformal RT to a total dose of 50 Gy in 25 fractions, with or without a boost to the tumor bed. New individual cardiac toxicities included: atrial fibrillation (AF) 98/878 (11.16%), heart failure (HF) 82/878 (9.34%), coronary artery disease (CAD) 46/878 (5.24%) and valvular disease 180/878 (20.50%). Mean heart doses were 6.62 ± 5.20Gy (MACE) and 5.76 ± 4.96Gy (controls) (p = 0.0916). Compared with controls, patients with MACE had significantly higher disease stage and more frequent histories of CAD, AF and HF. Maximum RT doses to the left atrium (LA) were associated with MACE, new-onset HF, AF and valvular disease, while mean RT dose to the left ventricle (LV) was associated with development of CAD (all p < 0.05).
CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates that patients treated with RT for BC may experience diverse CV toxicities during long-term follow-up. Higher doses to left-sided cardiac substructures, particularly the LA and LV, were associated with specific CV endpoints, while MHD was not associated with toxicity.

Title: Three-dimensional laparoscopic partial nephrectomy for hilar versus non-hilar tumors: outcomes from a large contemporary series.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The management of renal hilar tumors remains a technically demanding aspect of nephron-sparing surgery. Although robotic partial nephrectomy has been widely reported in this setting, evidence from large series of purely laparoscopic procedures performed with three-dimensional vision is still limited.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: We retrospectively evaluated 342 consecutive patients who underwent 3D laparoscopic partial nephrectomy between July 2022 and July 2025 at a high-volume tertiary center. Tumors were stratified as hilar (n = 55) or non-hilar (n = 287). The primary endpoint was warm ischemia time. Secondary endpoints included operative time, estimated blood loss, perioperative complications, need for postoperative ureteric stenting, renal function preservation, and trifecta achievement.
RESULTS: Median operative time was modestly longer in the hilar group (78 min vs 73 min, p = 0.04). Median warm ischemia time was also higher for hilar tumors (24 min vs 16 min, p <0.001) but consistently remained within the accepted threshold (<25 min). Estimated blood loss was comparable (270 ml vs 250 ml, p = 0.39). Overall complication rates were similar, though postoperative stent placement was more frequent in the hilar cohort (28% vs 7%, p <0.001). Median postoperative eGFR decline at 3 months was similar between groups. Trifecta achievement was 67.2% for hilar and 71.1% for non-hilar tumors (p = 0.27).
CONCLUSIONS: Three-dimensional laparoscopic partial nephrectomy for hilar tumors is associated with slightly longer operative and ischemia times and a higher need for postoperative stenting, but without an increase in major morbidity. In experienced hands, the functional and oncological outcomes were comparable between hilar and non-hilar tumors.

Title: Office-based transperineal laser ablation for benign prostatic hyperplasia: Functional outcomes and predictors of clinical improvement.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Transperineal laser ablation (TPLA) is an ultrasound-guided, office-based procedure for the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). This study evaluates short-term functional outcomes following TPLA and identifies predictors of clinical improvement.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: This cohort included men undergoing TPLA between January 1, 2025, and February 1, 2026, using a transperineal interstitial laser system (EchoLaser, Elesta SpA). Minimum follow-up was 6 months. Variables included age, body mass index (BMI), prostate-specific antigen (PSA), PSA density, testosterone, prostate volume, International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), peak urinary flow rate (Qmax), and post-void residual (PVR). Intraoperative variables included ablation time and energy delivered. Pre- and post- treatement differences were assessed using the Wilcoxon signed rank test. Spearman correlation analysis evaluated predictors of improvement.
RESULTS: Thirty-five of forty men met the inclusion criteria. Mean prostate volume was 71.6 cm3 (range 29.8-196). Mean IPSS improved from 23.5 to 10.6 (p <0.001). Qmax increased from 7.2 to 18.4 ml/s (p = 0.007). PVR decreased from 396.8 to 70.6 ml (p <0.001). Comorbidities included urinary tract infection or urosepsis history, hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, and anticoagulation use. Postoperative complications included three patients with urinary retention requiring catheterization and one patient with urosepsis requiring hospitalization. Greater improvement correlated with higher baseline IPSS and PVR (p <0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: Office-based TPLA produced significant short term functional improvement. Functional gains were comparable to those achieved with hospital based surgical interventions. Prospective, multicenter, randomized studies are warranted to further evaluate long term durability.

Title: Erratum: Nondipping Blood Pressure Pattern Is Associated with the Development of Myocardial Injury after Noncardiac Surgery: A Single-center Prospective Observational Study: Erratum.

Title: Associations of post-traumatic stress disorder and metabolic syndrome with accelerated brain aging in South African adults: A case-control study.
Abstract:
UNLABELLED: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and metabolic syndrome (MetS) are both associated with childhood trauma (CT) and accelerated brain aging. We examined the putative moderating effects of CT exposure on the associations of PTSD diagnosis and MetS status with brain aging in cases (n = 97) compared to trauma-exposed controls (n = 87). Brain age predictions were generated from T1-weighted magnetic resonance image scans using a pre-trained machine learning pipeline (brainageR). A measure of relative brain aging known as "predicted age difference" (PAD) was calculated by subtracting chronological age from the predicted brain age. Results showed that increased waist circumference was associated with a higher PAD, while CAPS-5 scores were associated with a lower PAD. MetS status was also associated with increased PAD in adults with lower CT exposure. The association between higher brain age difference scores and CT were more pronounced in participants with lower triglyceride levels. We found that increased waist circumference correlated with an increased PAD, independent of PTSD diagnosis. Future research should elucidate the possible mechanisms of accelerated brain aging and the protective factors that may slow its progression.
SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: Adults with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) frequently develop metabolic syndrome (MetS), and scientists have found that people with either condition may exhibit similar patterns of neurodegeneration in certain regions of the brain - a process known as brain aging. This study examined the extent to which PTSD, MetS, the PTSD-MetS comorbidity, and childhood trauma were associated with brain aging. While PTSD, MetS, and its interaction were not related to brain aging patterns, we identified risk factors for accelerated brain aging, including greater waist circumference, MetS among adults with lower childhood trauma, and lower triglycerides among those with greater childhood trauma. These results demonstrate that developmental, metabolic, and cardiovascular risk factors may also pose increased risks for accelerated brain aging in adulthood.

Title: The 'Upstairs-Downstairs' heart with complete main pulmonary artery agenesis and PDA-dependent pulmonary circulation: A rare structural intersection characterized by multi detector computed tomography.
Abstract: Superior-inferior ventricular arrangement is an exceedingly rare form of congenital cardiac malposition, representing fewer than 0.1% of all congenital heart diseases, and is almost invariably associated with complex intracardiac anomalies. We report a 3-year-old male who presented with persistent cyanosis, exertional dyspnea, and failure to thrive. Prospective ECG-gated CT angiography demonstrated situs solitus with levocardia. A superior-inferior ventricular arrangement was present, with the morphologic left ventricle positioned superior to the morphologic right ventricle. The great arteries were normally related, with a left-sided aortic arch. A large ventricular septal defect was identified. Pulmonary atresia was present, characterized by the absence of the right ventricular outflow tract, pulmonary valve, and main pulmonary artery. Native confluent branch pulmonary arteries were present and received pulmonary blood flow through a large patent ductus arteriosus supplying the left pulmonary artery, with additional small systemic-to-pulmonary collateral vessels. The morphologic right ventricle was dilated and hypertrophied, with associated enlargement of the right atrium. Pulmonary venous drainage was normal, and no abnormalities of the systemic venous drainage were identified. This case underscores the critical role of cardiac CT angiography in comprehensive anatomical delineation of rare and complex congenital cardiac malformations, with direct implications for surgical planning and prognostication.

Title: Why Sleep Matters in COPD: Cluster-Derived Sleep Phenotypes Reveal Distinct Physiological, Comorbidity and Survival Profiles.
Journal: International journal of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep disturbances are highly prevalent in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) but are not incorporated into current phenotypic classifications. We examined whether multidimensional sleep data identify clinically relevant patterns in COPD and whether these patterns are associated with all-cause mortality.
METHODS: In a clinical cohort of 205 patients with COPD, home-based sleep assessment was performed using the WatchPAT™ device. Fifteen complementary variables reflecting sleep duration and architecture, nocturnal oxygenation, sleep-disordered breathing, and daytime sleepiness were analysed using Partitioning Around Medoids clustering. The resulting phenotypes were characterised by pulmonary function, gas exchange, functional capacity, systemic biomarkers, and comorbidity burden. Longitudinal follow-up was available for 199 participants; survival was assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and Cox regression adjusted for age, sex, post-bronchodilator FEV1 and positive airway pressure (PAP) treatment.
RESULTS: Five distinct sleep phenotypes were identified: preserved sleep physiology (good sleepers, 20.5%), curtailed sleep duration (short sleepers, 33%), altered sleep architecture with REM suppression (light sleepers, 18.5%), predominant nocturnal hypoxaemia (hypoxic sleepers, 20%), and severe sleep-disordered breathing (apnoeic sleepers, 8%). Despite similar airflow limitation and COPD symptom burden, phenotypes differed in gas exchange, functional capacity, systemic inflammation, and cardiometabolic comorbidities. During a median follow-up of 4.2 years, 56 participants (28.1%) died. Compared with good sleepers, hypoxic sleepers had a higher hazard of death after adjustment for age, sex, and FEV1 (HR 2.80, 95% CI 1.05-7.44). Following adjustment for PAP treatment, a higher mortality hazard was also observed among untreated apnoeic sleepers (HR 6.16, 95% CI 1.56-24.38).
CONCLUSION: Multidimensional sleep phenotyping identified clinically distinct clusters of patients with COPD beyond conventional spirometric severity and apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI)-defined sleep-disordered breathing. These findings support sleep as a clinically relevant dimension of COPD heterogeneity, and warrant prospective validation of sleep-related traits and their clinical outcomes.

Title: Validity of Administrative ICD-10 Diagnosis Codes for Ventricular Arrhythmia and Cardiac Arrest in a French University Hospital.
Abstract:
PURPOSE: Drug-induced QT interval prolongation increases the risk of ventricular arrhythmias and cardiac arrest. Assessing these outcomes in electronic health databases and evaluating their association with drug exposure requires prior validation of administrative diagnostic codes. This study aimed to evaluate the positive predictive value (PPV) of International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision (ICD-10) codes for ventricular arrhythmias and cardiac arrest in the French hospital discharge summary database (Programme de Médicalisation des Systèmes d'Information (PMSI)).
METHODS: In a retrospective validation study, we examined PMSI data recorded at Amiens University Medical Center (Amiens, France). Hospital stays between September 2022 and August 2025 with ICD-10 codes for cardiac arrest (I46.0, I46.9), ventricular tachycardia (I47.2), or ventricular fibrillation/flutter (I49.0) were identified. Events were confirmed by electronic medical record review. PPVs with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. The study design prevented the estimation of sensitivity, specificity, and negative predictive values. Sensitivity analyses were stratified by year, and by type of care unit. Exposure to QT-prolonging medications prior to events was also assessed.
RESULTS: In a population of 182 patients (median age: 66 years; 75% males; in-hospital mortality rate: 45%), PPVs [95% CI] for all diagnosis codes were high: 0.98 [0.95; 1.00] for cardiac arrest with successful resuscitation, 0.96 [0.79; 1.00] for unspecified cardiac arrest, 0.99 [0.94; 1.00] for ventricular tachycardia, and 0.93 [0.87; 0.97] for ventricular fibrillation/flutter. Sensitivity analyses yielded consistent results. Overall, 49.7% of patients had been exposed to ≥1 QT-prolonging medications prior to a validated event, and 26.5% to ≥2 of these medications concomitantly.
CONCLUSION: The high PPVs in PMSI data supports the use of the evaluated ICD-10 codes for outcome identification in pharmacoepidemiological studies of electronic health databases in general, and those investigating QT-prolonging medication use and the risk of serious cardiac events in particular.

Title: Hypertension, Deep Retinal Perfusion, and Concurrent Visual Acuity in Retinal Vein Occlusion: A Cross-Sectional OCTA Study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: To investigate the cross-sectional association between hypertension and OCTA-derived retinal microvascular characteristics and to assess whether deep capillary plexus perfusion area (DCP-PA) provides additional explanatory information for concurrent visual acuity in retinal vein occlusion (RVO).
METHODS: This retrospective secondary cross-sectional analysis included 88 RVO-affected eyes from 88 patients. Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) and swept-source OCTA were assessed at the same visit. Multivariable linear regression evaluated associations between hypertension and six OCTA outcomes after adjustment for age, sex, RVO subtype, and hyperlipidemia, with Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction. The association between DCP-PA and concurrent logMAR BCVA was assessed using a clinical-structural model including age, sex, RVO subtype, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and total retinal thickness (TRT), followed by an extended model incorporating DCP-PA.
RESULTS: Hypertension was associated with lower DCP-PA (β=-1.71; 95% CI, -2.85 to -0.57; FDR-adjusted P=0.011) and lower DCP vessel length density (β=-3.29; 95% CI, -5.48 to -1.09; FDR-adjusted P=0.011). Lower DCP-PA remained independently associated with worse concurrent visual acuity after adjustment for clinical factors and TRT (β=-0.12 per mm2; 95% CI, -0.16 to -0.08; P<0.001). Hyperlipidemia was also associated with worse visual acuity (β=0.34; 95% CI, 0.18 to 0.49; P<0.001). Adding DCP-PA increased adjusted R 2 from 0.40 to 0.59 and reduced AIC from 94.60 to 61.99 (partial F=38.54; P<0.001). No significant interaction was observed between DCP-PA and RVO subtype (P=0.353).
CONCLUSIONS: Hypertension was associated with reduced deep retinal perfusion in RVO. Lower DCP-PA was independently associated with worse concurrent visual acuity and provided additional explanatory information beyond clinical factors and retinal thickness. These cross-sectional findings do not establish causality or prospective prognostic value.

Title: Postdischarge Class-Complete Secondary Prevention Medication Nonadherence After Ischemic Stroke: Overall and Comorbidity-Specific Patterns.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate postdischarge class-complete secondary prevention medication nonadherence after ischemic stroke and identify overall and comorbidity-specific factors associated with 180-day nonadherence.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using prospectively collected follow-up data from a stroke registry, including consecutive patients hospitalized with acute ischemic stroke. Medication use was assessed at discharge, 90 days, and 180 days after discharge. Class-complete discontinuation-that is, discontinuation of at least one of the secondary prevention medication classes prescribed at discharge, including antiplatelet agents, anticoagulants, lipid-lowering medications, antihypertensive medications, and glucose-lowering medications-was the primary outcome. Any-use adherence, defined as continued use of at least one secondary prevention medication class, was used for comparison. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify factors associated with 180-day class-complete nonadherence, with subgroup analyses among patients with hypertension and diabetes mellitus.
RESULTS: A total of 2549 patients with ischemic stroke were included. At 180 days, 1408 patients (55.2%) had discontinued at least one prescribed secondary prevention medication class, whereas only 738 (29.0%) had discontinued all prescribed classes; 1141 (44.8%) continued every class prescribed at discharge. Class-complete adherence declined from 59.4% at 90 days to 44.8% at 180 days, whereas any-use adherence was 85.9% and 71.0%, respectively. Each additional discharge medication class was associated with higher odds of 180-day class-complete nonadherence in a prespecified multivariable model (adjusted odds ratio [OR], 1.50; 95% CI, 1.27-1.79). Cardioembolism (OR, 2.11; 95% CI, 1.37-3.26), dyslipidemia (OR, 1.50; 95% CI, 1.09-2.07), and large-artery atherosclerosis (OR, 1.24; 95% CI, 1.03-1.49) were also associated with nonadherence; hypertension was of borderline significance (OR, 1.23; 95% CI, 0.99-1.54; P = 0.067). In subgroup analyses, the association with number of discharge medication classes was similar across the hypertension and diabetes mellitus subgroups, with no evidence of effect modification (P for interaction = 0.32 and 0.67), whereas the association with large-artery atherosclerosis was stronger among patients with hypertension (OR, 1.37; 95% CI, 1.08-1.73) or diabetes mellitus (OR, 1.43; 95% CI, 1.10-1.87) than among those without (P for interaction = 0.036 and 0.009, respectively).
CONCLUSION: Class-complete medication nonadherence was common within 180 days after ischemic stroke discharge and often reflected partial discontinuation rather than complete cessation of secondary prevention therapy. Medication-class-specific follow-up may help identify incomplete regimen continuation and guide targeted support for patients with greater treatment complexity, atherosclerotic stroke mechanisms, or chronic vascular comorbidities.

Title: Source-Specific PM2.5 Exposure and Atrial Fibrillation Risk in U.S. Older Adults: A Nationwide Cohort Study.
Abstract: Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) is associated with an increased risk of atrial fibrillation (AF), but the effects of individual PM2.5 sources remain unclear. We evaluated the relationship between long-term exposure to source-specific PM2.5 and incident AF among 26.3 million U.S. Medicare beneficiaries from 2000 to 2019. We resolved PM2.5 sources using the Multilinear Engine model based on PM2.5 components data from monitoring stations. Annual ZIP code-level exposures were assigned using inverse-distance weighting of monitoring stations within a 100 km buffer. Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate AF risk per interquartile range (IQR) increase in source-specific PM2.5 concentrations, adjusting for demographic and socioeconomic factors and other environmental covariates. Over 171.6 million person-years of follow-up, 4.44 million incident AF cases were identified. Exposure to PM2.5 from vehicle emissions (HR 1.029, 95% CI 1.028-1.030), heavy oil and coal combustion (HR 1.048, 95% CI 1.046-1.050), secondary sulfate (HR 1.056, 95% CI 1.053-1.058), and secondary nitrate (HR 1.032, 95% CI 1.030-1.034) was significantly associated with higher AF risk. In contrast, biomass burning and soil and dust exhibited only modest associations, and secondary organic aerosols (SOA) showed no overall effect. Regional analyses revealed geographic heterogeneity: fossil-fuel-related sources drove AF risk in most regions, secondary sulfate and nitrate had the strongest effects in the southern U.S., and SOA was more strongly associated with AF in the West. These findings highlight the differential toxicity and regional heterogeneity of PM2.5 sources in AF risk and emphasize the need for targeted, region-specific air quality regulations focusing on traffic and industrial emissions to mitigate AF incidence in older adults.

Title: Prediction of acute mountain sickness from overnight pulse oximetry during ascent to Everest Base Camp: a field-based machine learning study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acute mountain sickness (AMS) affects a large proportion of individuals ascending to high altitude every year. While AMS is not life threatening, if left untreated it can progress to serious illness (e.g., high altitude cerebral oedema). Current assessment tools rely on subjective symptom reporting and do not enable prospective prediction. Objective, field-deployable methods for early risk stratification remain limited. This study evaluated whether physiological biomarkers derived from overnight pulse oximetry can predict subsequent AMS during ascent to Everest Base Camp (EBC).
METHODS: A field study was conducted in the Khumbu region of Nepal. Healthy lowlanders (n = 139-144 across datasets) underwent overnight pulse oximetry recordings at Namche Bazaar (3,440 m) and Dingboche-level (4,371-4,730 m). A total of 125 physiological features were extracted from continuous, overnight oxygen saturation (SpO2) and heart rate recordings. Supervised machine-learning models were trained to classify physician-diagnosed AMS at Lobuche (~4,940 m) using: 1) physiological biomarkers alone and 2) biomarkers combined with clinical and contextual metadata. Model performances were assessed using repeated stratified k-fold cross-validation, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) as the primary metric.
RESULTS: Biomarker-only models demonstrated consistent above-chance discrimination at both altitudes (mean AUC 0.74 at both Namche and Dingboche-level). At lower altitude, predictive performance was achieved using a small set of physiological features, and inclusion of metadata did not improve model performance. At higher altitude, combining biomarkers with contextual variables improved discrimination (AUC 0.84 ± 0.08; sensitivity 0.73 ± 0.23). Selected features were primarily related to nocturnal oxygenation burden, desaturation dynamics, and heart rate variability.
CONCLUSION: Overnight pulse oximetry captures physiological signals associated with subsequent AMS development prior to symptom onset. These findings support the feasibility of objective, non-invasive risk stratification during early ascent. Integration of wearable monitoring with computational modelling may provide a complementary tool to support preventative decision-making along high-altitude trekking routes.

Title: Weight loss and blood pressure lowering with GLP-1 receptor agonists and multi-hormone receptor modulators in overweight and obesity: a systematic review and meta-regression of phase 3 clinical trials.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Obesity and hypertension frequently coexist, and weight-reduction is recommended as a core strategy for blood pressure (BP) management in adults with overweight or obesity. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) and emerging multi-hormone receptor modulators (MHRMs) induce substantial weight loss alongside modest BP reductions. However, the extent to which weight-loss is associated with BP lowering across these therapies remains unclear.
METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of phase 3 randomized controlled trials evaluating GLP-1RAs and MHRMs in adults with overweight or obesity (PROSPERO: CRD420251146441). We searched Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from 1946 to December 2025. Risk of bias was assessed using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. Placebo-adjusted changes in body weight and BP at each trial's primary endpoint were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis with inverse-variance weighting. Meta-regression assessed the association between weight loss and BP reduction.
FINDINGS: Thirty-seven trials including 50,171 participants were analysed. Thirty-six trials had low risk of bias across all domains. Across all trials, 50% of participants were females, 16% had type 2 diabetes and 57% had hypertension. Median treatment duration was 68 weeks. Mean placebo-adjusted weight loss was -10.1% (95% CI -11.3 to -9.0) accompanied by a -4.9 mmHg (95% CI -5.5 to -4.3) reduction in systolic BP. Between-trial meta-regression showed that 76% of the variance in systolic BP reduction was explained by differences in weight loss (R2 = 0.76; P < 0.01), corresponding to a reduction of 0.37 mmHg (95% CI 0.28 to 0.45) per 1% change in body weight.
INTERPRETATION: Across phase 3 trials of GLP-1RAs and MHRMs, greater weight loss was strongly associated with larger reductions in BP, supporting pharmacological weight-loss therapies as an adjunct strategy for BP management in obesity.
FUNDING: None.

Title: Predictors and Factors Associated With Delayed Primary Cleft Surgery in Bangladesh.
Abstract: Background Delayed primary cleft surgery remains a major challenge in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where barriers to timely access coexist with medically necessary postponements. Understanding factors associated with delayed surgery and the relative contribution of presentation-related and medical reasons may help improve comprehensive cleft care. This study aimed to identify predictors of delayed primary cleft surgery, characterize the distribution of reasons for surgical delay, and evaluate factors associated with delayed presentation among patients treated in a comprehensive cleft care program in Bangladesh. Methods A retrospective cohort study was conducted at the National Institute of Burn and Plastic Surgery (NIBPS), Dhaka, Bangladesh. Medical records of patients undergoing primary cleft surgery between January 2016 and December 2020 were reviewed. Of 792 records screened, 424 met the eligibility criteria after exclusion of secondary or revision procedures, syndromic clefts, and incomplete records. Delayed primary surgery was operationally defined as primary cleft lip repair performed after 9 months of age or primary cleft palate repair performed after 18 months of age, according to predefined study criteria. Demographic and clinical variables were analyzed using univariate and multivariable binary logistic regression to identify factors associated with delayed primary surgery. A secondary multivariable analysis evaluated factors associated with operationally defined delayed presentation. Six prespecified predictor variables were included in the multivariable models. Results Among 424 patients, 132 (31.1%) underwent delayed primary cleft surgery. Operationally defined delayed presentation was the most frequently identified reason for delayed surgery, accounting for 70 (53.0%) delayed cases, followed by congenital heart disease (16.7%), anaemia (12.1%), and other causes (18.2%). In multivariable analysis, urban residence was independently associated with lower odds of delayed primary surgery compared with rural residence (adjusted OR 0.642, 95% CI 0.418-0.988; p=0.044), whereas congenital heart disease was associated with higher odds of delayed primary surgery (adjusted OR 2.720, 95% CI 1.424-5.197; p=0.002). For delayed presentation, congenital heart disease was independently associated with lower odds of delayed presentation (adjusted OR 0.205, 95% CI 0.048-0.876; p=0.032). Residence, gender, cleft phenotype, other congenital anomalies, and anaemia were not significantly associated with delayed presentation. Conclusion Nearly one-third of patients experienced delayed primary cleft surgery, with delayed presentation being the most frequent documented contributor. Rural residence and congenital heart disease were independently associated with delayed primary surgery, whereas residence was not independently associated with delayed presentation. Congenital heart disease was independently associated with lower odds of delayed presentation, a finding that should be interpreted cautiously. These findings highlight the need to distinguish potentially preventable access-related delays from medically indicated postponements when planning strategies to improve timely cleft care.

Title: High Prevalence and Limited Perinatal Prediction of Kidney Dysfunction in Adolescents Born Extremely Preterm.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Extremely preterm birth (< 28 weeks' gestation) increases chronic kidney disease (CKD) risk. However, among those born extremely preterm, the prevalence of abnormal kidney health during adolescence and its perinatal predictors remain poorly defined.
METHODS: Adolescents from the Extremely Low Gestational Age Newborn -Environmental influences on Child Health Outcomes (ELGAN-ECHO) cohort (14 US hospitals) were assessed for abnormal kidney health defined as ≥ 1 indicator-chronic kidney disease in children (CKiD) U25 estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) < 90 ml/min per 1.73 m2, blood pressure (BP) ≥ 120/80 mm Hg, or microalbuminuria > 30 mg/g.Five feature selection methods screened perinatal covariate predictors using a 60 to 40 training-test split. Multiple imputation addressed missing data in sensitivity analyses. Area under the curve (AUC) was the primary performance metric.
RESULTS: Of the 675 adolescents (mean age 18 years), 354 (52%) had a classifiable kidney health status, as follows: 188 with all 3 measurements and 166 with partial measurements showing ≥ 1 abnormality. The prevalence of abnormal kidney health was 66% among complete cases (125/188) and 82% among all determinate cases (291/354). In the full cohort, prevalence ranged from 43% to 91% (bounding estimates accounting for missing data). Individual measurements revealed 30.5% with reduced eGFR, 42% with elevated BP, and 9% with microalbuminuria. Across all methods, perinatal covariates achieved random test-set discrimination (AUC: 0.48-0.55) for abnormal kidney health prediction, compared with training set AUCs of 0.66-0.72.
CONCLUSION: Abnormal kidney health is highly prevalent after extremely preterm birth, underscoring the importance of protocolized longitudinal kidney health surveillance throughout childhood to enable early identification of CKD and elevated BP in children born extremely preterm. The perinatal factors we examined did not meaningfully predict kidney health abnormalities and variable importance did not translate to individual-level prediction in this cohort.

Title: Cardiometabolic diseases and prescription patterns in a Kuwait tertiary-care hospital: A retrospective cross-sectional chart review.
Journal: Journal of Taibah University Medical Sciences
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Tertiary-care data can provide critical insights into clinical demographics in Gulf Arab settings where these data remain limited, despite reflecting hospital-based frequencies rather than population-level prevalence. This study aimed to descriptively characterize cardiometabolic disease and medication frequencies in a tertiary-care cohort.
METHODS: This retrospective cross-sectional chart review included adult patients with ≥1 ICD-10-coded chronic cardiometabolic condition at Mubarak Hospital, Kuwait, between January 1, 2022, and December 31, 2024. Disease and medication frequencies were summarized by age group (<35 years, 35 to < 65 years, and ≥65 years) and sex. Univariate and multivariate associations were evaluated. Binomial regression models estimated adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), adjusting for age or sex, nationality, and smoking status, with further adjustment for ischemic heart disease (IHD) in selected models.
RESULTS: Among 501 patients (54.1% female; mean age 63.7 ± 14.6 years), the most frequent conditions were hypertension (77.8%), diabetes mellitus (58.5%), dyslipidemia (44.7%), and IHD (23.6%). Lipid-lowering medications (76.05%) and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors/angiotensin receptor blockers (59.5%) were the most common medications. Disease frequencies increased significantly with age. Compared with those aged 35 to <65 years, patients aged ≥65 years had higher adjusted prevalences of type 2 diabetes (aPR: 1.17, 95% CI: 1.00-1.35), hypertension (aPR: 1.18, 95% CI: 1.07-1.30), and IHD (aPR: 2.37, 95% CI: 1.68-3.35). Males had a significantly higher adjusted prevalence of chronic kidney disease (aPR: 1.96, 95% CI: 1.20-3.19) and IHD (aPR: 1.69, 95% CI: 1.22-2.32) than females. Notably, the higher prevalence of aspirin/clopidogrel antiplatelet therapy in males (aPR: 1.37, 95% CI: 1.11-1.69) persisted even after further adjustment for IHD (aPR: 1.30, 95% CI: 1.05-1.60).
CONCLUSION: Within this selected cohort, the cardiometabolic burden was high and varied by age and sex. Multicenter Gulf studies with patient-level adjustment are needed to characterize the disease burden and prescribing frequencies.

Title: Periodontal diseases and coronary artery disease: epidemiological links, pathogenic mechanisms and prospects for comorbidity integrated management.
Journal: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
Abstract: Periodontal disease (PD) and coronary artery disease (CAD) are two highly prevalent chronic systemic disorders with overlapping population risk profiles. Accumulating observational, cellular, and genetic studies have suggested potential positive correlations between PD severity, periodontal pathogen load, and CAD incidence, coronary lesion severity, and major adverse cardiac events, whereas Mendelian randomization analyses may not support a direct causal link between the two illnesses. Several synergistic pathogenic pathways may mediate their association: periodontal pathogens may translocate into peripheral circulation to colonize atherosclerotic plaques and exert potential direct vascular toxicity; sustained systemic low-grade inflammation may disrupt endothelial homeostasis; molecular mimicry may induce cross-autoimmune vascular impairment; shared susceptibility loci and conventional cardiovascular risk factors may jointly amplify vascular damage. Standard non-surgical periodontal therapy may reduce systemic inflammatory burden and improve endothelial function, and clinical and microbial periodontal markers may serve as non-invasive biomarkers for CAD risk stratification. This review synthesizes epidemiological evidence and multilayered pathogenic mechanisms and proposes bidirectional collaborative interventions and multidisciplinary cardiostomatological management frameworks for comorbid patients. Further large-scale randomized controlled trials and multi-ethnic genetic analyses are still required to clarify causal inference and potential long-term cardiovascular benefits of periodontal intervention.

Title: Development of an interpretable machine-learning model to predict insufficient functional improvement after aquatic therapy in stroke.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early identification of stroke survivors who are unlikely to achieve clinically meaningful motor improvement after aquatic therapy may help optimize rehabilitation prescriptions and support precision rehabilitation. This study aimed to develop and validate machine-learning models based on pretreatment Fugl-Meyer Assessment (FMA) data to predict insufficient motor improvement after aquatic therapy, to examine whether actual aquatic-therapy exposure improves prediction, and to identify the most important predictors.
METHODS: We conducted a single-center retrospective study of patients with stroke who received the routine aquatic rehabilitation programme in the Department of Rehabilitation Medicine between January 2022 and December 2025. The primary outcome was insufficient improvement in total Fugl-Meyer motor function at day 56 ± 7 days after the start of aquatic therapy, defined as Δ FMA <10 points; total FMA was recalculated as FMA upper-extremity plus lower-extremity scores. Temporal validation was used: cases from January 2022 to December 2024 formed the training set, and cases from January to December 2025 formed the temporal validation set. Two modeling strategies were developed. Model A included baseline clinical information and the initial rehabilitation and aquatic-therapy plans available after prescription and before the first aquatic session. Model B added actual treatment-execution parameters accumulated through day 14 (allowable landmark window, days 12-16). ExtraTrees, Random Forest, XGBoost, logistic regression and K-nearest neighbors were compared, and model performance was assessed with the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration, decision-curve analysis (DCA) and Shapley additive explanations (SHAP).
RESULTS: A total of 1,320 patients were included, of whom 409 had insufficient FMA improvement after aquatic therapy. The development set included 786 patients and 241 events, and the temporal validation set included 534 patients and 168 events. In the temporal validation set, Random Forest performed best for Model A, with an AUC of 0.818 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.777-0.853] and Brier score of 0.172 (95% CI 0.160-0.186). At the frozen sensitivity-prioritized threshold of 0.408, Model A had an accuracy of 0.700, sensitivity of 0.857, specificity of 0.628, positive predictive value of 0.514, negative predictive value of 0.906 and F1 score of 0.643. Random Forest also performed best for Model B, with an AUC of 0.814 (95% CI 0.774-0.850) and Brier score of 0.174 (95% CI 0.163-0.186). The paired change in AUC was -0.004 (95% CI -0.022 to 0.014). Model A SHAP analysis highlighted planned aquatic-course duration, planned weekly aquatic frequency, baseline FMA-LE, baseline upper-extremity FMA and time from stroke onset to rehabilitation.
CONCLUSIONS: The interpretable Model A used routine clinical data and initial rehabilitation prescriptions available before the first aquatic session and was evaluated in a later cohort from the same center. Model B analysis illustrates how risk could be updated at day 14 once genuine execution records become available. These analyses do not show that model-guided treatment adjustment improves motor recovery; external validation and prospective clinical-impact evaluation are required before clinical use.

Title: Postischemic endothelial immune reprogramming in stroke.
Abstract: Large-vessel recanalization is essential in acute ischemic stroke, but it does not guarantee microvascular reperfusion. Endothelial responses may contribute to persistent tissue hypoperfusion through leukocyte trafficking and immunothrombosis. Many of these responses may begin during ischemia and may continue or intensify when blood flow returns. We therefore use postischemic or ischemia/reperfusion-associated terminology unless experiments isolate the contribution of reperfusion. We propose that endothelial immune reprogramming requires a coordinated molecular program, localization to a defined vascular segment and time, and a corresponding change in immune-regulatory function. An isolated increase in an adhesion molecule or circulating biomarker indicates activation or injury but cannot identify such a state. Barrier/stress, adhesive/chemotactic, and prothrombotic responses overlap. Experimental studies implicate endothelial signaling, leukocyte arrest, and platelet interactions with neutrophil extracellular traps, but have not established a common sequence of endothelial states. Human evidence comes mainly from circulating biomarkers, thrombectomy thrombi, post-mortem tissue, and perfusion imaging. The available findings have yet to link a defined cerebral endothelial state to downstream perfusion and clinical outcome in the same patients. Prospective studies should combine serial vascular biomarkers, repeated perfusion imaging, and longitudinal follow-up, with endothelial-enriched molecular profiling when tissue is available. Therapeutic studies should test whether modifying a reversible endothelial program relieves no-reflow while preserving later immune resolution and vascular repair. These approaches remain investigational.

Title: Artificial intelligence-enabled deep clinical phenotyping in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: from patient subtypes to precision care.
Abstract: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a clinical syndrome defined by shared manifestations but produced by diverse combinations of cardiometabolic, vascular, inflammatory, renal, pulmonary, atrial, skeletal-muscle, and aging-related mechanisms. This heterogeneity limits the value of classifications based only on left ventricular ejection fraction and helps explain why many mechanistically plausible interventions have produced neutral average results. Deep phenotyping can move the field from descriptive heterogeneity toward biologically coherent and clinically actionable subtypes by integrating clinical trajectories, advanced imaging, exercise and invasive hemodynamics, circulating biomarkers, multiomics, and digital physiology. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers methods to combine these high-dimensional data, but statistical clusters should not be equated with disease endotypes. A useful subtype must be reproducible across cohorts, anchored to plausible biology, associated with a distinct clinical course, and able to improve diagnosis, therapeutic selection, or clinical-trial design. This Review examines the translational continuum from experimental HFpEF models to human patient subtypes, summarizes the main deep-phenotyping domains and AI approaches, and proposes seven clinically interpretable subtype families: cardiometabolic-inflammatory, hypertensive-vascular aging, atrial myopathy, pulmonary vascular-right ventricular, cardiorenal-congestive, peripheral-frailty, and specific etiologic phenocopies. Current evidence supports a layered treatment strategy in which broadly effective therapies, particularly sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, are combined with phenotype-directed management of obesity, diabetes, mineralocorticoid receptor activation, atrial fibrillation, congestion, pulmonary vascular disease, and physical deconditioning. The central next step is prospective validation of dynamic subtype assignments in external populations and phenotype-enriched trials. Phenogroup labels should therefore be regarded as pragmatic, transitional proxies for dominant mechanisms when those mechanisms cannot yet be measured directly at the individual-patient level; their value lies in improving decisions while the field moves toward fully individualized mechanism-based treatment. Deep phenotyping will be clinically valuable only when it changes a decision and improves an outcome, rather than merely increasing descriptive complexity.

Title: Anticoagulants beyond coagulation: repurposing heparin to mitigate immunothrombosis and inflammatory cascades in sepsis.
Abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening syndrome caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, in which inflammation, coagulation, endothelial injury, and immune dysfunction interact to drive organ failure and death. Accumulating evidence identifies immunothrombosis as a central mechanism in this process, linking neutrophil extracellular traps, platelet activation, tissue factor expression, circulating histones, and glycocalyx degradation to microvascular collapse and multiple organ dysfunction. Although heparin has traditionally been used as an anticoagulant, its highly sulfated structure also permits interactions that are independent of antithrombin. In addition to inhibiting thrombin generation, heparin can neutralize extracellular histones, interfere with HMGB1- and lipopolysaccharide-related inflammatory signaling, inhibit heparanase, preserve endothelial glycocalyx integrity, and modulate leukocyte trafficking through selectin-related pathways. Most of these non-anticoagulant actions have been demonstrated in cell systems, animal models, human endotoxemia, or diseases other than sepsis, and should therefore be read as biological plausibility rather than as an established clinical effect. The clinical literature addresses three questions that should not be conflated: routine venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in critically ill patients, anticoagulation directed at sepsis-induced coagulopathy or disseminated intravascular coagulation, and experimental immunomodulatory repurposing. The most recent meta-analysis restricted to randomized trials found no significant mortality reduction with heparin across three trials and 426 patients (risk ratio 0.86, 95% confidence interval 0.60-1.24), and the disseminated intravascular coagulation subgroup was also inconclusive. Favorable associations reported in retrospective sepsis-induced coagulopathy cohorts justify prospective phenotype-enriched trials but do not identify established responders. This review summarizes the pathophysiological rationale, mechanistic basis, current clinical evidence, and major safety considerations of heparin use in sepsis, and highlights future directions including precision phenotyping, biomarker-guided therapy, and non-anticoagulant heparin derivatives. At present no heparin preparation, salt, dose, or biomarker threshold is validated for sepsis-specific immunomodulation.

Title: The Role of Comorbidities in Predicting 12-Month Survival in Patients with Liver Cirrhosis: A Study from Zahedan, Iran.
Journal: Middle East journal of digestive diseases
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Liver cirrhosis is a progressive disease characterized by the replacement of healthy liver tissue with scar tissue, leading to impaired liver function. Early diagnosis and management play a crucial role in improving patient outcomes. Comorbidities, including diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia, are known to influence the prognosis of cirrhosis. This study aimed to assess the relationship between comorbid diseases and the 12-month survival of patients with liver cirrhosis in Zahedan, Iran.
METHODS: A retrospective cohort of patients with cirrhosis was followed for 12 months. Laboratory indices, including blood glucose, lipid profile, and blood pressure, were monitored. Survival analysis was performed to evaluate the impact of comorbidities on patient survival using statistical methods such as Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression analysis.
RESULTS: Abnormal blood glucose levels, high blood pressure, and dyslipidemia significantly reduced the 12-month survival of patients with cirrhosis. Despite treatment with lipid-lowering medications, lipid disturbances remained a key factor in the survival prognosis. Additionally, factors like body mass index and smoking habits were also identified as influential but often overlooked in clinical practice.
CONCLUSION: This study underscores the importance of managing comorbidities in patients with cirrhosis to improve survival outcomes. The findings suggest that integrated care addressing both cirrhosis and its associated comorbidities can enhance patient prognosis. Further research is necessary to examine additional factors, such as physical activity, diet, and daily stress levels, which may also affect survival rates.

Title: Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome: a review of diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.
Abstract: The diagnosis and treatment of neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome (nTOS) remain challenging. Although consensus-based clinical frameworks exist, they lack robust externa validation. This study conducts a review of nTOS publications in the PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science databases, with a search cutoff date of December 2025. Current evidence suggests that the incidence of nTOS may be underestimated. Diagnosis should be based on a comprehensive evaluation, including medical history, systematic physical examination, ancillary examinations, diagnostic muscle block, and exclusion of other possible diseases. Treatment should be carried out in a phased manner. For mild cases, nonsurgical treatment is preferred. For patients who experience progressive neurological dysfunction, muscle atrophy, or failure of conservative treatment, timely surgery should be considered. Surgical decompression mainly involves the supraclavicular or axillary approaches. Surgical techniques include first rib resection, rib-sparing scalenectomy, pectoralis minor release, cervical rib resection. However, the optimal treatment remains controversial due to the limited availability of high-quality evidence. Future research should focus on elucidating the pathophysiology of nTOS, improving diagnostic accuracy through technological innovation, and optimizing treatment protocols through prospective multicenter studies.

Title: Lion Hearts: applying implementation mapping to plan the delivery of a family-based physical activity intervention in community CrossFit affiliates.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Community-based physical activity interventions face challenges in adoption, implementation, and sustainability. Lion Hearts is a family-based physical activity intervention designed to promote cardiovascular health among mothers and children aged 3-6 years. This study applied Implementation Mapping during intervention development to identify implementation determinants and develop stakeholder-informed strategies for subsequent pilot testing.
METHODS: The five iterative tasks of Implementation Mapping were applied through a co-design process with seven CrossFit affiliate owner-coaches: (1) conducting an implementation needs and assets assessment and identifying adopters and implementers; (2) specifying implementation outcomes, performance objectives, determinants, and change objectives; (3) selecting theoretical change methods and implementation strategies; (4) producing implementation protocols and materials; and (5) developing a prospective implementation-evaluation plan. Two 60-min co-design sessions were conducted approximately eight weeks apart. The first elicited barriers and facilitators to adoption and delivery within affiliate settings. Audio recordings were transcribed verbatim, and three researchers reviewed and coded both transcripts using structured matrices, supplemented by facilitator notes. Findings were synthesized using rapid qualitative analysis and integrated with behavioral theory and implementation science frameworks to identify implementation determinants and develop implementation strategies and materials. This study applied the five tasks of Implementation Mapping to identify implementation determinants and develop stakeholder-informed strategies, delivery supports, and a prospective evaluation plan for subsequent pilot testing.
RESULTS: Stakeholders identified implementation determinants related to coach knowledge and self-efficacy, participant engagement and competing demands, class structure and flow, scheduling, staffing, equipment availability, and compatibility with affiliate workflows. These findings informed implementation strategies and delivery supports targeting affiliate owners and coaches, including coach training resources, structured session templates, class-flow guidance, and fidelity-monitoring tools. Performance objectives and an implementation logic model were developed to specify hypothesized pathways linking determinants and strategies to prospective implementation outcomes. An evaluation plan was developed to assess reach, adoption, feasibility, acceptability, fidelity, and maintenance during subsequent pilot implementation.
CONCLUSION: Implementation Mapping and stakeholder co-design produced a theory-informed, contextually responsive implementation package for Lion Hearts. Although implementation outcomes have not yet been evaluated, the resulting strategies, materials, and prospective evaluation plan are positioned for testing and refinement in community fitness settings.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07147387.

Title: Left atrial appendage morphology and hemodynamics: potential new markers for individualized thromboembolic risk assessment in atrial fibrillation.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Traditional CHA₂DS₂-VASc scoring has well-recognized limitations in thromboembolic risk assessment for atrial fibrillation (AF), particularly in low-score patients who nevertheless thrombose, high-score event-free individuals, cancer patients, and post-ablation cohorts. The left atrial appendage (LAA) is the source of 98% of thrombi in non-valvular AF and exhibits marked inter-individual morphological and hemodynamic variability that traditional scores completely ignore.
AIMS: This narrative review critically evaluates current evidence on LAA morphology, hemodynamics, computational fluid dynamics/fluid-structure interaction (CFD/FSI) studies, and digital twin technology, and proposes a mechanism-driven, individualized risk assessment framework for AF-related thromboembolism.
METHODS: A literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE and Web of Science (1990-May 2026) using combinations of keywords related to LAA morphology, hemodynamics, AF, and thromboembolism. Priority was given to landmark original studies, high-quality observational studies with multivariable adjustment, meta-analyses, and contemporary CFD/digital twin studies. A narrative synthesis was adopted owing to heterogeneity in study designs and outcomes.
RESULTS: LAA morphological subtypes are associated with long-term stroke risk, with chicken-wing being protective (OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.05-0.91) and cauliflower carrying the highest risk (OR 8.02, 95% CI 0.92-27.86). However, risk is highly context-dependent, with chicken-wing unexpectedly increasing peri-ablation thromboembolic risk (OR 7.2, 95% CI 1.35-38.33) and windsock morphology independently predicting post-ablation AF recurrence (OR 2.72, 95% CI 1.21-6.12). Importantly, traditional morphological classification does not correlate directly with blood stasis (p = 0.365), whereas quantitative geometric parameters such as trabecular number, normalized stroke volume, and ostial area are far more sensitive predictors (R² = 74%). Digital twins integrating multimodal clinical, morphological, and hemodynamic data identify a high-risk phenogroup with a 70% thrombus history rate.
CONCLUSION: Based on these findings, we propose a practical two-tier assessment framework combining basic morphological classification with multimodal refined evaluation (digital twin) for intermediate-/high-risk or clinically challenging cases. This framework represents a paradigm shift from static clinical scores toward mechanism-driven, individualized risk management. Prospective validation of this approach is now warranted.

Title: Specific interventions as part of a quality improvement collaborative enhance care for ischemic stroke patients.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Adherence to guidelines for stroke care varies, despite evidence that managing fever, glycemia (sugar), and conducting swallowing screening (FeSS) reduces mortality and disability. We established a quality improvement collaborative to improve care processes for ischemic stroke, with a focus on these three recommendations. We then added two additional care process activities: screening for activities of daily living (ADL) and depression, collectively defined as FeSS+.
METHODS: In this multicenter intervention study (n = 24), we retrospectively analyzed 30 consecutive patient records per center of ischemic stroke patients in 2019, pre-intervention (measurement period 1 [MP1]), and in 2022, post-intervention (measurement period 2 [MP2]). All hospitals received feedback on their MP1 performance, and an optional e-learning tool on FeSS+ was also offered. We compared adherence between MP1 and MP2 and assessed the impact of the e-learning tool.
RESULTS: Data were collected from 580 patients during MP1 and 588 patients during MP2. E-learning tools were delivered to teams at 18 hospitals (75%). Adherence improved for temperature measurement (18 to 25%, p = 0.004) and swallowing screening (36 to 59%, p < 0.001). No significant changes were observed for glycemia, ADL, or depression screening. Improvements in adherence to glycemia management, swallowing screening, and depression screening were observed only among hospitals that disseminated the e-learning tool (p = 0.01, <0.001, <0.001, respectively). Temperature measurement improved more in hospitals without e-learning (OR 2.62 vs. 1.27; p = 0.03).
DISCUSSION: We observed improvements in measuring temperature and swallowing screening after receiving feedback. The dissemination of the e-learning tool was associated with increased adherence to glycemic measurement, swallowing screening, and depression screening, underscoring the role of specific interventions. However, overall adherence remained low, highlighting the need for continued quality improvement.
Publication Types: Journal Article; Multicenter Study; Observational Study

Title: Complement and immunoglobulin profiles in ANCA-associated vasculitis with renal involvement: a serotype-stratified analysis of disease activity and renal outcomes.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) is characterized by pauci-immune small-vessel inflammation driven predominantly by neutrophil activation, in contrast to immune-complex-mediated glomerulopathies in which complement consumption tracks disease activity and renal injury severity. Serum C3 at diagnosis has repeatedly been associated with renal and patient survival in AAV, yet it remains unresolved whether complement fractions reflect the extent of renal injury in a dose-dependent manner, as they do in lupus nephritis, and how complement relates to immunoglobulin class profiles across ANCA serotypes.
METHODS: This retrospective single-center cohort study included 73 patients with AAV (PR3-ANCA, n = 39; MPO-ANCA, n = 34) who had complete complement and immunoglobulin data at admission and at least 6 months of follow-up at a tertiary nephrology center. Serum C3, C4, IgG, IgA, and IgM were measured at baseline before the initiation of immunosuppressive treatment; no sample was obtained after plasma exchange had begun. Patients were stratified by ANCA serotype and chronic kidney disease (CKD) severity. Associations with disease activity, inflammatory indices, and 6-month outcomes were explored using non-parametric comparisons, Spearman correlations, false discovery rate (FDR) correction, and sensitivity analyses.
RESULTS: C3 and C4 lay within the reference interval in 97.3% and 86.3% of patients, respectively, and showed no gradient across CKD severity groups (C3 p = 0.453; C4 p = 0.550), whereas the inflammatory indices C-NLR and PLR differed across those groups. IgA was nominally higher in patients with MPO-ANCA than in those with PR3-ANCA (2.60 [1.92-2.88] vs. 2.11 [1.78-2.30] g/L, p = 0.011) but did not retain significance after FDR adjustment across the five immune parameters (q = 0.055), and all values lay within the reference interval. IgG correlated with ESR (ρ = +0.40, p < 0.001) and ΔeGFR at 6 months (ρ = +0.26, p = 0.037). Serum C4 was higher in the eight patients who did not achieve clinical remission (0.35 [0.28-0.44] vs. 0.28 [0.20-0.33] g/L, nominal p = 0.037; FDR q = 0.184; AUC 0.729, 95% bootstrap CI 0.473-0.953, an interval that includes 0.5). C3 correlated inversely with neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) (ρ = -0.24, p = 0.043).
CONCLUSIONS: Frank complement consumption was uncommon in this cohort, and neither C3 nor C4 graded renal injury severity, consistent with pauci-immune pathogenesis and in contrast to lupus nephritis. These data do not conflict with published cohorts in which relatively lower C3 predicted adverse renal outcomes; rather, they suggest that the prognostic signal resides in variation within the reference interval rather than in measurable consumption proportional to glomerular injury. The serotype difference in IgA and the association between C4 and failure to achieve remission are exploratory observations that did not withstand correction for multiple comparisons. Because induction-regimen coding was sparse and heterogeneous, no treatment-adjusted IgA model was retained. The C4 association was based on only eight non-remission events and, notably, ran in the opposite direction to a complement-consumption interpretation; it requires confirmation in larger, prospective cohorts.

Title: Mirror therapy for upper limb motor recovery after stroke: a meta-analysis.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To systematically evaluate the rehabilitation effect of mirror therapy (MT) on upper limb motor function in stroke patients, thereby providing evidence-based support for clinical rehabilitation decision-making.
METHODS: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) investigating MT for upper limb dysfunction after stroke were retrieved from the PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and EMBASE databases. The risk of bias in the included studies was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool 2.0 (RoB 2.0). A meta-analysis was performed, and the grade of evidence was determined using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) system.
RESULTS: A total of 21 RCTs were ultimately included. The meta-analysis showed that MT significantly improved the total score of the Fugl-Meyer Assessment Upper Extremity (FMA-UE) in stroke patients (Mean Difference [MD] = 5.45, 95% Confidence Interval [95% CI]: 3.50-7.41, p < 0.001). Hand function showed a statistically significant but clinically modest improvement (MD = 1.16, 95% CI: 0.03-2.29, p = 0.04); however, sensitivity analysis indicated that this statistical significance was not robust and depended on a small number of high-weight studies. A positive trend toward improvement was observed for shoulder-elbow-forearm function (MD = 1.79, 95% CI: -0.02 to 3.60, p = 0.05). However, no statistically significant improvement was found for wrist joint function (MD = 0.65, 95% CI: -0.17 to 1.47, p = 0.12). Heterogeneity was low across outcomes. No clear evidence of publication bias was detected; however, the number of studies was small for some outcomes, limiting the power of funnel plots and Egger's test. The overall quality of evidence was moderate to low.
CONCLUSION: MT may improve global upper limb motor function in stroke patients, with a more modest and less robust effect on hand function. The statistical significance of the hand-function finding depended on a small number of high-weight studies, and the evidence for hand function is of low quality; the overall evidence is low-to-moderate. Therefore, these findings, especially those for hand function, should be interpreted cautiously, and further high-quality studies are warranted.

Title: Case Report: mNGS-negative Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome with small bowel obstruction as the initial manifestation in a glucocorticoid-exposed COPD patient: a fatal case.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome (SHS) is a life-threatening condition in immunocompromised hosts with an extremely high mortality rate. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) demonstrates limited sensitivity for parasitic detection, and its clinical value remains to be fully elucidated. The conventional microscopy remains an indispensable tool for the diagnosis of parasitic infections.
CASE DESCRIPTION: A 73-year-old male patient with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and cerebral infarction presented with abdominal pain and distension for 7 days and no bowel movement for 3 days. He was diagnosed with incomplete small bowel obstruction at an outside hospital and treated with fasting, enemas, meropenem, and methylprednisolone. He was subsequently transferred to our hospital due to acute lower respiratory tract infection. Chest radiography revealed bilateral diffuse infiltrates, and his condition rapidly deteriorated, requiring admission to the intensive care unit (ICU), endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, and continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). Stool smear and retrospective sputum examination both identified larvae of Strongyloides stercoralis. However, mNGS of sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) obtained upon admission failed to detect any parasitic sequences. The patient was treated sequentially with albendazole and ivermectin, in combination with broad-spectrum antibacterial, antifungal, and antiviral therapy. He ultimately died on February 11, 2025, due to severe pneumonia, sepsis, and bone marrow suppression.
CONCLUSION: For immunocompromised hosts with multiple risk factors, particularly those exposed to glucocorticoids, active parasitic microscopic examination of stool and respiratory secretions should be pursued when unexplained pulmonary infiltrates coexist with gastrointestinal symptoms, even in the setting of negative mNGS results, to avoid missed diagnosis.
Publication Types: Case Reports; Journal Article; Research Support, Non-U.S. Gov't

Title: Central nervous system, cranial, and cerebrovascular conditions beyond the Kimonis criteria in patients with Gorlin syndrome: a retrospective cohort study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Gorlin syndrome is a multisystem developmental and cancer-predisposing disorder commonly caused by germline PTCH1 variants. The Kimonis clinical criteria capture the canonical phenotype; however, central nervous system (CNS), cranial, and cerebrovascular conditions documented beyond these criteria remain poorly defined.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective descriptive cohort study of 32 patients who fulfilled the Kimonis clinical criteria and received care at either or both hospitals in Japan. Clinical information through March 31, 2026, including sufficiently documented care elsewhere, was reviewed. The exploratory primary descriptive outcome was defined as the presence of at least one documented condition in three categories: structural CNS or cranial conditions, cerebrovascular disorders, or CNS neoplasms other than medulloblastoma. The three categories were considered separately.
RESULTS: A PTCH1 sequence variant or whole-gene deletion was documented in 24 of 32 patients. Eight patients had 10 documented findings representing eight conditions, including hydrocephalus, Chiari malformation, syringomyelia, moyamoya disease, and cerebral infarction. These findings were identified during routine longitudinal clinical care rather than systematic neuroimaging screening and therefore should not be interpreted as a prevalence estimate. Four patients underwent neurosurgical or cerebrovascular interventions.
CONCLUSION: Clinically relevant CNS, cranial, and cerebrovascular conditions documented beyond the Kimonis criteria may warrant consideration when new neurological, respiratory, or craniocervical symptoms arise. Awareness of these conditions may inform symptom-directed differential diagnosis and the selection of imaging modalities and anatomical coverage. These exploratory findings do not establish a unified neurological phenotype or causal relationship with Gorlin syndrome and do not support universal neuroimaging surveillance in asymptomatic patients.

Title: Efficacy and safety of portable ultrasound-guided pingyangmycin sclerotherapy for deep-seated oral and maxillofacial venous malformations: a retrospective observational study.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Intralesional sclerotherapy is the mainstay treatment for venous malformations (VMs). This study aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of ultrasound-guided pingyangmycin sclerotherapy for outpatients with deep-seated oral and maxillofacial VMs.
METHODS: This retrospective study included 49 outpatients with symptomatic deep-seated VMs in the oral and maxillofacial region who received portable ultrasound-guided pingyangmycin sclerotherapy between August 2023 and September 2025. The treatment response analysis after sclerotherapy included lesion volume reduction and symptom improvement. Ultrasound was used to calculate lesion volume. The assessment of global discomfort from the perspective of patients was calculated using the 0-10 numeric rating scale (NRS). The presence of complications was recorded during follow-up.
RESULTS: Among the 49 patients, the average number of sessions for each patient was 2 (range, 1-5). All patients experienced symptom relief after sclerotherapy. The median post-treatment NRS score was 0 (range, 0-1), compared with a median of 5 (range, 2-10) before sclerotherapy. Regarding lesion volume, twenty-one lesions (42.86%) demonstrated excellent response (≥90% reduction). Twenty-three lesions (46.94%) presented moderate response (≥50, <90% reduction). Five (10.2%) lesions showed mild reduction (<50% reduction). The mean lesion dimensions after treatments were 1.54 × 0.87 × 0.96 cm, with a corresponding calculated volume of 0.47 cm3, compared with average dimensions 3.27 × 1.69 × 1.85 cm (volume, 3.59 cm3) before sclerotherapy. A mean volume decrease of 82% was observed among all patients. Paired analysis showed significant improvement in both lesion volume and NRS score after the sclerotherapy. No severe complications occurred in this study.
CONCLUSION: Portable ultrasound-guided pingyangmycin sclerotherapy is a feasible and well-tolerated outpatient-based procedure for patients with deep-seated oral and maxillofacial venous malformations.

Title: LVEF-defined septic cardiomyopathy modifies the association between the prognostic nutritional index and mortality in adults with sepsis: a 72-h landmark analysis.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: The prognostic nutritional index (PNI) combines albumin and lymphocyte count and may capture nutrition-related immune-inflammatory status in sepsis. Whether its association with mortality differs by left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF)-defined septic cardiomyopathy (SCM) is unclear.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective 72-h landmark study of MIMIC-IV adults with Sepsis-3 who survived to the landmark, had clinically indicated pre-landmark echocardiographic LVEF assessment, and had calculable early PNI.
