OBJECTIVE: Gene therapies are increasingly being developed and evaluated to treat complex diseases with multiple genetic causes, including cardiovascular diseases (CVDs). However, these studies have not yet been reviewed systematically. We aimed to conduct a scoping review of randomised controlled trials of gene therapies for CVDs and create an evidence map of the included literature.
METHODS: We searched six databases for studies published from November 2018 to March 2025. Our search yielded 9106 records, and 1864 publications were reviewed at the full-text level.
RESULTS: We included 28 randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating interventions delivered by RNA interference (13 RCTs; 46%), antisense oligonucleotides (9 RCTs; 32%), plasmids (4 RCTs; 14%) and other vectors (adeno-associated virus and adenovirus; 2 RCTs; 7%). Cardiovascular indications included dyslipidaemia (12 RCTs; 43%), ischaemia (4 RCTs; 14%), transthyretin amyloidosis (4 RCTs; 14%), heart failure (2 RCTs; 7%) and other CVDs (6 RCTs; 21%). Samples included an average of 183 participants (range: 5–655); studies followed these participants for an average of 13 months (range: 3–97). Interventions were efficacious in most (22 RCTs; 85%) of the 26 studies that reported efficacy outcomes, but effects lasted less than 1 year in most studies (69%; 18 RCTs). Serious adverse events varied widely by study (range: 0%–62% of intervention group participants), but 19 RCTs reported that less than 10% of intervention group participants experienced a SAE.
CONCLUSIONS: Gene therapies for CVDs were reported to be efficacious in most RCTs, but their effects lasted less than 1 year in 69% of studies. Gene therapies for CVDs show promise in their efficacy and relative safety, but more research is needed to evaluate their long-term effects and risks.

Title: Discharge NT-proBNP predicts 2-year outcomes after TAVR but not after SAVR in preserved ejection fraction: a propensity-matched cohort study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Discharge N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) is a recognised prognostic marker after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), but its value after surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) remains uncertain, possibly reflecting differences in perioperative physiology.
AIMS: To compare the prognostic utility of discharge NT-proBNP after TAVR versus SAVR in patients with severe aortic stenosis and preserved ejection fraction, and to examine the association between NT-proBNP reduction and Left Ventricular Mass Index (LVMI) regression.
METHODS: This propensity-matched cohort study included 556 patients (TAVR, n=278; SAVR, n=278) with left ventricular ejection fraction ≥50% treated at a single centre (2019–2023). The primary endpoint was a 2-year composite of all-cause death or heart failure rehospitalisation.
RESULTS: After matching, baseline characteristics were well balanced. Discharge NT-proBNP >1000 pg/mL predicted lower event-free survival after TAVR (77.3% vs 91.4%; adjusted HR 3.21, 95% CI 1.96 to 5.26, p<0.001) but not after SAVR (83.8% vs 86.7%; adjusted HR 1.18, p=0.50; p for interaction=0.008). Longer aortic cross-clamp time progressively abolished NT-proBNP prognostic value in SAVR. NT-proBNP reduction correlated with LVMI regression regardless of procedure (β=2.2 per 10% ΔNT-proBNP%, p<0.001). A 6-month NT-proBNP ≤1000 pg/mL identified favourable outcomes irrespective of procedure (adjusted HR 0.51, p=0.002).
CONCLUSIONS: Discharge NT-proBNP predicts outcomes after TAVR but not SAVR, likely due to cardiopulmonary bypass-induced inflammation. NT-proBNP reduction correlates with LVMI regression irrespective of procedure. Risk stratification may be optimised by discharge measurement after TAVR and 6-month reassessment after SAVR.

Title: Predictors of outcome in adults with double outlet right ventricle.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Double outlet right ventricle (DORV) encompasses a range of congenital heart defects. Although survival to adulthood has improved, late risks, particularly life-threatening arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death (SCD) persist.
OBJECTIVES: We evaluated long-term outcomes in an adult DORV cohort, including SCD risk and device therapy.
METHODS: This multicentre, retrospective cohort study enrolled adults with DORV under follow-up at two UK tertiary centres from 2000 to 2023. Patients were classified by anatomical subtype and surgical strategy. The primary composite outcome was all-cause mortality, heart or heart–lung transplantation, aborted SCD or appropriate implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) shock.
RESULTS: Among 254 patients (median age 20 (IQR 17.6 to 29.2) years; 52.8% male), 61.4% had biventricular repair. Complex (n=90, 35.4%) and Fallot-type (n=79, 31.1%) DORV predominated. Over a median 12.4 (7.4 to 17.3) years, 47 (18.5%) patients died: heart failure (40.4%) and SCD (25.5%) were leading causes. Aborted SCD occurred in 4 (1.6%) cases, 4 (1.6%) underwent heart transplantation and 10 (4.0%) received appropriate ICD shocks. One in eight patients experienced ventricular tachycardia and one in three developed supraventricular tachycardia. In exploratory multivariable analysis restricted to patients with biventricular repair, older age, pulmonary hypertension and baseline QRS >180 ms were associated with the composite outcome.
CONCLUSIONS: Amongst adult survivors of DORV, late mortality due to heart failure and SCD was considerable, whereas transplantation was uncommon. In the biventricular-repair subgroup, older age, baseline QRS >180 ms and pulmonary hypertension were associated with adverse outcome in exploratory analysis; these findings require validation.

Title: Different perfusion responses to bypass surgery in moyamoya disease and intracranial atherosclerotic disease: a prospective perfusion MRI study.
Small dense low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and risk of cardiovascular events in general adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies.
Abstract:
ABSTRACT: 
OBJECTIVES: Small dense low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (sdLDL-C) is considered one of the most atherogenic lipid fractions, but its association with cardiovascular events and whether this differs by assessment method remain uncertain. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies to quantify this association.
DESIGN: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohorts; PROSPERO registered (CRD420261411427).
DATA SOURCES: PubMed, ProQuest Health & Medical Collection, MEDLINE (Ovid) and Web of Science Core Collection were searched from inception to June 2026.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: Prospective cohort studies of community-based or population-based adults reporting HRs for incident cardiovascular events across baseline sdLDL-C categories were eligible.
DATA EXTRACTION AND SYNTHESIS: Data were extracted independently by two reviewers. Random-effects restricted maximum likelihood models pooled HRs for the highest versus lowest sdLDL-C categories and for quartile (Q)2, Q3 and Q4 versus Q1 comparisons, stratified by sdLDL-C assessment method. Sensitivity analyses, risk-of-bias assessment, Bayesian hierarchical relative-to-an-identified-distribution (RIDIT)-based modelling and Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations (GRADE) assessment were performed.
RESULTS: Fourteen studies were included, comprising 738 114 participants and 77 839 incident cardiovascular events. In the highest-versus-lowest comparison, the pooled HR was 1.47 (95% CI 1.32 to 1.63). The association was stronger for directly measured than calculated sdLDL-C (HR 1.64, 95% CI 1.38 to 1.94 vs HR 1.37, 95% CI 1.21 to 1.54). Between-study heterogeneity was substantial in several analyses. Pairwise quantile and Bayesian RIDIT-based analyses supported a graded positive exposure–risk pattern. Leave-one-out analyses did not materially change the estimates, and Egger’s tests showed no small-study effects. Risk of bias was low to moderate. GRADE certainty was moderate for calculated sdLDL-C and low for the overall and directly measured analyses.
CONCLUSION: Higher baseline sdLDL-C is associated with increased incident cardiovascular event risk in general adult populations and may serve as an accessible marker of atherogenic cardiovascular risk.

Title: MetCool ACS: study protocol for a multicentre quasi-randomised trial of metformin in patients without diabetes after acute coronary syndrome in Poland.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Despite advances in coronary intervention and secondary prevention, patients without diabetes who experience acute coronary syndrome (ACS) remain at elevated cardiovascular risk. Metformin has pleiotropic cardiovascular effects beyond glucose lowering, but its role after ACS in people without diabetes is uncertain.
METHODS AND ANALYSIS: MetCool ACS is a multicentre, prospective, quasi-randomised, open-label trial enrolling 1000 adults without diabetes hospitalised for ACS and treated with successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stent implantation. Allocation is determined by the second digit of the Polish national identification number: even digits allocate to metformin and odd digits to standard care (allocation 1:1). Participants allocated to metformin will receive dose-escalated therapy to 850 mg three times a day (2550 mg/day) for 24 months, followed by 6 months of post-treatment follow-up (total 30 months). The primary endpoint is unplanned coronary revascularisation (PCI or coronary artery bypass grafting) within 30 months after the index ACS-related revascularisation. Secondary endpoints include cardiac death, all-cause death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke and safety outcomes. Time-to-event outcomes will be analysed using appropriate survival analysis methods, including Kaplan-Meier estimates, log-rank testing and Cox proportional hazards models, with competing-risk methods applied where appropriate. Detailed statistical methods will be prespecified in the statistical analysis plan. Protocol version: 3.1/2023 (10 January 2023).
ETHICS AND DISSEMINATION: The study was approved by the Bioethics Committee at the Military Institute of Medicine (Resolution 55/WIM/2020; 18 November 2020) and the Bioethics Committee at the Military Chamber of Physicians (Resolution 31/23; 27 October 2023). All participants provide written informed consent. Results will be disseminated primarily through peer-reviewed publication and scientific meetings. The trial is covered by clinical trial insurance, including coverage for potential claims arising from harm related to participation in the trial. Any compensation for trial-related harm will be provided in accordance with applicable regulations and the terms and conditions of the insurance policy.
TRIAL REGISTRATION NUMBERS: EudraCT 2020-004962-21; EU CT 2024-516589-13-00; NCT05305898.

Title: Associations between short-term PM2.5 exposure and major cardiovascular events in high-risk population: a nationwide case-crossover study.
Abstract:
ABSTRACT: 
OBJECTIVES: While particulate matter with a diameter ≤2.5 µm (PM2.5) is a recognised major modifiable risk factor with well-documented short-term impacts on acute cardiovascular events in the general population, data regarding its effects on high-risk populations with significant atherosclerotic risk are limited. This study aims to identify the association between short-term exposure to PM2.5 and acute major cardiovascular events in Thailand.
DESIGN: A time-stratified case-crossover design.
SETTING: The nationwide Cohort Of patients with high Risk for cardiovascular Events-Thailand registry (CORE-Thailand registry).
PARTICIPANTS: A total of 1121 individuals from the registry who experienced four-point major adverse cardiovascular events (4P-MACEs) between 2011 and 2019.
PRIMARY OUTCOME MEASURE: The primary exposure was defined as short-term PM2.5 exposure, with the primary outcome being a first-time MACE, which included acute myocardial infarction, stroke, heart failure hospitalisation and all-cause death.
METHODS: Using a time-stratified case-crossover design, the analysed events included non-fatal myocardial infarction, non-fatal stroke, heart failure hospitalisation and all-cause death. Daily PM2.5 concentrations during the event and control periods were obtained from nearby air quality monitors. Conditional logistic regression models assessed odds ratio (ORs) for 4P-MACE per 10 µg/m³ increase in PM2.5 exposure over lag periods from 0 to 7 days.
RESULTS: The participants had a mean age of 69.9 years and 55.8% were male. Most had pre-existing atherosclerotic cardiovascular diseases (74.6%), diabetes mellitus (58.4%), hypertension (98.1%) and dyslipidaemia (83.3%). Significant associations were observed for both single-day (lag 1 to lag 4) and average-days (lag 01 to 07) PM2.5 exposures. A 10 µg/m³ increase in PM2.5 was associated with increased odds of MACEs, with ORs of 1.06 (95% CI 1.01 - 1.11) for single-day lagged exposures and varying ORs from 1.06 to 1.08 for average-days lagged exposures (lags 01 to 04).
CONCLUSIONS: Short-term PM2.5 exposure significantly increased the risk of MACE in the Thai population with high atherosclerotic risk. These findings underscore the urgency of public health interventions aimed at mitigating air pollution exposure, especially among vulnerable groups.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: The study is registered with the Thai Clinical Trials Registry (TCTR20130520001).

Title: Association between the triglyceride-glucose-waist circumference index and obstructive sleep apnoea: a hospital-based case-control study in China and the development of machine learning models.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVES: We aimed to examine the association between the triglyceride-glucose-waist circumference (TyG-WC) index and obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) and to develop machine learning (ML) models to identify OSA.
DESIGN: Case–control study and development of six ML models.
SETTING: A sleep medicine centre at a tertiary hospital in China.
PARTICIPANTS: 534 patients with OSA diagnosed by polysomnography between 2017 and 2025, matched with 534 OSA-free individuals.
PRIMARY AND SECONDARY OUTCOME MEASURES: The primary outcome was the association between TyG-WC and OSA, assessed using multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, education, marital status, hypertension, diabetes, smoking and alcohol use. Secondary outcomes were the dose-response and threshold effects, subgroup interactions, external consistency testing in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), sensitivity analyses and development of ML models (LightGBM, XGBoost, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbours, Naive Bayes) incorporating TyG-WC and the same clinical variables, evaluated for discrimination, calibration and clinical utility, interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP).
RESULTS: TyG-WC was linearly associated with OSA (adjusted OR=1.067, 95% CI 1.055 to 1.079; p<0.001; p for non-linearity=0.827), and this association remained robust in NHANES and sensitivity analyses. Significant interactions were observed by age and hypertension status. In the test set, six ML models demonstrated good predictive performance (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC)=0.732–0.803). XGBoost achieved the highest discrimination (AUC=0.803, 95% CI 0.755 to 0.851), with no evidence of miscalibration (Brier score=0.183; Hosmer-Lemeshow p>0.05) and positive net benefit across threshold probabilities. SHAP identified TyG-WC as the most influential predictor across all ML models.
CONCLUSIONS: TyG-WC was associated with OSA. ML models incorporating TyG-WC and clinical variables achieved good performance, supporting TyG-WC’s potential as an accessible risk marker.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Not applicable.

Title: Predicting Major Amputation Rates in Diabetic Hindfoot Ulcers With Critical Infection and Ischemia: A Risk-Factor-Based Model.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Diabetic hindfoot ulcers pose a substantially greater risk of progressing to major amputation than forefoot or midfoot ulcers. Patients with these ulcers often experience severe psychological distress at the prospect of major limb loss. Consequently, patients, their families, and healthcare professionals prioritize understanding the actual risk of major amputation based on the patient's current clinical status. However, practical tools addressing this critical and common concern remain limited. In a previous preliminary study, we proposed a model for predicting major amputation rates in diabetic hindfoot ulcers. Nonetheless, that model, which relied solely on ischemia and infection, demonstrated limited accuracy. The present study aimed to refine the prediction of major amputation in diabetic hindfoot ulcers by 1) identifying additional risk factors and 2) evaluating amputation rates according to these factors.
METHODS: A retrospective analysis was conducted involving 1,663 hospitalized patients diagnosed with diabetic foot ulcers. From this group, 50 patients with hindfoot ulcers presenting with critical ischemia and infection were included. A total of 88 baseline clinical and laboratory parameters were evaluated to determine key risk factors.
RESULTS: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) ≥ stage 3, hemoglobin < 10.35 g/dL, and albumin < 3.75 g/dL emerged as independent predictors of major amputation (P < 0.05). Univariable logistic regression demonstrated a strong positive correlation between the number of identified risk factors and the rate of major amputation. Patients without these three risk factors did not undergo major amputation, even in the presence of critical infection and ischemia. Conversely, amputation risk increased to 6% for individuals with one risk factor, 27% for those with two, and 67% for patients with all three (P < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: CKD, low serum hemoglobin, and low serum albumin were identified as significant risk factors for major amputation in patients with diabetic hindfoot ulcers complicated by critical infection and ischemia. The risk of major amputation increases substantially with the presence of multiple risk factors, from 6% amputation rate with one factor to 67% with three factors. Nevertheless, prospective studies with larger sample sizes are warranted to validate this risk-factor model.

Title: Effect of Sleep Hygiene on Metabolic Syndrome in an Adult Rural Population in India: Protocol for a Cross-Sectional Study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Metabolic syndrome (MetS) refers to a group of conditions including high blood pressure, excess weight, high blood glucose, and abnormal cholesterol and triglyceride levels that together substantially increase the risk of heart disease and diabetes. Poor sleep hygiene is associated with a higher likelihood of type 2 diabetes, while sleep duration can affect the development of various MetS components. Approximately 25% of adults worldwide currently have MetS, and this prevalence is projected to increase to 50% by 2035. However, there is a distinct lack of evidence about the specific impact of sleep hygiene on cardiometabolic health within the rural Indian population. This study will focus on addressing this literature gap by evaluating these risk factor associations by using validated tools to help develop targeted community interventions.
OBJECTIVE: This study aims to estimate the prevalence of poor sleep quality and cardiometabolic risk factors in a rural Indian population and to determine the association between sleep hygiene and cardiometabolic risk factors.
METHODS: This study will be a community-based, cross-sectional, analytical study, and data collection will be carried out by trained personnel using validated tools during house-to-house visits. In this cross-sectional study of 281 rural Indian adults aged ≥40 years, sleep quality will be assessed via the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (a score >5 indicates poor sleep), alongside direct measurements of blood pressure, fasting plasma glucose, BMI (≥25 kg/m² for obesity), waist circumference, and the Madras Diabetes Research Foundation-Indian Diabetes Risk Score for diabetes risk. Data will be collected through a door-to-door approach, with informed consent entered into Google Forms, and quality checked via training and regular reviews. Using R software, analyses will include prevalence estimates with 95% CIs; chi-square or t tests for associations between poor sleep and cardiometabolic risks; and logistic regression (P<.05) adjusted for confounders such as diet, stress, and physical activity.
RESULTS: This study began in January 2025 with conceptualization and ethics approval obtained in June 2025. Data collection commenced in August 2025 following Clinical Trial Registry-India registration, with 53 participants enrolled as of May 5, 2026. Standardized tools (GAD-7, PHQ-9, and GPAQ) were incorporated to assess key confounding variables. Data collection is projected to finish by January 2027, with final analysis and study conclusion expected by March 2027.
CONCLUSIONS: The relationship between MetS and sleep hygiene warrants greater attention, particularly as poor sleep habits become increasingly prevalent alongside MetS. This study will deepen the understanding of their connection, paving the way for targeted interventions and prevention strategies.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: Clinical Trial Registry-India CTRI/2025/08/092892; https://tinyurl.com/3sak2h9x.
INTERNATIONAL REGISTERED REPORT IDENTIFIER (IRRID): DERR1-10.2196/90117.

Title: Spanish catheter ablation registry. 25th official report of the Heart Rhythm Association of the Spanish Society of Cardiology (2025).
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: We report the results of the 2025 Spanish catheter ablation registry.
METHODS: This retrospective registry included catheter ablation procedures performed at participating hospitals in Spain and recorded in the REDCap database using a dedicated data collection form.
RESULTS: A total of 109 centers participated, reporting 33 435 ablations. Atrial fibrillation was the most commonly treated arrhythmia (14 452 cases), with single-shot techniques being the most frequently used approach (63%) and a marked increase in pulsed field ablation (37% vs 21% in 2024). The remaining arrhythmia substrates remained at similar levels. The overall acute success rate was 95%, the complication rate was 1.6%, and the mortality rate was 0.04%. There was a marked increase in outpatient procedures (33% vs 18% in 2024), particularly atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia ablation (50%) and cavotricuspid isthmus ablation (45%). A total of 467 pediatric ablations were performed in 38 centers. Accessory pathway ablation was the most common procedure (65.3%), with a 97% success rate.
CONCLUSIONS: A similar number of centers participated, with a slight increase in the number of procedures compared with 2024. Atrial fibrillation remained the most frequently treated arrhythmia. Acute success, complication, and mortality rates remained stable. The accreditation process for centers and professionals is well-established, with a stable number of annual accreditations. Full English text available from: www.revespcardiol.org/en.

Title: Late-pregnancy maternal serum alkaline phosphatase levels and risk of early postpartum cardiometabolic disease: A municipality-wide electronic health record-based cohort study in Tianjin, China.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To investigate the association between gestational age-standardized maternal alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels and early postpartum cardiometabolic disease.
METHODS: The study included 166,986 singleton pregnancies from the Tianjin Health and Medical Data Platform in Tianjin, China (2009-2023). Maternal serum ALP levels measured within two weeks before delivery were gestational age-standardized and categorized into quartiles. Primary outcomes were early postpartum cardiometabolic diseases including hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, cardiovascular disease (CVD), and a composite outcome comprising these conditions. Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
RESULTS: During a median follow-up of 4.7 years, compared with the highest gestational age-standardized ALP quartile, the lowest quartile was associated with higher risks of postpartum hypertension (HR: 1.18, 95% CI: 1.09, 1.28), diabetes mellitus (HR: 1.23, 95% CI: 1.10, 1.37), CVD (HR: 1.17, 95% CI: 1.07, 1.28), and composite outcome (HR: 1.13, 95% CI: 1.08, 1.20). Exploratory analyses showed limited incremental discrimination after adding gestational age-standardized ALP to models containing adverse pregnancy outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: Lower gestational age-standardized maternal ALP levels before delivery were associated with a higher risk of early postpartum cardiometabolic disease. Further studies across ethnically and geographically diverse populations are warranted to validate these findings.

Title: Association of Spinal Epidural Lipomatosis With Systemic Lipid Metabolism in Patients With Lumbar Spinal Stenosis: A Propensity Score-Matched Study.
Journal: The spine journal : official journal of the North American Spine Society
Abstract:
BACKGROUND CONTEXT: Spinal epidural lipomatosis (SEL) is often regarded as a local consequence of obesity, yet its relationship with systemic lipid metabolism and symptom severity in lumbar spinal stenosis remains unclear. Apolipoprotein B (ApoB) is central to atherogenic lipid transport and ectopic fat deposition. Examining the association between systemic lipid metabolic abnormalities, including elevated ApoB levels, and epidural fat accumulation may provide insights into the metabolic pathogenesis and clinical relevance of SEL.
PURPOSE: To determine whether SEL is associated with systemic lipid metabolic abnormalities and greater preoperative symptom burden in patients undergoing surgery for lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS).
STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective, propensity score-matched cohort study.
PATIENT SAMPLE: A consecutive series of 1,145 patients who underwent posterior decompression for symptomatic LSS between December 2023 and December 2025. After 1:1 propensity score matching, 90 patients with SEL were compared with 90 patients without SEL.
OUTCOME MEASURES: Serum lipid and other biochemical markers, epidural fat/spinal canal (EF/SpC) index on lumbar magnetic resonance imaging, Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), and visual analog scale (VAS) scores for leg and back pain.
METHODS: SEL was diagnosed and graded on preoperative lumbar MRI according to the Borré classification, using the epidural fat/spinal canal index. Propensity score matching was performed for age, sex, body mass index (BMI), smoking history, drinking history, hypertension, and diabetes. Biochemical variables and preoperative clinical scores were compared between matched SEL and non-SEL patients. Conditional logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with SEL. BMI-adjusted partial Spearman correlation analyses were performed to evaluate associations between the EF/SpC index and biochemical markers. Regression-based trend analyses were conducted to assess changes in lipid-related markers across increasing SEL severity grades.
RESULTS: Among 1,145 patients with LSS, 105 (9.2%) met the diagnostic criteria for SEL. After matching, 90 patients with SEL were compared with 90 non-SEL controls. The SEL group had higher apolipoprotein B (ApoB) levels than controls, as well as higher low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, triglycerides, and total cholesterol. ApoB remained independently associated with SEL in conditional logistic regression (odds ratio per 0.1 g/L, 1.141; 95% confidence interval, 1.019-1.277; P=0.022). Within the SEL group, the EF/SpC index correlated positively with triglycerides (ρ=0.43, q<0.001) and ApoB (ρ=0.40, q=0.002), while atherogenic lipid markers increased progressively with SEL severity. Patients with SEL also showed higher Oswestry Disability Index and leg-pain visual analog scale scores, whereas back-pain scores were similar between groups.
CONCLUSION: In patients undergoing surgery for LSS, SEL was associated with a more atherogenic lipid profile after matching for BMI and other major baseline characteristics, as well as greater preoperative disability and leg pain. The association of ApoB with SEL, together with the graded relationships of ApoB and triglycerides with epidural fat burden, suggests that SEL may reflect systemic lipid metabolic dysfunction rather than local epidural fat deposition alone.

Title: Temporal trends and outcomes of intravascular imaging in chronic total occlusion interventions: insights from the PROGRESS-CTO registry.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: In this study we investigated temporal trends, indications, practice variation, and outcomes associated with intravascular imaging (IVI) use in a large, multicenter chronic total occlusion (CTO) percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) registry.
METHODS: We analyzed CTO PCIs performed at 76 US and international centers in 2012-2026 in the PROGRESS-CTO registry. Patients were categorized according to IVI use. P value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.
RESULTS: Among 18,024 CTO PCIs, IVI was used in 10,569 procedures (58.6%). IVI use increased over time. Intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) was the predominant modality, accounting for 98.1% of IVI-guided procedures. Following 1:1 propensity score matching, technical (85.8% vs 78.8%; p < 0.001) and procedural success (83.6% vs 78.1%, p = 0.003) remained higher in the IVUS-to-cross group. Difference was also pronounced when IVUS was used to cross ambiguous proximal cap: technical success was 85.1% versus 75.9% (OR, 1.81; 95% CI, 1.49-2.21), and procedural success was 83.0% versus 75.1% (OR, 1.63; 95% CI, 1.34-1.99). Centers contributing <100 cases had lower IVI use than centers contributing ≥100 cases (47.7% vs 58.7%; p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: IVI use during CTO PCI continues to increase. Procedures in which IVUS was used to facilitate lesion crossing were associated with higher technical and procedural success rates and similar in-hospital MACE rates. The association with success was also pronounced when IVUS was used to resolve proximal cap ambiguity. IVI use varied significantly among participating centers, highlighting differences in practice patterns and adoption of IVI during CTO PCI.

Title: Late gadolinium enhancement dispersion mapping predicts major arrhythmic events in patients with prior myocardial infarction.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Myocardial scar heterogeneity is a key determinant of ventricular arrhythmias after myocardial infarction (MI). Late gadolinium enhancement dispersion mapping (LGE-DM) quantifies structural complexity, but its prognostic role in ischemic cardiomyopathy remains unevaluated.
METHODS: We retrospectively included 364 consecutive patients with prior MI (>90 days). For each LGE image, a parametric map was generated and each enhanced pixel scored (0-8) based on surrounding signal distribution; the global dispersion score (GDS) was calculated as the mean pixel score, quantifying pixel-to-pixel heterogeneity. The endpoint was a composite of sudden cardiac death (SCD), resuscitated cardiac arrest, sustained ventricular tachycardia, or appropriate ICD therapies.
RESULTS: During a median follow-up of 4 years, 42 arrhythmic events occurred. Patients with events showed significantly higher GDS than event-free patients (0.53 vs 0.32, P < 0.0001). Multivariable Cox regression confirmed GDS as an independent predictor (HR 1.16 per 0.1-unit increase, 95% CI 1.03-1.29), while LVEF and LGE extent were not, and GDS remained independently associated with events when LGE extent was forced into the model (HR 1.12 per 0.1-unit increase, P = 0.005). In patients with LVEF >35%, GDS was the only independent predictor across all multivariable models. Harrell's C-index was 0.682, with an optimism of 0.012 on bootstrap resampling. ROC analysis identified GDS >0.5 as a provisional cut-off derived within the same cohort (apparent AUC 0.74 overall; 0.81 in the LVEF >35% subgroup). Kaplan-Meier analysis confirmed worse prognosis in patients with GDS >0.5 (overall: p = 0.0002; LVEF >35%: p < 0.0001).
CONCLUSIONS: LGE dispersion independently predicts malignant ventricular arrhythmias post-MI, outperforming LGE extent and LVEF. GDS may improve SCD risk stratification particularly in patients with LVEF >35%, a population not adequately targeted by current LVEF-based criteria. External validation is required before the proposed threshold can be used clinically.

Title: The Society of Thoracic Surgeons (2026) Expert Consensus Document on Management of Borderline Left Heart Excluding Unbalanced Atrioventricular Septal Defect and Strategies for Biventricular Conversion.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Strategies to recruit the left ventricle in borderline left heart (BLH), whether utilizing primary or staged recruitment strategy, are challenged by lack of consensus regarding optimal substrate, timing, and technique.
METHODS: A panel of experienced congenital cardiac surgeons, cardiologists and imaging experts were convened to develop key questions related to BLH management, excluding unbalanced atrioventricular septal defect, from neonatal period through 1 year, using the PICO (Patients/Population, Intervention, Comparison/Control, Outcome) framework. Literature searches were performed for each question. Using a modified Delphi method, consensus statements were developed.
RESULTS: For neonates with BLH, primary biventricular repair should be adopted cautiously, and only with favorable anatomic and physiologic criteria determined by echocardiography and/or magnetic resonance imaging. Neonates in the 'grey-zone', with smaller mitral and aortic valve sizes, endocardial fibroelastosis, indexed left ventricular diastolic volume < 25 ml/m2 and ascending aortic flow < 2.0 L/min/m2, should undergo staged recruitment to potentially facilitate growth of left-sided structures and more durable surgical rehabilitation of left ventricular inflow and outflow. Timing and type of subsequent procedures should be guided by interval cardiac catheterization and magnetic resonance imaging data. Initial palliation of grey-zone neonates can be accomplished with either surgical Norwood or hybrid stage 1 with possible atrial level restriction, and subsequent endocardial fibroelastosis resection along with aortic and mitral valve repair as components of successful complete biventricular conversion.
CONCLUSIONS: Biventricular approaches in BLH should be guided by integration of anatomic and physiologic criteria, with most neonates recommended for staged recruitment rather than primary repair.

Title: Prognostic Value of Late Gadolinium Enhancement Findings in Isolated Left Ventricular Dilatation and Dilated Cardiomyopathy.
Journal: Journal of cardiovascular magnetic resonance : official journal of the Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) and isolated left ventricular dilatation (ILVD) are defined as left ventricular (LV) dilatation, with reduced or preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), respectively. We aimed to assess the prognostic value of late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) findings, including LGE extent, location, and number of areas to predict all-cause death in ILVD and DCM, separately.
METHODS: Between 2008 and 2021, we conducted a bicentric retrospective study including all consecutive ILVD and DCM patients referred for cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR). The primary outcome was all-cause death. A propensity-score matching was performed to balance characteristics between ILVD and DCM populations. Cox regressions were performed to determine the prognostic value of each LGE feature.
RESULTS: Of 2,752 patients (age 52±8 years, 56% males), 408 (15%) patients died after a median (interquartile range) follow-up of 9 (7-12) years, including 268 (16%) of 1,668 DCM patients and 140 (13%) of 1,084 ILVD patients. Overall, 737 (27%) patients had LGE, including 472 (28%) of 1,668 DCM patients and 265 (24%) of 1,084 ILVD patients. After propensity-score matching, in ILVD patients with LGE (N=265), the LGE extent (hazard ratio [HR] 1.38, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.06-1.78, p=0.015), multiple LGE areas (HR=3.39, 95% CI: 1.66-6.92, p<0.001), and its septal location (HR=2.68, 95% CI: 1.59-4.52, p<0.001) were strong prognosticators of death after adjustment. Similarly, after propensity-score matching, in DCM patients with LGE (N=277), the LGE extent (HR=1.39, 95% CI: 1.06-1.83, p=0.018), multiple LGE areas (HR=2.70, 95% CI: 1.20-6.08, p=0.017), and its septal location (HR=2.82, 95% CI: 1.47-5.41, p=0.002) were strongly associated with death. The CMR LGE score performed well in participants with LGE (area under the curve [AUC] at 10 years, 0.79 [95% CI: 0.69-0.89]).
CONCLUSIONS: LGE findings were strongly and independently associated with death in both ILVD and DCM patients, with each successive LGE characteristic providing significant incremental prognostic value beyond traditional prognosticators, including LVEF.

Title: Fatigue, Anxiety and Depression 12 Months After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Population Based Cohort Study.
Abstract:
AIM: To determine the prevalence and factors associated with fatigue, anxiety, and depression 12 months after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA); examine their associations with health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and functional recovery; and compare symptom burden with population norms.
METHODS: This prospective, population-based cohort study included adults (≥18 years) who received EMS-attempted resuscitation and survived to hospital discharge following non-traumatic OHCA in Victoria, Australia, between July 2019 and June 2022. Survivors were identified from a statewide OHCA registry and completed a 12-month telephone interview. Primary outcomes were fatigue (Modified Fatigue Impact Scale), anxiety and depression (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale). Secondary outcomes included HRQoL (EQ-5D, SF-12), functional recovery (GOSE), living arrangement, and return to work.
RESULTS: Of 1068 eligible 12-month survivors, 728 (68.2%) completed follow-up (median age 61 years; 555 [76.2%] male). Fatigue was reported by 35.8% (250/699), anxiety by 22.6% (162/716), and depression by 18.0% (129/716). Higher symptom burden was associated with lower EQ-5D and SF-12 scores, worse GOSE outcomes (all p<0.001) and reduced return-to-work rates. Compared with population norms, survivors reported greater fatigue (SMD 0.64; 95%CI, 0.50-0.78;p<0.001), and depression (SMD, 0.12; 95%CI, 0.02,0.21;p=0.02) but lower anxiety (SMD, -0.27; 95%CI, -0.35 to -0.18;p<0.001). In adjusted models, younger age, preexisting anxiety or depression, diabetes and initial non-shockable arrest were associated with higher symptom burden, whereas EMS-witnessed arrests were associated with lower symptom burden.
CONCLUSIONS: Fatigue, anxiety, and depression were common at 12 months after OHCA and are associated with poorer recovery. Fatigue exceeded population norms and may be an under-recognised component of cardiac arrest survivorship.

Title: Regional implementation of a prehospital advanced life support program with video-assisted physician direction and outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: The smart advanced life support (SALS) program was introduced to provide prehospital advanced life support under real-time video-assisted physician direction for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). This study evaluated the association between regional SALS implementation and OHCA outcomes.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort study used difference-in-differences and event-study analyses with data from the OHCA surveillance system in South Korea and included adult OHCA cases (aged ≥19 years) from 2 years before through 4 years after SALS implementation in August 2015. The exposure was region-level implementation of SALS. Outcomes were the prehospital time interval, prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), survival to discharge, and favorable neurological outcome. Pre- to post-implementation changes were compared between regions with and without SALS.
RESULTS: A total of 129,207 cases were included. SALS regions had greater increases in the prehospital time interval (4.12 minutes; 95% confidence interval [CI], 2.91 to 5.33) and prehospital ROSC (1.35 percentage points; 95% CI, 0.56 to 2.15) than regions without SALS. No significant additional improvements were observed in survival to discharge (-0.35 percentage points; 95% CI, -1.31 to 0.62) or favorable neurological outcome (-0.35 percentage points; 95% CI, -1.08 to 0.37). Event-study analyses suggested differential pre-intervention trends for prehospital time, but not for the other outcomes.
CONCLUSION: SALS regions showed greater increases in prehospital time and prehospital ROSC without significant improvements in survival to discharge or favorable neurological outcome, but the finding for prehospital time should be interpreted cautiously because differential pre-intervention trends were observed.

Title: Association Between Capnographic Changes During Pulse Checks of Varying Durations and Clinical Outcomes During Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation: A Multicenter Study From Türkiye (CaPTuRe).
Abstract:
AIM: To investigate the association between capnographic changes during pulse checks of different durations and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) outcomes.
METHODS: This multicenter, prospective, controlled, quasi-randomized study categorized patients according to pulse check duration: Group A (≤5 seconds) and Group B (>5 to ≤10 seconds). Five measurements were obtained during the first six CPR cycles. Four capnographic parameters were evaluated for each measurement: Post-CPR end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO2), Pre-CPR ETCO2, loss rate (percentage decrease between Post- and Pre-CPR ETCO2), and recovery time (time required to regain the previous cycle's Post-CPR ETCO2).
RESULTS: The study included 252 cardiac arrest patients (Group A, n=124; Group B, n=128). In Group A, patients with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) had markedly lower loss rates and shorter recovery times than non-survivors, together with higher pre- and post-CPR ETCO2 values (all p<0.001). Group A also had a higher ROSC rate than Group B (36.3% vs. 19.5%; p=0.005). Logistic regression identified pulse check duration as an independent predictor of ROSC, with Group A having 2.39-fold higher odds of ROSC than Group B (odds ratio [OR]=2.39, 95% confidence interval [CI]=1.347-4.242; p=0.003). Pre-CPR ETCO2 was strongly negatively correlated with loss rate (ρ=-0.770), whereas Pre- and Post-CPR ETCO2 values (ρ=0.96) and loss rate and recovery time (ρ=0.89) were strongly positively correlated.
CONCLUSION: Pulse checks completed within 5 seconds were associated with more favorable capnographic dynamics and higher ROSC rates than those lasting 6-10 seconds. These findings are hypothesis-generating and warrant prospective validation.

Title: Association between burst-suppression with identical bursts and multimodal measures of cerebral oxygenation after cardiac arrest.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Burst-suppression with identical bursts (BSIB) is an electroencephalographic (EEG) pattern associated with severe post-cardiac arrest brain injury (PCABI). Whether modifiable mechanisms of brain injury underlie BSIB is unknown. We hypothesized BSIB is associated with impaired cerebral oxygen metabolism, reflected as pathologically elevated jugular bulb venous oxygen saturation (SjvO2), higher brain tissue oxygen tension (PbtO2), normal jugular bulb venous-to-arterial carbon dioxide gradient (PbCO2 gap, and lower intracranial pressure (ICP) compared to other EEG patterns.
METHODS: This single-center retrospective study included patients resuscitated from cardiac arrest who underwent EEG and SjvO2 or PbtO2 monitoring. We categorized EEG patterns as BSIB, malignant without BSIB, and non-malignant. Using mixed effects linear regression, we examined associations between EEG and SjvO2, PbCO2 gap, PbtO2, and ICP.
RESULTS: The SjvO2 and PbtO2 cohorts included 109 and 33 patients, respectively. SjvO2 did not differ between BSIB and malignant EEGs (β=3; 95% CI, -0.6 to 7.0), butwas higher with BSIB compared to non-malignant patterns (β=12; 95% CI, 7.0 to 16.0). BSIB was associated with lower PbCO2 gap compared to malignant (β=-1.4; 95% CI, -2.6 to -0.3) and non-malignant (β=-2.6; 95% CI, -4.1 to -1.0) patterns. PbtO2 was highest with BSIB, but not significantly higher compared to malignant patterns in our adjusted model (β=4.0; 95% CI, -4.7 to 13.0). ICP was lower in those with BSIB compared to malignant patterns (β=-19.0; 95% CI, -32.5 to -5.6). Interpretation BSIB may represent a distinct subtype of PCABI characterized by impaired oxygen metabolism with preserved oxygen delivery and diffusion.

Title: Safety outcomes of semaglutide by chronic kidney disease severity in the FLOW trial.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: People with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) often experience medication intolerance and side effects that worsen with lower estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). This prespecified secondary analysis assessed the safety of semaglutide by baseline eGFR.
METHODS: FLOW (NCT03819153) was a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial testing the efficacy of subcutaneous semaglutide 1.0 mg once-weekly on a primary kidney outcome (50% or more eGFR reduction, kidney failure, or death due to kidney or cardiovascular causes) in participants with T2D and CKD. Safety data were collected selectively and included serious adverse events (SAEs), AEs leading to treatment discontinuation, and prespecified AEs of special interest (AESIs). In this descriptive assessment, systematically collected safety data were reported numerically by baseline eGFR.
RESULTS: Of 3533 participants, 1767 received semaglutide and 1766 received placebo. Fewer SAEs were reported with semaglutide than placebo across baseline eGFR subgroups (45.1% versus 50.4% in the 60 or more ml/min per 1.73 m2 subgroup, and 56.4% versus 60.4% in the under 30 ml/min per 1.73 m2 subgroup). SAEs related to infections and infestations; cardiac disorders; respiratory, thoracic and mediastinal disorders; and metabolism and nutrition disorders were generally less frequent with semaglutide than placebo, regardless of baseline eGFR. Treatment discontinuations due to AEs were higher with lower baseline eGFR across treatment groups (60 or more ml/min per 1.73 m2: semaglutide 11.2%, placebo 11.3%; under30 ml/min per 66 1.73 m2: semaglutide 18.8%, placebo 18.7%). Discontinuations specifically due to gastrointestinal AEs were reported more frequently with semaglutide (4.5%) than placebo (1.1%), regardless of baseline eGFR. Frequencies of AESI were similar between treatment groups across baseline eGFR subgroups.
CONCLUSIONS: In this safety assessment, SAEs were reported less frequently with semaglutide than placebo, with corresponding patterns observed for treatment discontinuations and AESIs. No unexpected safety concerns were identified across the spectrum of eGFR represented in the FLOW trial.

Title: A study using the REIN registry suggests a statin therapy benefits for secondary prevention in patients receiving dialysis.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: While statins are effective for cardiovascular prevention in the general population, their benefit in patients with CKD G5D (kidney failure treated by dialysis) remains uncertain. Previous randomized controlled trials included mixed populations for primary and secondary prevention while excluding patients with recent cardiovascular events, leaving a knowledge gap regarding statin effectiveness for secondary prevention immediately following an atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) event. Here, we address this gap by providing real-world evidence.
METHODS: We conducted a landmark-based observational study, informed by the target trial framework using the French Renal Epidemiology and Information Network (REIN) registry and merged with data from the French national healthcare system database from 2010 to 2023. We included adults with CKD G5D who experienced an ASCVD event. We used inverse probability of treatment weighting to balance baseline characteristics between statin initiators and non-initiators, thereby estimating the average causal effect on all-cause mortality. Results focus on the relative and absolute risk difference and the life expectancy gain using delta restricted mean survival time (dRMST).
RESULTS: The study cohort included 5534 patients (median age: 75 years; 67% male). During the ten years of follow-up, statin use was associated with a reduced risk of mortality. The survival curves reached a maximum absolute difference at year four (risk difference -6.2% (95% CI: -10.2; -2.2); relative risk 0.88 [95% CI: 0.81; 0.96]). Life expectancy extended significantly over time with a mean survival gain of 69 days at five years (95% CI: 14-125) and reaching 135 days at ten years (95% CI: 31-239). No difference was identified between groups regarding hospitalizations for rhabdomyolysis or toxic hepatitis.
CONCLUSIONS: In patients receiving dialysis, statin initiation following an ASCVD event is safe and associated with a modest-to-moderate ten-year cumulative survival benefit. While interpreted within observational limitations, this real-world evidence supports their use in this secondary prevention setting.

Title: The Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort (CRIC) study measured hepcidin, cardiovascular, kidney and metabolic outcomes in chronic kidney disease.
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Abnormal iron homeostasis plays a critical role in extra-hematopoietic disorders. The relationship of hepcidin, the master iron regulator, to clinical outcomes, has not been characterized in a large cohort of chronic kidney disease (CKD).
METHODS: To determine if plasma hepcidin level predicts cardiovascular (CV), kidney, and metabolic outcomes in patients with CKD, we studied 3826 patients enrolled in the Chronic Renal Insufficiency Cohort (CRIC) study. Hazard ratios for hepcidin tertiles were estimated from Cox Proportional Hazards regression for primary outcomes of incident heart failure (HF), end stage kidney disease (kidney failure) or halving of the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), and new onset diabetes or prediabetes. Secondary outcomes included atherosclerotic events and all-cause and CV mortality.
RESULTS: The median and interquartile range of plasma hepcidin level was 43 (22, 77) ng/mL. Higher plasma hepcidin levels were associated with older age, male sex, non-Hispanic Black race, diabetes, lower eGFR, higher albuminuria, increased plasma levels of iron indices, C-terminal fibroblast growth factor 23, and markers of inflammation (high-sensitivity C-reactive protein and interleukin-6). We found no association between plasma hepcidin level and the risk for incident HF or prediabetes/diabetes. However, compared to the middle tertile, the highest hepcidin tertile was independently associated with increased risk for kidney outcomes (hazard ratio 1.19; 95% confidence interval 1.09, 1.30) and atherosclerotic events (hazard ratio 1.34; 95% confidence interval 1.09, 1.64), while the lowest hepcidin tertile was associated with increased risk for all-cause and CV mortality in fully adjusted multivariable models including iron indices and inflammation.
CONCLUSION: Both low and high plasma levels of hepcidin are associated with adverse clinical outcomes.

Title: Hypertensive Intraventricular Hemorrhage in a Chinese Population: Clinical Characteristics, Treatment, and Outcomes.
Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) is associated with high mortality and poor outcomes in survivors. This study described the clinical characteristics and treatment outcomes of patients with hypertensive IVH (HIVH) in a large single-center Chinese cohort.
METHODS: We conducted retrospective analysis of prospectively maintained stroke registry at a tertiary medical center in China from September 2018 to January 2026. Patients with hypertensive IVH were included, while those with vascular-structural lesions or trauma were excluded. Demographic data, clinical treatments, and outcomes were analyzed.
RESULTS: In total, 489 patients with HIVH were enrolled, including 49 (9.9%) with primary IVH (pIVH) and 440(90%) with secondary IVH (sIVH). Panventricular hemorrhage was the most common overall HIVH pattern (31%), and 170 patients (35%) received external ventricular drainage (EVD). The overall 30-day mortality rate was 26%, and the 90-day mortality rate was 29%, respectively. Multivariate analysis showed that larger hematoma volume (OR=1.02, p=0.001), lower admission GCS score (OR=1.37, p<0.001), and older age (OR=1.03, p=0.011) were independent risk factors for 90-day mortality in patients with HIVH. Subgroup analysis showed that the EVD group had significantly lower 90-day cumulative mortality risk than the non-EVD group (HR=0.57, 95%CI 0.41-0.79, p<0.001), but no significant difference in favorable functional outcome at 90 days [modified Rankin Scale (mRS) 0-2: 22% vs 27%, p=0.265]. Additionally, the EVD group had significantly prolonged hospital stay (21 days vs 13 days, p<0.001). Furthermore, there was no significant difference in 90-day mortality risk between pIVH and sIVH (HR=0.94, 95%CI 0.51-1.75, p=0.848), but pIVH had significantly higher favorable functional outcome rates (mRS 0-2: 65% vs. 21%, p < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Parenchymal brain injury was the predominant factor associated with prognosis in patients with HIVH. EVD was associated with lower mortality but did not improve functional outcomes.

Title: Shock Index-Creatinine as a Predictor of In-Hospital Clinical Outcomes in Patients with Anterior Wall ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction Undergoing Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early risk stratification in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is essential but established scores such as TIMI and GRACE require multivariable computation. The Shock Index-Creatinine (SIC) is a simpler bedside alternative, yet Indian data are sparse.
OBJECTIVE: To assess whether admission SIC predicts in-hospital adverse events in anterior wall STEMI patients undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI).
METHODS: Two hundred consecutive patients with anterior wall STEMI undergoing primary PCI at a tertiary care centre in northern India were prospectively enrolled over 12 months. SIC was computed at admission as (Shock Index × 100) - Cockcroft-Gault creatinine clearance. The primary outcome was in-hospital death; secondary outcomes were heart failure, cardiogenic shock, contrast-induced acute kidney injury (CI-AKI), and life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia. Discrimination was assessed by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC).
RESULTS: The cohort was 73.0% male with a mean age of 54.5 years; in-hospital mortality was 10.0% (n = 20). Admission SIC was markedly higher in non-survivors than survivors (82.0 ± 42.4 versus -20.1 ± 19.4; p < 0.001). AUCs were 0.992 for mortality and cardiogenic shock, 0.971 for CI-AKI, 0.909 for ventricular arrhythmia, and 0.907 for heart failure (all p < 0.001). A SIC ≥ 20 predicted death with 95.0% sensitivity and 98.9% specificity.
CONCLUSIONS: In this Indian cohort, admission SIC was a powerful bedside predictor of adverse in-hospital events after primary PCI for anterior wall STEMI. The unusually high discriminative performance requires external validation in larger multicentre populations before routine clinical adoption.

Title: Dose-Response Profiles in Incretin and Multi-Agonist Obesity Pharmacotherapy.
Journal: Clinics and research in hepatology and gastroenterology
Abstract: Incretin and multi-agonist therapies have transformed obesity pharmacotherapy, but dose selection remains less mature than efficacy assessment. This critical narrative review examines nonlinear relationships among administered dose, systemic exposure, weight and cardiometabolic benefit, gastrointestinal tolerability, treatment persistence, and maintenance. Across established and newer programs, average efficacy generally increases with dose, yet incremental gains may narrow at higher exposure while adverse-event burden and discontinuation can increase. The maturity of evidence is heterogeneous, and later-stage programs should not be interpreted as clinically equivalent to agents supported mainly by earlier-phase dose-ranging data. Moreover, an "optimal dose" is not an endpoint-independent quantity: the exposure most appropriate for weight loss may differ from that relevant to glycemic control, cardiovascular benefit, body composition, tolerability, or maintenance. We therefore distinguish nominal dose from exposure and present response-guided titration as a hypothesis-generating framework for prospective testing, not as an evidence-based dosing algorithm. Existing continuation and withdrawal studies support the importance of ongoing pharmacological treatment after successful weight loss but do not establish a minimum or optimal de-intensified maintenance dose. Future trials should jointly model efficacy, safety, body composition, patient-reported outcomes, pharmacokinetics, and discontinuation to test objective-specific, patient-level dosing strategies.

Title: Epidemiological comparison of cirrhosis to other long-term health conditions in the United Kingdom.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Although cirrhosis is a serious long-term health condition (LTC), it tends to receive little attention from healthcare policymakers. Here, we sought to describe how cirrhosis compares to other LTCs to inform priority-setting discussions.
METHODS: We analysed data from the Our Future Health (OFH) study, a cohort of ∼1.7 million individuals from England, United Kingdom. Self-reported diagnosis status for cirrhosis and 15 benchmark LTCs (including type 1 diabetes, type 2 diabetes, Parkinson's disease, chronic kidney disease, schizophrenia, and stage 4 cancer) were ascertained from the enrolment questionnaire. Each LTC was profiled with respect to: sociodemographic characteristics; mortality; comorbidity burden; and late diagnosis. Furthermore, information on each LTC's trajectory (i.e., increasing, stable, or decreasing over time) was determined from background mortality data over the last decade.
RESULTS: The study cohort included 1,613,777 participants, of whom 2,606 (0.2%) reported a diagnosis of cirrhosis. Mortality elevation for participants with cirrhosis versus without was substantial (HR: 7.46; P<0.001, with adjustment for age/sex) and comparable to dementia (HR:7.60), stage 4 cancer (HR:7.06), whilst higher than schizophrenia (HR:4.46) and heart failure (HR:4.01). People with cirrhosis had more co-existing health conditions/diseases than other LTCs (i.e., elevated prevalence for 58/145 distinct health conditions; second only to stage 4 cancer). Area-based deprivation score was third highest for cirrhosis, behind COPD and schizophrenia. Late diagnosis of cirrhosis was commonplace, with <15% of new-onset liver failure reporting cirrhosis at enrolment. Cirrhosis also exhibited an upward trajectory, with mortality increasing by ∼20% in the last decade.
CONCLUSION: Cirrhosis is an anomaly LTC with respect to its deprivation, comorbidity, mortality, upward trajectory, and late diagnosis profile. Our data provide comparative evidence to inform priority-setting discussions with policymakers.
IMPACT AND IMPLICATIONS: Various levers are available to policy makers for reducing incidence of liver cirrhosis. However, other health conditions are often prioritised by policy makers ahead of cirrhosis; the decision-making process around this is not always transparent nor grounded in evidence. This study explores the characteristics of cirrhosis relative to other long-term conditions through a public-health lens. Our findings may guide priority-setting discussions between policy makers, advocates and other stakeholders and may shift current discourse onto a more empirical footing.

Title: Risk Factors and Clinical Outcomes of Reocclusion after Endovascular Treatment for Acute Ischemic Stroke: An Updated Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression.
Journal: Journal of neuroradiology = Journal de neuroradiologie
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early reocclusion after endovascular treatment (EVT) for acute ischemic stroke is underrecognized; its determinants and impact remain poorly defined.
METHODS: Random-effects meta-analysis of early reocclusion after successful EVT (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library through January 2026). Crude odds ratios (ORs) were pooled and certainty rated with GRADE. Post hoc sensitivity analyses included only same-site reocclusion definitions.
RESULTS: Ten studies (3,381 patients) were included; 244 (7.2%) reoccluded. Reocclusion was associated with lower 90-day functional independence (OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.17-0.38) and higher mortality (OR 1.86, 1.29-2.68), both moderate certainty. Reocclusion was more frequent with large-artery atherosclerosis (OR 2.24, 1.41-3.55; same-site 3.04, 1.73-5.33) and less frequent with cardioembolism (OR 0.40, 0.28-0.57) and atrial fibrillation (OR 0.39, 0.26-0.59), mutually confounded associations reflecting one embolic-versus-atherothrombotic axis. Prestroke antiplatelet therapy (OR 0.43, 0.28-0.67) lost significance under the same-site definition (0.60, 0.31-1.16). Exploratory data (two cohorts) linked eTICI 2c-3 reperfusion with less reocclusion (OR 0.44, 0.28-0.69). No study reported when etiology was adjudicated; the atherosclerosis association may be partly outcome-induced.
CONCLUSIONS: Early reocclusion is uncommon but carries a substantial prognostic penalty. Its determinants appear to lie in the vascular substrate rather than thrombectomy technique; prospective studies with uniform same-site definitions and systematic follow-up imaging are needed.

Title: Myocardial Infarction Within 6 Months before Total Shoulder Arthroplasty is Strongly Associated with Postoperative Complications.
Journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: As total shoulder arthroplasty (TSA) is increasing in volume, limited data exist regarding how recent myocardial infarction (MI) influences postoperative outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of MI timing, type, treatment, and anatomical location on rates of postoperative cardiac, medical, and surgical complications following TSA.
METHODS: A national insurance database, PearlDiver, was queried to identify patients with a history of MI within two years prior to TSA. These patients were propensity-matched 1:4 to controls without prior MI based on demographics and comorbidities. The MI cohort was stratified by timing (0-6 months, 6-12 months, 12-18 months, 18-24 months), and subgroup analyses were performed by MI type (Type 1 vs. Type 2), ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) vs Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI) classification, percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT), and infarct location.
RESULTS: A history of MI within 2 years preceding TSA had a strong association with higher odds of postoperative MI (OR 5.67; 95% CI, 3.86-8.32). The strongest association was observed when MI occurred within 6 months of TSA (OR 9.95; 95% CI, 6.50-15.24). Type 1 MI was strongly associated with postoperative MI, particularly within 6 months (OR 10.86; 95% CI, 6.96-16.95). Type 2 MI within 6 months was strongly associated with postoperative MI (OR 10.69; 95% CI, 2.50-45.63), DVT (OR 9.81; 95% CI, 2.30-41.79), and PJI (OR 5.24; 95% CI, 1.60-17.18). Both STEMI (OR = 6.17) and NSTEMI (OR = 5.77) were strongly associated with postoperative MI. Anterior MI was strongly associated with postoperative MI (OR 7.22; 95% CI, 3.36-15.49), whereas inferior MI was strongly associated with 90-day mortality (OR 6.46; 95% CI, 1.85-22.60).
CONCLUSION: MI within 2 years and specifically 6 months of TSA was associated with higher odds of postoperative complications. MI timing, subtype, treatment, and location should be carefully weighed when considering TSA in this high-risk population.

Title: A multifaceted intervention to increase bystander CPR rates after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in France: a stepped-wedge, cluster-randomised, controlled trial.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is a key determinant of survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but rates remain suboptimal worldwide. We evaluated whether a multifaceted intervention targeting emergency dispatch systems and community response could increase bystander-initiated CPR before emergency medical service (EMS) arrival.
METHODS: We conducted a stepped-wedge, cluster-randomised trial in 15 French EMS agencies. The intervention combined dispatcher training for early recognition of cardiac arrest and telephone-assisted CPR, activation of trained volunteers through a geolocation smartphone application, and structured audit and feedback provided to EMS agencies. Consecutive adults (≥18 years) with non-traumatic OHCA were included. Randomisation was stratified by tercile of OHCA volume managed by each EMS in 2015. The intervention was implemented during a 1-month transition period before the intervention period at each EMS centre. A dedicated protocol guided dispatchers to identify cardiac arrest from unresponsiveness and abnormal breathing, then gave scripted compression-only instructions and activated volunteers, targeting recognition within 60 s of call pick-up and first compression within a further 60 s. The primary outcome was bystander-initiated CPR before EMS arrival. The trial was prospectively registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03633370) and is completed.
FINDINGS: Of the 15 EMS agencies initially randomised, two withdrew before recruitment began and were replaced, and one enrolled no patients. Therefore, between Aug 27, 2018, and Feb 20, 2022, 14 EMS agencies recruited a total of 2160 patients. The intention-to-treat analysis included 1684 patients (686 control, 998 intervention) enrolled across the 12 originally randomised EMS agencies. The mean age for all patients included in the intention-to-treat analysis was 67 years (SD 15), and 1205 (71·6%) were male. Bystander-initiated CPR before EMS arrival occurred in 421 (61·4%) patients in the control group and 708 (70·9%) patients in the intervention group (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 1·54 [95% CI 1·09-2·19]; p=0·017). Estimates were consistent across six prespecified sensitivity analyses (OR range, 1·38-1·55), remaining significant in four, but not after adjustment for cluster-specific secular trends (1·38 [0·98-1·94]) or baseline characteristics (1·39 [0·97-1·98]). No intervention-related adverse events were reported.
INTERPRETATION: A multifaceted intervention was associated with increased bystander-initiated CPR after OHCA, although the estimate was sensitive to the modelling of secular trends, and it did not translate into improved clinical outcomes. These findings support further investigation of coordinated community-based strategies to strengthen the early links in the chain of survival at a population level.
FUNDING: Direction Générale de l'Offre de Soins.
Publication Types: Journal Article; Multicenter Study; Randomized Controlled Trial

Title: Apnea-hypopnea index-oxygen desaturation index (AHI-ODI) discordance in obstructive sleep apnea: association with symptom burden and cardiometabolic comorbidity: A retrospective cross-sectional study.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: The apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) counts respiratory events but not the depth or duration of accompanying desaturation. We examined AHI-ODI discordance (AHI minus oxygen desaturation index, ODI) and its associations with daytime symptom burden and prevalent cardiometabolic comorbidity.
METHODS: Single-center retrospective cross-sectional study of 200 adults with OSA (January 2023-January 2025). Five indices (AHI, ODI, mean SpO2, T90 and AHI-ODI discordance) were examined; excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS; Epworth Sleepiness Scale ≥ 11) was the primary outcome. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, BMI and an AHI-ODI × sex interaction.
RESULTS: The cohort was 77.5% male, median age 57 years (48.8-64.2). For EDS, AHI-ODI discordance showed the numerically highest AUC (0.639, p < 0.001), followed by T90 (0.627), and mean SpO2 and ODI (0.609 each); AHI was not significant (0.546, p = 0.264). No pairwise difference was significant. AHI-ODI discordance remained independently associated with EDS after adjustment (OR 1.04 per event/h, 95% CI 1.01-1.07, p = 0.008), with no significant sex interaction. Among secondary outcomes, T90 showed the highest AUCs for diabetes mellitus (0.644) and hypertension (0.615), and mean SpO2 for heart failure (0.608). No index discriminated against previous stroke or atrial fibrillation.
CONCLUSIONS: AHI-ODI discordance was independently, but only modestly, associated with EDS, whereas oxygenation indices were related to prevalent cardiometabolic comorbidity. The discrimination was insufficient, and all reported cut-offs are exploratory. AHI-ODI discordance is not a measure of sleep apnea-specific hypoxic burden.

Title: Time-Varying Spatial Ventricular Gradient Orientation Is Associated With Anthracycline Heart Failure.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Anthracycline use is limited by cardiotoxicity resulting in heart failure (HF). The spatial ventricular gradient (SVG) is a vectorcardiographic measurement of myocardial electrical heterogeneity associated with sudden death and incident HF. It is unclear if serial measurement of SVG after anthracycline initiation can help predict subsequent HF.
OBJECTIVES: The objective of the study was to determine if time-varying SVG measurements are associated with anthracycline HF.
METHODS: Retrospective, single-center study of adult patients with cancer treated with anthracyclines between 1992 to 2019. Standard 12-lead electrocardiograms obtained within 6 months before and up to 5 years after anthracycline initiation were analyzed. Patients with prior HF or ≤1 electrocardiogram within 5 years were excluded. Median vectorcardiograms were constructed, and the SVG vector was obtained by integrating under the X, Y, and Z QRST complexes. Multivariable competing-risks regression was performed with SVG parameters included as time-varying covariates, incident HF as the main outcome, and death as a competing outcome.
RESULTS: Among 594 patients (median age 61 years, 48% male), 83 (14%) developed HF within 5 years. In multivariable competing-risks regression, time-varying SVG azimuth (circular angle in the transverse plane) was independently associated with HF (P = 0.0024), demonstrating a 9.4-fold gradient in risk across values. Leftward/anterior azimuth values were the lowest risk areas, whereas posterior/rightward orientations were the highest risk.
CONCLUSIONS: Time-varying SVG azimuth was independently associated with HF risk in patients treated with anthracyclines. Assessing dynamic changes in SVG azimuth during anthracycline treatment may enhance early identification of patients at risk for HF and inform the use of cardioprotective strategies during cancer therapy.

Title: Atrial Fibrillation in Valvular Heart Disease: Assessing the Impact of Genetics in the UK Biobank.
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Atrial fibrillation (AF) in valvular heart disease (VHD) is generally attributed to pressure or volume overload with atrial remodeling, but the independent contribution of genetic predisposition remains unclear.
OBJECTIVES: The authors evaluated the predictive value of a previously developed AF polygenic risk score (PRS) across VHD subtypes in the UK Biobank.
METHODS: In this prospective cohort study (UK Biobank, 2000-2022), incident AF and VHD status were defined using ICD codes. VHD subtypes included mitral valve (MV) disease (MV prolapse [MVP], mitral regurgitation, mitral stenosis) and aortic valve (AV) disease (aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation). PRS was categorized into quintiles and grouped as low, intermediate, and high.
RESULTS: Among 452,841 participants with available PRS, 385 had MVP, 1,058 mitral regurgitation, 81 mitral stenosis, 421 aortic regurgitation, and 509 aortic stenosis. In Cox models, PRS was independently associated with incident AF in MV disease (HR: 1.7, P = 0.03 for intermediate PRS; HR: 2.3, P = 0.002 for high PRS), with the strongest effect in MVP (HR: 3.1, P = 0.03 for high PRS). In AV disease, PRS was not significantly associated with AF risk (P = 0.93 and P = 0.07 for intermediate and high PRS, respectively). Interaction analyses confirmed attenuation or absence of the PRS effect in AV disease (P = 0.04 and P = 0.004 for intermediate and high PRS, respectively), whereas no significant interaction was observed in MV disease (P = 0.80 and P = 0.11, respectively).
CONCLUSIONS: In VHD, AF PRS predicts AF risk, but the genetic impact differs by subtype. AV disease shows minimal genetic contribution, suggesting predominantly hemodynamic risk, while MV disease-particularly MVP-shows substantial genetic influence.

Title: Effects of Target Heart Rate Attainment Method on Metabolic, Perceptual, and Performance Responses During Heart Rate-Clamp Exercise in Recreationally Active Female Subjects.
Journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
Abstract: Mitchinson, CJ, Benitez, B, Kwak, M, Snell, E, Kuhn, AN, and Bergstrom, HC. Effects of target heart rate attainment method on metabolic, perceptual, and performance responses during heart rate-clamp exercise in recreationally active female subjects. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study used a test-retest design to examine ramp and immediate protocols for attaining a target heart rate (HR) and the subsequent effects on metabolic, respiratory, perceptual, and performance responses during HR-clamp cycle ergometry. Fifteen recreationally active female subjects (22 ± 5 years) completed a graded exercise test to determine maximal oxygen consumption (V̇O2max) and maximal HR (HRmax), followed by 4 randomized, 20-minute HR-clamp trials at 86% HRmax using either a ramp (gradual increases in power output [PO]) or immediate (instantaneous application of target PO) protocol, each performed twice. Oxygen consumption (V̇O2), minute ventilation (V̇E), respiration rate (RR), rating of perceived exertion (RPE), PO, and time to target HR were assessed at HR attainment and averaged across the HR-clamp trials. Analyses included linear mixed models fitted with fixed effects and random intercepts, and one-way repeated measures ANOVAs with intraclass correlation coefficients to examine test-retest reliability (p < 0.05). Time to target HR did not differ between protocols (p = 0.958). However, the ramp protocol elicited a greater V̇O2, RR, V̇E, and PO at HR attainment (p < 0.001-0.035) and a greater V̇O2 and PO across the HR-clamp trials (p = 0.008-0.017) compared with the immediate protocol, whereas RPE did not differ between protocols (p = 0.118-0.984). The ramp protocol demonstrated greater systematic error for metabolic and performance measures, whereas the immediate protocol showed less systematic error and comparable reliability. These findings indicated that the method used to attain a target HR significantly alters the physiological stimulus of HR-clamp exercise, and practitioners and researchers should carefully consider protocol selection when prescribing or interpreting HR-clamp exercise.

Title: Clinical and Financial Value of Cardiac Point-of-Care Ultrasound During Traumatic Cardiac Arrest.
Journal: The western journal of emergency medicine
Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Traumatic cardiac arrest is associated with poor survival and significant consumption of hospital resources. Determining which patients have survivable injuries allows for judicious use of resources. Our aim was to determine whether cardiac activity on point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) during traumatic cardiac arrest was associated with increased patient survival and the charges of continued resuscitation in patients that do have cardiac activity on POCUS.
METHODS: We conducted this single-center retrospective study at an urban, Level I trauma center of consecutive patients arriving in traumatic cardiac arrest from August 2016-December 2023 who had a cardiac POCUS performed during the initial resuscitation efforts. Our primary outcome was to determine whether cardiac activity on POCUS during the arrest was associated with increased patient survival to neurologically intact hospital discharge. Secondary objectives included determining whether there was a correlation between cardiac activity on POCUS during traumatic cardiac arrest and survival to hospital admission. Additionally, we evaluated hospital charges and length of stay associated with continued resuscitation in patients who demonstrated cardiac activity on ultrasound.
RESULTS: We identified 134 patients in traumatic cardiac arrest, of whom 74 (55.2%) had a cardiac POCUS performed and met inclusion criteria. A total of 17 patients had cardiac activity noted on the initial POCUS, with two (11%) surviving to hospital discharge (95% CI, 1.3-39.7). The two survivors initially categorized as being in traumatic cardiac arrest were ultimately found to have medical etiologies and not trauma. Of the 57 patients who had no cardiac activity noted on POCUS, none survived to hospital discharge (95% CI, 0-6.3%). More patients survived to hospital admission who had cardiac activity on their initial POCUS compared with those who had no cardiac activity (odds ratio [OR], 49.8; 95% CI, 5.5-446.9; P < .001). More patients survived to hospital discharge as well, but this was not statistically significant (OR, 18.6; 95% CI, 0.84-406.7, P = .06). Traumatic cardiac arrest patients who had present cardiac activity had longer code times prior to terminating efforts (26.6 vs 7.7 minutes, P < .001) and had higher overall charges per patient ($91,321 vs $10,032), P < .001).
CONCLUSION: The absence of cardiac activity on POCUS in patients with traumatic cardiac activity is likely to be fatal. The presence of cardiac activity was associated with increased resuscitation times, charges, and survival to hospital admission but not necessarily to hospital discharge.

Title: Hemodynamic Effects of Interfacility Dexmedetomidine Infusions During Transport of Patients with Alpha-2-adrenergic Agonist Withdrawal.
Journal: The western journal of emergency medicine
Abstract:
BACKGROUND: In the Philadelphia region, there has been an increase in the potency of illicit opioids as well as the addition of nonopioid adulterants. Currently, medetomidine, a veterinary anesthetic that acts as an alpha-2-adrenergic agonist, is a common adulterant in the illicit opioid supply, causing both unique overdose and withdrawal syndromes. Although opioid withdrawal alone is not deadly, with added adulterants, especially medetomidine, this is no longer the case. Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-2-adrenergic agonist frequently used for sedation in the emergency department and intensive care unit. Dexmedetomidine is also used off-label to treat the life-threatening withdrawal from alpha-2-agonists.
